question: For a vaginal hysterectomy, what should I use for the vaginal prep and how does that differ from the abdominal skin prep?
reference: For vaginal surgery, perform vaginal cleansing with either 4% aqueous chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). For abdominal surgical site skin preparation, use an alcohol-based agent unless contraindicated — chlorhexidine-alcohol is an appropriate choice (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence).
source_text:
Multimodal medications

pain from different physiological pathways with the goal
of optimizing pain control and minimizing unwanted side
effects from narcotic pain medications. They can be used
throughout the continuum of perioperative care, beginning
in the preoperative area prior to surgery, continuing intraoperatively through coordination with anesthesia, and carried
on in the postoperative period. While the body of literature
specific to multimodal protocols in urogynecology is growing, most of the information has originated from other specialties or general gynecology [52–55].

question: My pre-op patient's BP is still high on her antihypertensives and she tells me she drinks heavily on weekends — could the alcohol be why her meds aren't working, and how much BP drop could she get by cutting back?
reference: Yes — excessive alcohol use is recognized to increase resistance to the effects of antihypertensive medications. This may be due to poor adherence to the medication regimen and/or altered pharmacokinetics of the antihypertensive agent, which is metabolized by the liver under the influence of acute or chronic alcohol ingestion. Adhering to low alcohol consumption guidelines will enhance drug efficacy. Limiting alcohol may delay or prevent the onset of hypertension and can decrease systolic blood pressure by about 2–4 mmHg. Also relevant to her weekend pattern: binge drinking raises systolic and diastolic pressure during the drinking episode, with a drop below baseline in the immediate post-drinking period (usually early morning hours), and binge drinking on weekends/holidays has been identified as a stroke risk factor in young people. Note that low alcohol consumption shows little BP difference compared with abstainers and has some cardioprotective effect, so you should not discourage drinking within recommended guidelines — but neither should you encourage someone to start drinking as a risk-reduction strategy.
source_text:
Nursing Best Practice Guideline
Binge drinking raised systolic and diastolic pressure during the drinking episode, and there was a drop in
both pressures to below baseline levels in the immediate post-drinking period, usually in the early morning
hours.

Furthermore, binge drinking was found to be a risk factor for stroke in young persons who
consumed alcohol on weekends and holidays, prime drinking times.

As well, moderate to heavy alcohol
use was related to intracerebral hemorrhage.

Although there is no direct evidence, this study would suggest
a link between alcohol, hypertension and stroke (Seppa & Sillanaukee, 1999).

Multiple population cohort and cross-sectional trials have shown little difference in blood pressure in
clients with low alcohol consumption and abstainers.

There is also evidence to support the limited
consumption of alcohol for its cardio protective effects.

Nurses need to be aware of this evidence and
should not discourage consumption within the recommended guidelines nor should they encourage the
initiation of drinking as a method of risk factor reduction related to the associated potential health risks of
overuse (Williams et al., 2004).

Adoption of healthy lifestyle behaviours is an important factor in prevention of high blood pressure and
lowering blood pressure in those known to be hypertensive.

By limiting the use of alcohol individuals may
delay/prevent the incidence of hypertension and decrease systolic blood pressure by 2-4 mmHg (Institute of
Clinical Systems Improvement, 2004; NIH, 2003).

Adherence to low alcohol consumption guidelines will enhance
drug efficacy.

It has been recognized that excessive use can increase resistance to the effects of
antihypertensive medications (NIH, 2003).

This resistance may be a result of poor adherence to the
medication regime and/or a change in pharmakinetics of the antihypertensive agent metabolized by the
liver that is under the influence of acute or chronic alcohol ingestion (Lip & Beevers, 1995).
source_title: Nursing Management of Hypertension

question: For a myeloma patient on lenalidomide and steroids, what can I give for clot prevention and what aspirin dose, and how long do we keep it going?
reference: For people with myeloma receiving chemotherapy with thalidomide, pomalidomide or lenalidomide plus steroids, consider pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with either aspirin 75 mg or 150 mg, or LMWH. Continue the prophylaxis for as long as the patient is receiving chemotherapy. Note that aspirin used in this indication was off label as of March 2018, as was LMWH in people under 18.

question: At what point do we need to start talking about ECMO referral for a pregnant patient with flu or COVID pneumonia?
reference: ECMO should be considered in fulminant cases of primary influenza pneumonia or SARS-CoV-2 — i.e. when respiratory compromise is severe and rapidly progressive rather than waiting for further deterioration. The most recent MBRRACE report specifically flagged the need for updated guidance on referral pathways for ECMO therapy, so escalate early and involve the team who can arrange transfer. Be alert that severe respiratory compromise with high mortality can also arise from secondary necrotising haemorrhagic pneumonia caused by group A streptococcal exotoxins or PVL-producing S. aureus following influenza or other viral respiratory infection, and that pulmonary haemorrhage from primary influenza has been reported. For suspected SARS-CoV-2, assess according to the RCOG guidance Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection in Pregnancy.
source_text:
Women suspected of SARS-CoV-2 should be assesses
according to the RCOG guidance Coronavirus (COVID-19) infection in pregnancy [2]. [Evidence level 4]
During 2009–12, an upsurge in influenza combined with a
low vaccination rate, diagnostic delay and lack of treatment accounted for 43% of all infection-related deaths in pregnancy (36
women); [5] in stark contrast to only one death during the three
years of the subsequent report when vaccination increased, [63]
and two in the 2023 MBRRACE report [4].

Influenza related morbidity and mortality is associated with a
body mass index (BMI) of over 30 kg/m2.

Early birth may be indicated during the third trimester of pregnancy.

Pulmonary haemorrhage due to primary influenza has been reported [64, 65].

Secondary bacterial infection with pneumococci, betahaemolytic streptococci and S. aureus occur typically after influenza and other viral respiratory infections.

GAS exotoxins
[66, 67] and S. aureus associated PVL [68, 69] produce a secondary necrotising haemorrhagic pneumonia with severe respiratory compromise and a high mortality rate [43]. [Evidence level 3]
Initiating extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)
should be considered in fulminant cases of primary influenza
pneumonia or SARS-CoV-2 [4].

The need for updated guidance
on referral for ECMO therapy was highlighted in the recent
MBRRACE report [4].

For more information on SARS-CoV-2
see the RCOG guidance Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection in
Pregnancy [2].

question: My patient is ASA 3 because of known COPD and she's booked for an elective hysterectomy — do I need to get lung function and blood gases done, or should I be calling someone?
reference: For a patient who is ASA grade 3 (or 4) because of known or suspected respiratory disease, don't just order lung function/arterial blood gas routinely — instead consider seeking advice from a senior anaesthetist as soon as possible after the preoperative assessment, who can advise on whether these tests are needed. Note that for this patient (ASA 3), kidney function testing and an ECG should both be offered.

question: When we're rewriting our unit's PPH protocol, are we allowed to change any of the WHO recommendations to fit what we actually have available here?
reference: Yes, but with limits. The recommendations are meant to be adapted into locally appropriate protocols that meet the specific needs of your country and health service — which may mean developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols. However, any modifications should be restricted to the weak recommendations only, and the justification for each change must be documented explicitly and transparently. The adaptation should be a well-planned, participatory, consensus-driven process, ideally involving local professional societies. Alongside the protocol change, you also need to create an enabling environment for its use — for example, widening the availability of uterotonics and supporting changes in practitioner behaviour so evidence-based practice can actually happen.
source_text:
Guideline implementation
The successful introduction of evidence-based policies related to the prevention and
management of PPH into national programmes and health care services depends on
well-planned and participatory consensus-driven processes of adaptation and imple
26
mentation. These processes may include the development or revision of existing
national guidelines or protocols based on this document.
The recommendations contained in the present guideline should be adapted into
locally-appropriate documents that are able to meet the specific needs of each
country and health service. Modifications to the recommendations, where necessary,
should be limited to weak recommendations and justifications for any changes made
in an explicit and transparent manner.
An enabling environment should be created for the use of these recommendations
(for example, by widening the availability of uterotonics), including changes in the
behaviour of health care practitioners to enable the use of evidence-based practic
es. Local professional societies may play important roles in this process and an allinclusive and participatory process should be encouraged. The WHO’s Department of
Reproductive Health and Research has published specific guidance on the introduc
tion of the WHO’s reproductive health guidelines and tools in national programmes.

question: Which practices did WHO actually build the Safe Surgery Checklist from — everything in their review, or just a subset?
reference: Only a subset. WHO's review graded practices at different levels, including 'suggested' practices (ones that should be considered for any operation). Because the review didn't make clear how its findings should be put into practice, WHO focused specifically on the 'highly recommended' practices at the end of the review for each objective, and used those to build two things: the WHO Safe Surgery Checklist and a set of recommended 'surgical vital statistics' for measurement. These were then finally reviewed and tested at pilot sites around the world.
source_text:

‘suggested’: a practice that should be considered for any
operation
While the review was relatively comprehensive, it did not make clear
how the findings were to be operationalized. Therefore, at the end of
the review for each objective and in order to provide simple means for
practitioners to ensure and improve standards of safety, we focused on
the ‘highly recommended’ practices and used them to construct two
products: the WHO Safe Surgery Checklist and a set of recommended
‘surgical vital statistics’ for measurement.
These guidelines have undergone final review and testing at pilot sites
around the world (see Appendix A). There is wide recognition that every
country can improve the safety of its surgical care and that this is a
critical matter of public health, affecting hundreds of millions of people
worldwide each year. By creating a culture of safety, WHO Patient
Safety is seeking to promote practice standards that reduce injuries
and save lives.

question: Se seguiamo le pazienti solo fino alla dimissione, quante infezioni del sito chirurgico ci stiamo perdendo? Vale la pena fare la sorveglianza a 30 giorni dopo la dimissione?
reference: Sì: nei dati italiani del Sistema Nazionale di Sorveglianza delle Infezioni del Sito Chirurgico (355 reparti chirurgici, 2009-2011), il 60% delle SSI è stato diagnosticato proprio attraverso la sorveglianza post-dimissione a 30 giorni. Senza il follow-up dopo la dimissione si perderebbe quindi la maggior parte dei casi. Il tasso complessivo rilevato era del 2,6% (1.628 SSI su 60.460 interventi), con i valori più alti nella chirurgia del colon (9,0%) e del retto (7,0%), seguiti da laparotomia (3,1%) e appendicectomia (2,1%). Da notare inoltre che una SSI comporta una degenza aggiuntiva media di circa 7-13 giorni.

question: We're 3 hours into an open debulking case with about 1800 mL blood loss — do I need to redose the cefazolin, and does her BMI of 38 change the dose?
reference: Yes. Prophylactic antibiotics should be redosed in prolonged operations after 1–2 times the half-life of the drug chosen — for cefazolin that is at about 3 hours — and also when blood loss exceeds 1500 mL, so this patient meets both triggers for a repeat dose. In addition, the dose should be increased in obese patients (BMI >35 or >100 kg), so her BMI of 38 warrants a higher dose. (The initial dose should have been given IV within 60 min before skin incision.)
source_text:
The dose should be increased in obese patients (BMI N 35 or
N100 kg) [56], and repeated after 1–2 times the half-life of the chosen
medication in prolonged operations (eg. 3 h for cefazolin, half-life:

h) and in case of blood loss N1500 ml [57]. For patients allergic to
penicillin/cephalosporin, a combination of clindamycin and gentamycin
IV or a quinolone (eg. ciproﬂoxacin) can be used. Laparoscopic operations not contaminated by the genitourinary or digestive tracts do not
require antimicrobial prophylaxis [58].
Skin preparation before surgery traditionally includes a shower, hair
removal and the use of skin antiseptic solution. One Cochrane review
addressed the topic of showering or bathing with different antiseptic solutions before surgery [59]. Showering using plain soap is as effective as
chlorhexidine in reducing surgical site infection. Compared to shaving,
hair clipping in the operating room immediately prior to surgery is associated with lower rates of SSI [60]. However, there is no clear evidence
that hair removal reduces SSI, irrespective of the method chosen
(shaving, hair clipping or depilatory cream). Therefore, hair removal
should be avoided and if deemed necessary hair clipping is preferred.
Skin antiseptic is highly recommended. A RCT showed a 40% reduction in SSI when using chlorhexidine gluconate and isopropyl alcohol 70% compared to an aqueous solution of 10% povidone-iodine
for skin cleansing in different clean-contaminated interventions
[61]. Chlorhexidine–alcohol therefore is preferred over aqueous
povidone-iodine solution although care must be taken to avoid ignition when electrocautery is used [62].
Summary and recommendation:
IV antibiotics should be administered routinely within 60 min before
skin incision. The dose should be repeated in case of prolonged operations or severe blood loss and increased in obese patients.
Hair clipping is preferred if hair removal is mandatory.
Chlorhexidine–alcohol is preferred to aqueous povidone-iodine
solution for skin cleansing.
Evidence level:
Antibiotic prophylaxis: High.
Hair clipping: High.
Chlorhexidine–alcohol: High.
Recommendation grade:
Antibiotic prophylaxis: Strong.
Hair clipping: Strong.
Chlorhexidine–alcohol: Strong.

question: Do we actually need a written protocol for transferring a PPH patient to a higher level of care, or is it enough to have our hemorrhage treatment protocol on the unit?
reference: Both are recommended. Health facilities should have formal protocols for the prevention and treatment of PPH (weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), and separately should have formal protocols for referral of women to a higher level of care (weak recommendation, very-low-quality evidence). So a hemorrhage treatment protocol alone is not sufficient — a distinct referral/escalation protocol is also recommended. Additionally, PPH treatment simulations are recommended for both pre-service and in-service training, and monitoring the use of uterotonics after birth for PPH prevention is recommended as a process indicator for programmatic evaluation.

question: My post-op patient on chronic diuretics has a magnesium of 1.2 mg/dL and is complaining of leg cramps and tremors — what am I watching for and how do we correct it?
reference: A magnesium of 1.2 mg/dL is below the normal range of 1.5-2.4 mg/dL, so this is hypomagnesemia — commonly caused by diuretics, undernutrition, and long-term alcohol use disorder. Beyond the leg cramps and tremors, watch for nausea, vomiting, lethargy, weakness, tetany, and arrhythmias. Treatment is to increase magnesium in the diet and give magnesium either PO or IV.

question: My post-op patient's heels are looking red and marked under her TED stockings — do I take them off, and what do I use instead?
reference: Yes — stop using the anti-embolism stockings if you see marking, blistering or discolouration of the skin (especially over the heels and bony prominences), or if she reports pain or discomfort. If she's suitable for it, offer intermittent pneumatic compression as an alternative, but not if she has a known allergy to the material it's made from. Advise her to wear the device for as much time as possible. Also remember stockings should come off daily for hygiene and skin inspection, and skin should be checked 2 or 3 times a day in people with significantly reduced mobility, poor skin integrity or any sensory loss.

question: If we're doing a manual removal of a retained placenta, do I need to give antibiotics, and which one?
reference: Yes — give a single dose of antibiotics when manual removal of the placenta is performed. Recommended options are ampicillin or a first-generation cephalosporin (weak recommendation, very-low-quality evidence).

question: For a post-caesarean woman we think is septic, do I need to get both sets of blood cultures before the first dose of antibiotics, and how far apart should they be?
reference: Yes — take two sets of blood cultures (each set with an aerobic and an anaerobic bottle) before any antibiotics are given, drawn sequentially within minutes of each other. Sampling a larger volume of blood improves the yield of pathogens. However, do not delay treatment: start empirical antibiotics straight away without waiting for microbiology results. In women at high risk of sepsis, the investigations and care should begin immediately.

question: Our ergometrine vials have been sitting in the theatre drug cupboard at room temperature — is that okay to give for PPH prevention, or do we need to switch to something else?
reference: No — ergometrine/methylergometrine requires refrigerated transport and storage at 2–8 °C. If that cold chain cannot be guaranteed, its quality and effectiveness may be adversely affected, and in that situation another effective uterotonic should be considered instead.

however, it requires refrigerated transport and storage (2–8 °C). In settings
where this cannot be guaranteed, the quality and effectiveness of ergometrine/

uterotonic can be considered.

question: For a pregnant patient on calcium supplements, does the dose matter for preterm birth risk — I've heard low-dose might actually be worse?
reference: Yes, the dose subgroups point in opposite directions. In the high-dose subgroup, calcium reduced preterm birth: 744/7744 (9.6%) vs 817/7735 (10.6%) with placebo/no treatment, RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.66–0.99), about 1 to 36 fewer per 1000 — moderate certainty. In the low-dose subgroup, preterm birth was more frequent with calcium: 45/330 (13.6%) vs 29/330 (8.8%), RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.00–2.41), up to 124 more per 1000 — but this estimate is very low certainty (very serious risk of bias and imprecision), so it should not be treated as established harm. The main pooled analysis showed no clear difference: 789/8074 (9.8%) vs 846/8065 (10.5%), RR 0.86 (0.70–1.05), low certainty. Note the passage does not state the actual mg cut-off defining low versus high dose.

question: What proportion of ED attendances could actually be handled by a GP instead — is there a figure we can quote when we're pushing for a primary care service alongside our emergency department?
reference: Royal College of Emergency Medicine survey data suggest around 20% of people attending emergency departments could be treated by GPs. A joint report from the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, Royal College of Physicians and Royal College of Surgeons has proposed that every emergency department should include a primary care out-of-hours facility. However, note that although extended GP access in surgeries is a current health policy requirement, the impact of such provision on reducing emergency department attendances for acute illness is unknown, and the specific effect of GPs on secondary care and the wider urgent and emergency care system still needs systematic research evaluation.
source_text:
Why this is important
Royal College of Emergency Medicine survey data suggest that around 20% of people who
attend emergency departments could be treated by GPs. Extended access to GPs in their
surgeries is a requirement of current health policy, but the impact of such provision on
reducing emergency department attendances of people with acute illnesses is unknown.
An alternative approach, proposed in a joint report from the Royal College of Emergency
Medicine, Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, Royal College of Physicians, and
Royal College of Surgeons, is that every emergency department should include a primary
care out-of-hours facility. This approach deserves systematic research evaluation focused
on the specific impact of GPs on secondary care and the wider urgent and emergency
care system.
Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence review 17:
GPs within or on the same site as emergency departments.
source_title: NICE NG94 - Emergency and Acute Medical Care in Adults

question: We've given three doses of carboprost 250 micrograms IM for atonic bleeding and she's still oozing — how many more doses can we give before we need to think about theatre?
reference: Carboprost 250 micrograms IM can be repeated every 15 minutes up to a maximum total of 2 mg (eight doses). However, if significant atonic haemorrhage continues after the third dose without significant improvement — i.e. 30 minutes or more after the first dose — the team should consider transferring her to the operating theatre for examination under anaesthesia, while being aware of the impending need for laparotomy and/or hysterectomy.

question: How much blood loss after delivery counts as postpartum haemorrhage, and what's the window I should be watching for it?
reference: PPH is commonly defined as blood loss of 500 ml or more within 24 hours after birth. The first 24 hours after birth is the critical monitoring window, since most PPH deaths occur during that period — and the majority could be avoided by giving prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labour plus timely, appropriate management.
source_text:
Introduction
Postpartum Haemorrhage (PPH) is commonly defined as a blood loss of 500 ml or
more within 24 hours after birth. PPH is the leading cause of maternal mortality in
low-income countries and the primary cause of nearly one quarter of all maternal
deaths globally. Most deaths resulting from PPH occur during the first 24 hours after
birth: the majority of these could be avoided through the use of prophylactic utero
tonics during the third stage of labour and by timely and appropriate management.
Improving health care for women during childbirth in order to prevent and treat PPH
is an essential step towards the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals.
The primary objective of this guideline therefore is to provide a foundation for the
strategic policy and programme development needed to ensure the sustainable
implementation of effective interventions for reducing the global burden of PPH.
source_title: WHO Recommendations for the Prevention and Treatment of Postpartum Haemorrhage

question: My post-op patient is being switched to immediate-release tramadol — can I schedule it PRN for breakthrough pain, and how long should she stay on it?
reference: No — immediate-release tramadol isn't meant to be used as an 'as needed' medication. It's prescribed for moderate to moderately severe pain when other analgesics can't be tolerated or aren't effective, and it's intended for pain episodes lasting less than a week. If the patient has chronic, ongoing pain, the extended-release form is the appropriate option instead.

question: How much daily weight gain in my post-op patient do I need to call the provider about?
reference: Report any weight change greater than 1 kg in 24 hours to the provider. Be sure the weight is measured consistently — same scale and same type of clothing — so the change is reliable. Alongside this, monitor edema location and extent using the 1+ to 4+ scale, track intake and output over 24 hours (watching for decreasing urine output relative to fluid intake as a sign of developing fluid volume excess), and check labs such as serum osmolarity, serum sodium, BUN, and hematocrit. For patients on IV fluids, also auscultate lung sounds for crackles and ask about dyspnea, reporting any new abnormal findings to the provider.

question: What AUDIT score should make me flag a pre-op patient as a problem drinker, and what do I do next?
reference: A total AUDIT score of 10 or more (out of a possible 40, with each item scored 0-4) indicates problem drinking. If alcohol overuse is suspected or identified, counsel the client on the negative health effects of alcohol and consider referral to an alcohol treatment specialist or program. Note that the AUDIT emphasizes heavy drinking and frequency of intoxication rather than signs of dependency; in its WHO pilot across six countries, sensitivity averaged 80% and specificity 98% for detecting excessive alcohol consumption. Also relevant to pre-op assessment: about half of clients with excessive alcohol use have blood pressures >160/90, and these readings normalize with abstinence, since the effect appears to come from alcohol consumed in the days immediately before measurement and is rapidly reversible.
source_text:
The AUDIT tool takes slightly longer to administer and consists of

questions. Responses are scored from 0-4 with a total possible score of 40 points. A score of 10 or more
points indicates problem drinking. This tool places the emphasis on heavy drinking and frequency of
intoxication rather than signs of dependency. The tool was developed by the World Health Organization
(WHO). In its initial pilot in six different countries, the sensitivity averaged 80% and specificity averaged
98% for detecting excessive alcohol consumption (Haggerty,1994).
If alcohol overuse is suspected or identified, the client should be counseled on the negative health effects
and referral to an alcohol treatment specialist or program may be appropriate (Cushman, 2001).
Examples of the CAGE questions and AUDIT tools are listed in Appendix L, along with a list of other
assessment tools. This list of tools is not all-inclusive, and some of the tools are designed for use with
specialized populations or as part of a broader substance use evaluation.
Research has shown that approximately half of clients with excessive alcohol use have blood pressure
readings >160/90, and these values were found to normalize during abstinence. Similar trends were found
within a broader population base leading researchers to believe the blood pressure effects of alcohol are
due to alcohol consumed in the days immediately prior to measurement and the effect is rapidly reversible
(Seppa & Sillanaukee, 1999).

question: At what blood sugar level should I start an insulin infusion on my post-op gyn onc patients, and what do I need to watch for?
reference: Hyperglycemia above roughly 180–200 mg/dL should be treated with an insulin infusion along with regular blood glucose monitoring (strong recommendation, high-level evidence). The key risk to monitor for is iatrogenic hypoglycemia — the most common adverse effect of intensive insulin therapy, which can cause morbidity such as seizures and brain damage — so the goal is to control significant hyperglycemia while avoiding driving the glucose too low.

question: When drugs aren't stopping a PPH from uterine atony, what surgical step do we set up for first, and what's the order of escalation from there?
reference: Move to surgical intervention sooner rather than later once pharmacological measures fail. Intrauterine balloon tamponade is the appropriate first-line 'surgical' intervention for most women when uterine atony is the only or main cause of bleeding. Conservative surgical interventions (e.g. brace/compression sutures — keep a laminated diagram of the brace suture technique in theatre) can be attempted as second line, depending on clinical circumstances and available expertise. Do not delay hysterectomy — resort to it sooner rather than later, especially with placenta accreta or uterine rupture, and ideally a second experienced clinician should be involved in that decision when feasible. If retained products are suspected, a pelvic ultrasound may help exclude retained products of conception, and surgical evacuation of retained placental tissue should be done or supervised by an experienced clinician.

question: How much blood loss after delivery counts as a postpartum hemorrhage, and within what time frame?
reference: PPH is commonly defined as blood loss of 500 ml or more within 24 hours after birth. It affects about 5% of all women giving birth worldwide. Severe complications such as organ dysfunction or death generally follow substantial blood loss that compromises the mother's haemodynamic stability, and uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH as well as a leading cause of PPH-related maternal mortality.
source_text:
Background
An estimated 303 000 women and adolescent girls died as a result of pregnancy and
childbirth-related complications in 2015, and around 99% of these deaths occurred in lowresource settings (1).

Obstetric haemorrhage, especially postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), is
responsible for more than a quarter of all maternal deaths worldwide (1).

In most low-income
countries, PPH is the leading cause of maternal deaths.

Thus, improving access to safe
and effective interventions to prevent PPH is critical to World Health Organization (WHO)
strategic priorities (particularly universal health coverage) for achieving the targets of the
third Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 3) (2,3).

International human rights law includes fundamental commitments of States to enable
women and adolescent girls to survive pregnancy and childbirth, as part of their enjoyment
of sexual and reproductive health and rights, and living a life of dignity (4).

WHO envisions
a world where “every pregnant woman and newborn receives quality care throughout
pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period” (5).

To provide good-quality care, skilled
health personnel at all levels of the health system need to have access to appropriate
medications and training in relevant procedures (6).

Health care providers, health managers,
health policy-makers and other stakeholders also need up-to-date, evidence-informed
recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices, in order to optimize quality of care
and improve health care outcomes.

PPH is commonly defined as a blood loss of 500 ml or more within 24 hours after birth,
and affects about 5% of all women giving birth around the world (7,8).

Severe maternal
complications, such as organ dysfunction or death, generally occur following substantial
blood loss that compromises maternal haemodynamic stability.

Uterine atony is the most
common cause of PPH and a leading cause of PPH-related maternal mortality worldwide (1).
source_title: WHO Recommendations for Uterotonics for Prevention of PPH

question: When we're revamping our maternity unit's quality improvement work, do we actually need to bring women and community members into it, or is it enough for staff to define the quality standards ourselves?
reference: Community members should be brought in — community participation in quality-improvement processes for maternity services is strongly recommended (based on low-quality evidence) because it improves quality of care from the perspectives of women, communities and health care providers alike. Communities should be involved in jointly defining and assessing quality, not just consulted after standards are set by staff. In addition, you should put mechanisms in place that ensure women's voices are meaningfully included in that process.
source_text:
Community participation in quality improvement processes
■

is recommended to improve quality of care from women’s, communities’ and health care
providers’ perspectives. Communities should be involved in jointly defining and assessing
quality. Mechanisms that ensure women’s voices are meaningfully included are also
recommended. (Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Source

question: How long does a trip have to be before we count travel as a VTE risk factor in a pregnant patient, and does it only count if she flew?
reference: Any long-distance travel of more than four hours counts as a VTE risk factor in pregnancy — it is not restricted to air travel. Although NICE antenatal care guidance and the RCOG Scientific Impact Paper on air travel specifically identify long-haul flights as increasing VTE risk, this guidance extends the risk factor to all travel over four hours regardless of mode. Note that pregnancy-specific data are limited, so this is extrapolated from studies in non-pregnant patients.

question: During a PPH, what's the scribe actually meant to be doing, and should the team leader be checking in with them?
reference: The scribe is the team member who records events on the structured PPH proforma, and this role is crucial to managing the haemorrhage. The proforma functions as a checklist of the available interventions, so the team leader should be actively communicating with the scribe throughout the PPH to confirm no steps have been missed. Accurate documentation matters for ongoing clinical management, continuity of care and teamwork, and poor documentation increases the risk of medicolegal consequences. The PPH should also be notified through the clinical incident reporting or risk management system.

question: Our unit is being asked to justify hiring a dedicated ERAS nurse — is that role actually recommended, and how do we show it's worth the cost?
reference: Yes — a patient care coordinator or a dedicated ERAS perioperative nurse is recommended as helpful for communication and patient compliance (strong recommendation, low quality of evidence). There is some upfront cost in starting the protocol, but this has been shown to be offset by reduced length of stay and fewer complications that follow from increased compliance. To demonstrate the value, compliance should be closely tracked, since it is directly tied to outcomes, and patient-reported outcomes should be consistently collected and documented so the institution can monitor, understand, and compare functional recovery in a patient-centered way. Implementation should be led by people familiar with current institutional protocols, with regular auditing and protocol updates communicated from the ERAS team to perioperative staff.

question: We're starting the surgical safety checklist in our gynae theatres next month — should we roll it out in all our ORs at once or just start in one room?
reference: Start small — test the checklist in one operating room with one team, and only move forward once problems have been addressed and enthusiasm builds. In WHO's original evaluation, sites that tried to implement it in multiple operating rooms simultaneously or hospital-wide met the most resistance and had the hardest time getting staff to use it effectively. Once that first team is comfortable, spread it to another operating room, discuss the effort with other surgical departments and surgeons, and make sure the people originally involved are actually using the checklist in their own rooms. Begin with a core group who are enthusiastic, including at least one person from surgery, anaesthesia and nursing, and work with the interested staff rather than trying to convince the most resistant ones at this early stage. Involve hospital leaders and administrators if you can, emphasizing lower complication rates and potential cost savings. You can customize the checklist for your setting, but don't delete safety steps simply because they can't be accomplished, and address resistance as it arises — clinicians with good experiences using it make the best champions.

question: When exactly do we need to run the sign-out checks — can I do them after the surgeon steps out to dictate, or does it have to be before?
reference: No — sign-out must be completed before the surgeon has left the room, and before the patient is moved out of the operating room. A practical time to start it is during wound closure. Any of the team can initiate it — circulating nurse, surgeon or anaesthetist. As part of it, the checklist coordinator confirms with the surgeon and team exactly what procedure was actually done, since it may have changed or expanded during the case — either by asking "What procedure was performed?" or confirming "We performed X procedure, correct?" The purpose is to hand off important information to the teams caring for the patient after surgery.
source_text:
Before patient leaves operating room
These safety checks should be completed before removing
the patient from the operating room. The aim is to facilitate
the transfer of important information to the care teams
responsible for the patient after surgery. The checks can
be initiated by the circulating nurse, surgeon or anaesthetist
and should be accomplished before the surgeon has left the
room. It can coincide, for example, with wound closure.
Since the procedure may have changed or expanded
during the course of an operation, the Checklist coordinator
should confirm with the surgeon and the team exactly what
procedure was done. This can be done as a question,
“What procedure was performed?” or as a confirmation,
“We performed X procedure, correct?”
source_title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist Implementation Guide

question: My post-op patient with suspected sepsis is hypotensive — how big should each fluid bolus be, and at what point do I need to call for senior help?
reference: Give isotonic electrolyte crystalloid (balanced crystalloid, or 0.9% saline as commonly carried by ambulance services) in a stepped approach using 250 ml boluses, reassessing the patient after each bolus. If there is no improvement after a bolus, seek senior clinical advice. In particular, once 1,000 ml has been given with no or only limited change in the indicators of hypoperfusion, escalate for senior advice because of the risk of fluid overload. Note this covers initial management only — fluid management may be adapted later as more clinical information becomes available.

question: At what blood loss volumes do we call a PPH minor versus major, and when does it count as severe?
reference: Primary PPH is traditionally defined as blood loss of 500 ml or more from the genital tract within 24 hours of birth. It is classed as minor at 500–1000 ml and major at more than 1000 ml. Major is further subdivided into moderate (1001–2000 ml) and severe (more than 2000 ml). Bear in mind that in women with a lower body mass (e.g. less than 60 kg), a lower blood loss volume may already be clinically significant. Bleeding that is abnormal or excessive from the birth canal between 24 hours and 12 weeks postnatally is classed as secondary PPH.
source_text:
Purpose and scope
Primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is the most common form of major obstetric haemorrhage.

The traditional
deﬁnition of primary PPH is the loss of 500 ml or more of blood from the genital tract within 24 hours of the birth
of a baby.2 PPH can be minor (500–1000 ml) or major (more than 1000 ml).

Major can be further subdivided into
moderate (1001–2000 ml) and severe (more than 2000 ml).

In women with lower body mass (e.g. less than 60 kg), a
lower level of blood loss may be clinically signiﬁcant.3 The recommendations in this guideline apply to women
experiencing a primary PPH of 500 ml or more.

Secondary PPH is deﬁned as abnormal or excessive bleeding from the birth canal between 24 hours and 12 weeks
postnatally.4 This guideline also includes recommendations speciﬁc to the management of secondary PPH.

Women with pre-existing bleeding disorders and women taking therapeutic anticoagulants are at increased risk of PPH;
this guideline does not include speciﬁc recommendations for the management of such situations or for managing
haemorrhage in women who refuse blood transfusion.

Guidance on these topics is available from other sources.5–8
This guideline has been developed primarily for clinicians working in consultant-led obstetric units in the UK;
recommendations may be less appropriate for other settings where facilities, resources and routine practices differ.

There is increasing emphasis on the availability of births at home or in midwife-led units.9 Obstetricians and
midwives should develop guidelines for the management of obstetric emergencies that may occur in the community,
including PPH.
source_title: GTG52 - Prevention and Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

question: For a C-section, how quickly after the baby is out do I need to get the uterotonic in, and does giving it mean we can't delay cord clamping?
reference: Give the uterotonic immediately after birth of the baby (or babies) — preferably within one minute — to maximize efficacy. This applies to both vaginal births and caesarean sections. Giving a uterotonic for PPH prevention does not need to interfere with delayed cord clamping, which WHO still recommends; the two can be done together. For injectable uterotonics, administration must be by skilled health personnel trained to give them.
source_text:
The use of an effective uterotonic for the prevention of PPH during the third stage
of labour is recommended for all births. To effectively prevent PPH, only one of the
following uterotonics should be used:
"
" oxytocin (Recommendation 1.1)
"
" carbetocin (Recommendation 1.2)
"
" misoprostol (Recommendation 1.3)
"
" ergometrine/methylergometrine (Recommendation 1.4)
"
" oxytocin and ergometrine fixed-dose combination (Recommendation 1.5).
Justification
"
" When used for PPH prevention, oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, ergometrine/
methylergometrine, and a fixed-dose combination of oxytocin and ergometrine
demonstrated clinical benefits especially in terms of PPH reduction compared with
no uterotonics. Although they all have variable undesirable effects, ranging from
minor to significant, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) agreed that these
undesirable effects do not outweigh the clinical benefits for any of these uterotonic
options when considered in the context of not using any uterotonic. Evidence
suggests that there is probably no important variability in, or uncertainty about,
how much women value the health outcomes associated with these uterotonics.
In spite of the differences in resource requirements, acceptability and feasibility
of implementing the individual uterotonic options (as presented below), the GDG
placed its emphasis on avoiding PPH and its complications where any of these
uterotonic options is all that is available for care, and therefore recommended that
any of these options can be applied for PPH prevention.
Remarks
"
" This recommendation applies to women undergoing a vaginal birth or caesarean
section. For injectable uterotonics, skilled health personnel who are trained to
administer them are required.
"
" To maximize efficacy, uterotonics are best given immediately (preferably within
one minute) after the birth of the baby or babies. Administration of a uterotonic for
prevention of PPH need not impede the delaying of cord clamping, as recommended
by WHO (13).
"
" The GDG advised that all women are to be provided with information – ideally
during antenatal care – on the need for an effective uterotonic to prevent PPH.
source_title: WHO Recommendations for Uterotonics for Prevention of PPH

question: If our patient's postpartum bleeding isn't settling with IV oxytocin, what's the next drug and dose we should be pulling up?
reference: If IV oxytocin is unavailable or the bleeding doesn't respond to it, give IV ergometrine, an oxytocin-ergometrine fixed-dose combination, or a prostaglandin — including sublingual misoprostol 800 µg (strong recommendation, low quality evidence). Tranexamic acid is also recommended if oxytocin and other uterotonics fail to stop the bleeding, or if the bleeding may be partly due to trauma (weak recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Continue uterine massage, and if there is still no response to uterotonics (or they aren't available), use intrauterine balloon tamponade for PPH due to atony; bimanual uterine compression and external aortic compression are temporizing measures until appropriate care is available. If bleeding persists despite uterotonics and conservative measures, proceed to surgical intervention, or uterine artery embolization if resources allow.

question: My patient had a hysterectomy and came out with a JP drain in place — do I need to keep giving her the prophylactic cefazolin doses until the drain comes out?
reference: No. For clean and clean-contaminated procedures such as this, no additional prophylactic antimicrobial doses should be given once the surgical incision is closed in the operating room, even if a drain is left in place. This is a Category IA strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. Prophylaxis should be given preoperatively, timed so a bactericidal serum and tissue concentration is present at the time of incision, but it is not continued postoperatively because of the drain.

question: My pre-op patient just told me his smoking has never caused him any problems so he doesn't want to hear about quitting — how should I respond without getting into an argument?
reference: Don't meet resistance with confrontation — roll with it. Ignore the antagonistic part of the comment and focus on the underlying issue, using reflection to create dissonance rather than warning or chastising him. For example: "I hope your health continues to stay that way. I would like you to consider getting your lungs checked, because early stages of cancer and lung disease may not have symptoms. That way you can make a better decision about whether you want to keep smoking. I am worried that your smoking is going to make your heart disease much worse in the future. However, the decision to smoke or quit smoking is yours." This lets him hear the information without feeling criticized, and makes clear the decision is his. Pair this with supporting his self-efficacy — ask "What worked before?" or "What do you think helped you be successful last time?" to draw out his strengths and past successes, and give genuine support for successes and even for contemplated changes, since he must be able to imagine success is possible before he will attempt change.
source_text:
It not only gives taking medication a specific, definable purpose
but also allows us to ask clients about behaviours that do not support the goal.

Roll with resistance – Ignore antagonistic elements in the client’s comments in order to focus on the
important underlying issues. For example, the client says, “Look, I haven’t had any real problems with
my smoking so far, so don’t worry about it.” Instead of rejecting this comment by saying, “If you continue
smoking, I can assure you that you will suffer some major consequences,” the healthcare provider can
roll with the expressed resistance by saying, “I hope your health continues to stay that way. I would like
you to consider getting your lungs checked because early stages of cancer and lung disease may not have
symptoms. That way, you can make a better decision about whether you want to keep smoking. I am
worried that your smoking is going to make your heart disease much worse in the future. However, the
decision to smoke or quit smoking is yours.” Do not meet resistance with confrontation but instead utilize
reflection to create dissonance. This allows the client to hear information without being chastised. In the
end, the decision belongs to the client.

Support self-efficacy – A person’s belief in the possibility of change (Bandura, 1977; 1982) is an important
motivator. Clients, based on their abilities and the resources and strengths they possess, need to be
encouraged by the healthcare provider. Questions such as: “What worked before?” or “What do you think
helped you to be successful last time?” provide valuable information about the client’s strengths.
Examine past successes (or failures) and offer genuine support for the successes. It is important to notice
not only actual changes in behaviour, but also contemplated changes, expressed in a positive manner.
The client must be able to imagine that success is a possibility before actually trying to change.
source_title: Nursing Management of Hypertension

question: Before I discharge a postpartum woman, what specific warning signs should I tell her to call us about right away?
reference: Teach her the danger signs for the four main postnatal complications and tell her to report any health concern to a health care professional: (1) PPH — sudden profuse blood loss or persistent increased blood loss, faintness, dizziness, palpitations/tachycardia; (2) pre-eclampsia/eclampsia — headache accompanied by one or more of visual disturbances, nausea, vomiting, epigastric or hypochondrial pain, feeling faint, or convulsions (particularly in the first few days after birth); (3) infection — fever, shivering, abdominal pain and/or offensive vaginal loss; (4) thromboembolism — unilateral calf pain, redness or swelling of the calves, shortness of breath or chest pain. Also give her general information about the normal physiological process of recovery after birth and that some health problems are common.

question: For a C-section, do we give the prophylactic antibiotic before the skin incision or wait until after the cord is clamped?
reference: Give the prophylactic antibiotics before the skin incision, not intraoperatively after umbilical cord clamping. This is a strong recommendation (based on moderate-quality evidence). Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for all women having either elective or emergency caesarean section (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), and a single dose of a first-generation cephalosporin or penicillin should be used in preference to other antibiotic classes (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence).

question: If we can only get one monitor for our theatre — pulse oximeter or capnograph — which one should we prioritise for our gynae cases?
reference: Prioritise the pulse oximeter. Although the weight of evidence is that oximetry and capnography together improve safety, much of the safety gain can be obtained from oximetry alone. Oximetry gives early warning in a greater variety of situations than capnography: it will alert you to problems in every situation that capnography would detect — perhaps later, but still in time to act — whereas there are many situations in which oximetry is potentially life-saving and capnography alone might not help. Oximetry is also less expensive (oximeters are typically under US$1000, and far cheaper in some places) and easier to maintain than capnography. Budget separately for probes, though — they are easily damaged and their replacement cost over time is likely to equal or exceed the cost of the device itself, so buy reliable, resistant probes.
source_text:
While the cost of pulse oximetry has fallen dramatically over the past

years, concern about capital outlay and resource constraints is
germane. Oximeters are relatively inexpensive (e.g. less than US$1000)
and may be much cheaper in many places, such as China, where they
are available at a fraction of this price. When calculated over the life
of the machine and the number of patients on whom it can be used,
this simple monitoring device becomes exceedingly cost–effective. In
addition, harm due to anaesthetic mishaps is not cost-free, and a single
error averted with pulse oximetry justifies its initial cost.
The devices themselves have excellent visual and auditory outputs, are
reliable and robust and do not require much maintenance. The probes
are, however, readily damaged and their replacement represents a
relatively high proportion of the overall cost of oximetry. It is not easy to
calculate the cost per patient of use of pulse oximetry, but the cost of
probes over time is likely to equal or exceed that of the actual device.
Reliable, resistant probes are needed. The cost of capnography is
somewhat higher, and maintenance is a little more challenging than for
oximetry.
Conclusion: Mandated use of pulse oximetry and capnography in
the developed world has stood the test of time. In settings with limited
resources, the issue is somewhat less clear because of arguments
about priorities for health-care funds. The overwhelming weight of
evidence is that these techniques together improve safety, but it
seems likely that much of the gain can be obtained from oximetry
alone. Oximetry appears to provide early warning in a greater variety
of situations than capnography (46). It will alert clinicians to problems
in every situation that would be detected by capnography, perhaps
later but certainly in time for action to be taken. Conversely, there are
many situations in which oximetry is potentially life-saving and in which
capnography alone might not be as helpful. Finally, oximetry is less
expensive and less difficult to maintain than capnography.
source_title: Safe Surgery Saves Lives: The Second Global Patient Safety Challenge
source_section: Evidence on monitoring with pulse oximetry and capnography

question: If we're expecting more than 500 ml blood loss on a case, what IV access should be in place before we make the incision?
reference: When there's a significant risk of losing more than 500 ml (7 ml/kg in children), it is highly recommended that at least two large bore intravenous lines or a central venous catheter be placed before skin incision. The team should also confirm that fluids or blood are available for resuscitation. If the anaesthetist doesn't know the expected blood loss for the case, they should discuss it with the surgeon before the operation starts — and the surgeon will restate expected blood loss again before skin incision as a second safety check for anaesthesia and nursing staff.
source_text:
Does the patient have a risk of >500 ml blood loss (7 ml/kg in children) ?
In this safety step, the Checklist coordinator asks the anaesthesia
team whether the patient risks losing more than half a litre of blood
during surgery in order to ensure recognition of and preparation for this
critical event. Large volume blood loss is among the most common
and important dangers for surgical patients, with risk of hypovolaemic
shock escalating when blood loss exceeds 500 ml (7 ml/kg in
children). Adequate preparation and resuscitation may mitigate the
consequences considerably.
Section I. | Introduction
103
Section IV. | Implementation Manual for the World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist
103
Surgeons may not consistently communicate the risk of blood loss
to anaesthesia and nursing staff. Therefore, if the anaesthetist does
not know what the risk of major blood loss is for the case, he or she
should discuss the risk with the surgeon before the operation begins. If
there is a significant risk of a greater than 500 ml blood loss, it is highly
recommended that at least two large bore intravenous lines or a central
venous catheter be placed prior to skin incision. In addition, the team
should confirm the availability of fluids or blood for resuscitation. (Note
that the expected blood loss will be reviewed again by the surgeon
before skin incision. This will provide a second safety check for the
anaesthetist and nursing staff.)
At this point this phase is completed and the team may proceed with
anaesthetic induction.

question: For our ERAS prolapse patients, when should we start the preop teaching and does it need to be written or is verbal enough — and should family be in the room?
reference: Start the ERAS discussion at the preoperative visit, explaining what the ERAS protocol involves and why it's being used in their perioperative care. Ideally give information in both written and oral form — don't rely on verbal alone. Written leaflets, videos, and psychological preparation all reduce anxiety and raise satisfaction (video education in a same-day discharge sacrocolpopexy protocol yielded high satisfaction in 98% of patients). Yes, include a support person: the patient plus a relative or care provider should meet with all members of the team for counseling and detailed information, so the team can clarify the patient's expectations and explain the postoperative plan. The aim is to set expectations about the surgical and anesthetic procedures and give the postoperative care plan; this also helps reduce pain and nausea and improves well-being. This is a strong recommendation, though based on low-quality evidence.
source_text:
and counseling
A large contributor to the success of ERAS protocols is
clear communication between the patient and physician.
Discussion of ERAS can be initiated at the preoperative
visit, with an explanation of what an ERAS protocol entails
and why it is being utilized in the patient’s perioperative
care. The goal of preoperative counseling is to set expectations about surgical and anesthetic procedures and to provide information regarding a care plan in the postoperative
period [2]. Preoperative education (with the help of educational leaflets, video, etc.) and psychological preparation

the chosen approach, education with thorough anticipatory
guidance is essential for patient engagement in and preparation for their own care.
Preoperative education is also effective in reducing pain
and nausea and improving well-being when added to an
existing ERAS protocol [2]. Interventions and endpoints in
this field vary widely, but most studies show that counseling
provides beneficial effects with no evidence of harm.
Recommendation
Ideally, patients should receive information in both written
and oral form. The patient and a support person, such as a
relative or care provider, should meet with all members of
the team for counseling, detailed information, and opportunities to understand the patient expectations and to explain
the postoperative plan.

question: For our same-day gyn surgery patients, what's the best way to catch surgical site infections after they go home — mailing surveys to the surgeons or calling the patients?
reference: No single detection method can be recommended; the choice depends on your available resources and data needs, and which operations you decide to monitor. That said, response rates differ a lot by method: questionnaires mailed to surgeons yield high response rates (72% to over 90%), telephone questionnaires to patients are more variable (38%, 81%, and 85% in different studies), and questionnaires mailed to patients yield quite low rates (15% and 33%). Direct methods such as home visits by nurses combined with a surgeon-completed survey at the 2-week postoperative clinic visit achieved essentially 100% ascertainment but are impractical for widespread use. Whatever method you use, apply the CDC NNIS definitions of SSI without modification in the outpatient setting.
source_text:
Methods chosen will necessarily reflect the hospital’s unique

question: For a post-op patient on our ward who I think might be septic, should I be using NEWS2 to score her, or is that only for certain patients?
reference: Yes — use NEWS2 for people aged 16 or over with suspected sepsis who are in an acute hospital setting (also acute mental health settings or ambulances), provided they are not currently pregnant and have not recently been pregnant. If your patient is currently or recently pregnant, NEWS2 is not the tool to use. In community or custodial settings, an early warning score should only be considered rather than routinely used. Whatever the setting, assess with a structured set of observations face-to-face to stratify risk when sepsis is suspected.

question: How long before her anaesthetic does my pre-op hysterectomy patient actually need to stop clear fluids, and can I give her a carbohydrate drink?
reference: Clear fluid fasting only needs to be 2 hours prior to the anaesthetic — this has been shown to be safe without increasing aspiration risk, and it helps avoid dehydration. Complex carbohydrate drinks can be given: they have been shown to be beneficial in colorectal surgery, reducing length of stay, and patients like them. Also avoid long-acting sedative premedication, as it can impair postoperative mobility, and mechanical bowel preparation should generally be avoided in gynaecological surgery. Do give antibiotics before incision and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis, as there is evidence of benefit.
source_text:
Perioperative care
Admission on the day of surgery has many advantages – these
include reduction in preoperative bed usage.

Dehydration is
avoided by reducing the period of ﬂuid fasting to 2 hours
prior to anaesthetic, which has been shown to be safe without
an increase the risk of aspiration.13 The use of complex
carbohydrate drinks have been shown to be beneﬁcial in
colorectal surgery,14 reducing the length of stay and liked by
patients.15 Mechanical bowel preparation can be associated
with morbidity and there is no evidence that it improves the
outcome for patients having elective rectal surgery, in whom
bowel continuity is restored.16 The role of mechanical bowel
preparation should therefore be investigated and generally
avoided in patients undergoing gynaecological surgery.

Long-acting
sedative
premedication
can
impair
postoperative mobility.17 Antibiotics prior to incision and
venous thromboembolic prophylaxis should be included as
there is evidence for their beneﬁt.18,19
Enhanced recovery pathways advocate minimal access
techniques.20,21 If considered necessary for the procedure to
be performed safely, abdominal incisions should be as small as
possible.

Nasogastric, abdominal and vaginal drains have little
beneﬁt and should be avoided as they increase morbidity and
prolong hospital stay.22–24 The routine use of vaginal packs
has been questioned, not only because they are uncomfortable
for patients but also because they may hinder, if not prevent,
mobilisation.

However, because of the lack of evidence, a
departmental approach for their use should be adopted to
ensure consistency.

This is another area for research.
source_title: Enhanced recovery in gynaecology

question: For our open abdominal hysterectomy patients, what proportion should actually end up needing a PCA pump, and what should we be giving instead?
reference: PCA should be needed in fewer than 5% of patients undergoing laparotomy. Instead, pain should be managed with an opioid-sparing multimodal approach: routine pre-operative oral acetaminophen, celecoxib, and gabapentin to reduce pain and opioid requirements, with non-opioids (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, gabapentin, dexamethasone) as first-line post-operatively. Give all post-operative medications orally in patients tolerating a diet; IV acetaminophen should not be used routinely since it is equally effective as the oral form but much more expensive. IV medications can be used for breakthrough pain, but PCA should rarely be required.
source_text:
Opioid Sparing Multimodal Post-operative Analgesia
Post-operative pain after gynecologic surgery plays a major role 
in patient quality of life and it may also be associated with higher 
rates of complications, longer hospital stays, increased readmission rates, and higher cost.172 173 When patients rely on opioid alone 
for post-operative analgesia, this may cause nausea, sedation, 
and fatigue while increasing the risk of addiction, thus leading to 
associated financial and social costs.174–176 Avoiding opioid use 
within a multimodal post-operative analgesia pathway, with greater 
emphasis on non-opioid medications, preserves or improves patient 
experience and functional recovery after surgery.37 177 Non-opioid 
alternatives include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, gabapentin, and dexamethasone.

Pre-operative education should stress the use of non-opioid alternatives as first-line 
therapy, and set expectations for post-operative pain control.

When used together, analgesics with different mechanisms of 
action may be synergistic, a concept which lays the foundation 
for post-operative pain management within ERAS protocols.178 
We recommend routine pre-operative administration of oral acetaminophen, celecoxib, and gabapentin to reduce pain and opioid 
requirements.179 Intravenous acetaminophen should not be used 
routinely, recognizing its equivalent efficacy to the oral preparation at much higher expense.

In general, oral administration of all 
post-operative medications in patients who can tolerate a diet is 
preferable to the intravenous route.

While intravenous medications 
may be required for breakthrough pain, patient-controlled analgesia 
should be required in <5% of patients undergoing laparotomy.
source_title: Guidelines for perioperative care in gynecologic/oncology: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations — 2019 update

question: For a pregnant patient just diagnosed with a leg DVT, should I keep her on bed rest with the leg up, or get her walking — and do compression stockings go on straight away?
reference: In the initial management of DVT, elevate the leg and apply a graduated elastic compression stocking to reduce oedema. She should not be kept immobile — mobilisation is encouraged, with the graduated elastic compression stocking in place.
source_text:
Additional therapies
Should graduated elastic compression stockings be employed in the acute management of VTE in pregnancy?
In the initial management of DVT, the leg should be elevated and a graduated elastic compression
stocking applied to reduce oedema. Mobilisation with graduated elastic compression stockings
should be encouraged.
What is the role of inferior vena cava filters in the management of VTE in pregnancy?
Consideration should be given to the use of a temporary inferior vena cava filter in the peripartum
period for patients with iliac vein VTE to reduce the risk of PE or in patients with proven DVT and
who have recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation.
source_title: GTG37b - Thrombosis and Embolism during Pregnancy Acute Management

question: We're at a rural unit and a post-op patient with suspected sepsis is waiting on ambulance transfer that'll take over an hour — do we hold antibiotics until she reaches the ED, and does she need her sepsis risk rescored on handover?
reference: No, don't wait. Where combined transfer and handover time to the emergency department is more than 1 hour, antibiotics should be given pre-hospital to people meeting high-risk criteria (see table 1): GPs in remote and rural locations where transfer routinely exceeds 1 hour should have mechanisms in place to give antibiotics in pre-hospital settings, and ambulance services should consider whether they need mechanisms to give antibiotics to people at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis if a GP has not already given them. Paramedics considering giving antibiotics should follow local guidelines and the recommendations on choice of antibiotic therapy. And yes — when ambulance or acute hospital staff take over care of someone whose sepsis risk was originally evaluated in the community (or a custodial setting), they must re-evaluate that risk of severe illness or death from sepsis using NEWS2.

question: If one of our postpartum patients suddenly collapses and we suspect a massive PE, what do I need to get organised and how fast — and what anticoagulant do they go on?
reference: Contact the on-call medical team immediately and arrange an urgent portable echocardiogram or CTPA within 1 hour of presentation. Intravenous unfractionated heparin is the preferred initial treatment for massive PE with cardiovascular compromise, so your unit should have a guideline in place for administering it. If massive PE is confirmed — or in extreme circumstances even before confirmation — immediate thrombolysis should be considered. Decisions between IV unfractionated heparin, thrombolytic therapy, or thoracotomy with surgical embolectomy are made on an individual basis by a multidisciplinary team including senior physicians, obstetricians and radiologists.

question: My pregnant patient on LMWH has developed an itchy rash at her injection sites — do I just switch her to a different LMWH brand, or does she need something else?
reference: If she's unable to tolerate heparin because of allergic skin reactions and there's no evidence of HIT, you can switch to an alternative LMWH preparation — but be aware the cross-reactivity rate between different heparin preparations is 33.3%, so the reaction may recur. If the problem persists on the alternative LMWH, or if she has confirmed HIT, escalate and consider danaparoid, a low-molecular-weight heparinoid; a review of 91 pregnancies in 83 women found danaparoid to be an effective and safe antithrombotic in pregnancy for women intolerant of heparin. For context, heparin-induced skin reactions were seen in 22 of 111 pregnant women (19.8%) in a prospective observational study, all due to allergic delayed-type hypersensitivity, with a median onset of 50.5 days (range 5–184 days) after starting treatment.

Women should be taught to self-inject and can then be managed as outpatients until delivery;
arrangements should be made to allow safe disposal of needles and syringes. A clinical audit

Prolonged unfractionated heparin use during pregnancy may result in osteoporosis and

pregnancies in 83 women concluded that danaparoid is an effective and safe antithrombotic

question: My post-op hysterectomy patient still has her Foley in from surgery yesterday — how soon should it come out if there's no ongoing indication?
reference: Remove it as soon as possible postoperatively, preferably within 24 hours of surgery, unless there are appropriate indications for continued use (Category IB). So if she has no ongoing indication, the catheter should already be coming out now rather than being left in.
source_text:
Suprapubic versus indwelling urethral

Low-quality evidence suggested a benefit of suprapubic catheters over indwelling urethral 
catheters in selected populations.37,62,104,107,108,128-133,135,136 This was based on a decreased risk of 
bacteriuria/unspecified UTI, recatheterization, and urethral stricture, and increased patient 
comfort and satisfaction. However, there were no differences in SUTI and an increased risk of 
longer duration of catheterization with suprapubic catheters. Studies involved primarily 
postoperative and spinal cord injury patients. Our search did not reveal data on differences in 
complications related to catheter insertion or the catheter site.

Q2A.5. Clean intermittent versus sterile intermittent

Moderate-quality evidence suggested no benefit of using sterile over clean technique for 
intermittent catheterization.63,73,105,117-122 No differences were found in the risk of SUTI or 
bacteriuria/unspecified UTI. Study populations included nursing home residents and adults and 
children with neurogenic bladder/spinal cord injury.

Evidence Review Table 2A. What are the risks and benefits associated with different 
approaches to catheterization? 
2A.1. 
Consider using external catheters as an alternative to indwelling urethral catheters in 
cooperative male patients without urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction. 
(Category II)

2A.2. 
Intermittent catheterization is preferable to indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheters 
in patients with bladder emptying dysfunction. (Category II)

2A.3. 
If intermittent catheterization is used, perform it at regular intervals to prevent bladder 
overdistension. (Category IB)

2A.4. 
For operative patients who have an indication for an indwelling catheter, remove the

question: We've got a suspected environmental outbreak on our surgical unit — do we need to step up cleaning in the OR area, and what agent should we be using?
reference: Yes — increased cleaning is essential whenever there is an outbreak in which environmental sources play a role. Health-care facilities should be visibly clean at all times as a baseline for minimizing infection. As for which cleaning and disinfecting agent to use, that depends on many factors, so follow your own facility's existing policies and procedures on cleaning and disinfection rather than choosing an agent ad hoc.
source_text:
Surgical site infections are second in frequency,
accounting for about 20% of all HCAIs.

Bloodstream infections associated with the use
of an intravascular device and pneumonia
associated with ventilators each account for
an additional 11% of HCAIs.

Evidence shows that infection rates can be
reduced if health-care workers comply with
infection prevention and control guidelines
and patients leave hospital as soon as possible.

Many HCAI patients (about 25%) are in ICUs
and more than 70% of the infections in these
patients are due to microorganisms resistant
to one or more antibiotics [13].

Preventing health care-associated infection–five
priority training areas for students
Over the course of their training, students will
work in many environments in which there is
a risk of transmission of infection.

Students should
approach every situation as having the potential
to lead to the infection of a patient or health-care
workers, including themselves.

This means that
students will need to routinely undertake activities
to prevent infection, such as using correct hand
hygiene techniques, using PPE (e.g. gloves and
gowns) appropriately, ensuring that instruments
and devices have undergone recommended
sterilization procedures, and adhering to policies
and recommendations to prevent infections in
specific situations, including the use of proper
aseptic technique and practising safe waste
management, especially concerning the disposal
of sharps.

Priority areas in which all health-care workers,
including students, need to take action are
described below.

Environmental cleanliness
Environmental cleanliness in the hospital is
essential for minimizing infections.

Health-care
facilities should be visibly clean.

Increased cleaning
is essential when there are outbreaks in which
environmental sources play a role.

The choice
of cleaning and disinfecting agent will depend
on many factors and each facility should have
existing policies and procedures on these issues.

question: Half our surgeons roll their eyes at the safety checklist and say it's a waste of time — what actually needs to happen from above to get them on board?
reference: Buy-in has to be visibly driven by leadership. The chiefs of surgery, anaesthesia and nursing must publicly state that safety is a priority and that the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist helps achieve it. They should demonstrate this by using the Checklist in their own cases and by regularly asking staff how implementation is going. Without demonstrable leadership, imposing the Checklist is likely to breed discontent and antagonism. Alongside this, adapt the Checklist to your local routines and expectations rather than treating it as rote recitation, and build a team by first recruiting the clinicians most likely to be supportive, including colleagues from as many disciplines as possible (surgery, anaesthesia, nursing). It also takes practice for teams to learn to use it effectively — the aim is a simple, efficient set of priority checks that improve teamwork and communication, not to frustrate workflow.
source_text:
It will take practice for teams to learn to use the Checklist

For the

To demonstrate

If

Previous quality improvement work has provided a

Experience with the pilot study

A number

Commitment by all clinical team

question: If I'm not sure the incision edges are holding well, should I still take out all the sutures at once or stagger them?
reference: Don't take them all out if approximation is questionable. Remove alternate sutures (every second one) first, then reassess skin approximation. If the wound is well-healed, all sutures can come out at the same time, but if there are concerns about approximation, delay removing the remaining sutures for several days to avoid dehiscence. Applying Steri-Strips before suture removal can also lessen the chance of dehiscence. Watch the wound line for any separation during removal and stop the procedure if you have concerns. Remember the provider must assess the wound and give an order for suture removal — nonabsorbable sutures are usually removed within 7 to 14 days, depending on healing and the extent of surgery.
source_text:
Checklist for Intermittent Suture Removal

Checklist for Intermittent Suture Removal 
Sutures are tiny threads, wire, or other material used to sew body tissue 
and skin together. They may be placed deep in the tissue and/or 
superficially to close a wound. The most commonly seen suture is the 
intermittent suture. 
Sutures may be absorbent (dissolvable) or nonabsorbent (must be 
removed). Nonabsorbent sutures are usually removed within 7 to 14 days. 
Suture removal is determined by how well the wound has healed and the 
extent of the surgery. See Figure 20.32

for an example of suture removal. 
Sutures must be left in place long enough to establish wound closure with 
enough strength to support internal tissues and organs. If sutures are 
removed too early in the wound healing process, dehiscence can occur. 
The wound line must be observed for separations during the process of 
suture removal and the procedure stopped if there are any concerns. 
The health care provider must assess the wound to determine whether or 
not to remove the sutures and provide an order for the removal of sutures. 
Alternate sutures (every second suture) may be removed first, and then 
the remaining sutures removed after adequate approximation of the skin 
tissue is determined. If the wound is well-healed, all the sutures may be 
removed at the same time, but if there are concerns about approximation, 
the removal of the remaining sutures may be delayed for several days to 
avoid dehiscence. Steri-Strips may be applied prior to suture removal to 
lessen the chance of wound dehiscence. See Figure 20.33.
