question: My postpartum patient is high-risk for sepsis — what lactate level means I need to escalate, and how fast do the IV antibiotics need to go in?
reference: A serum lactate of 4 mmol/l or more should trigger immediate escalation of care, including considering discussion with the critical care team. Lactate should be measured urgently in any woman with features indicating high risk of sepsis. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics should be given within one hour in women at high risk of sepsis, whether or not septic shock is present.
source_text:
KEY RECOMMENDATIONS
• Consider sepsis as a possible diagnosis in all women during pregnancy, and in the intrapartum and postpartum period, with a
suspected infection and whose clinical condition rapidly deteriorates. [Good Practice Point (GPP)]
• If sepsis is suspected in the community, urgent escalation and referral to hospital is indicated. [GPP]
• Monitoring of a woman with suspected sepsis should be performed using an early warning system modified for obstetrics,
managed through a multidisciplinary approach with early escalation and senior input. [GPP]
• Serum lactate should be measured urgently in women with features indicating a high risk of sepsis.

Serum lactate of 4 mmol/l or
more should prompt immediate escalation of care, including consideration of discussion with critical care team. [Grade D]
• Any relevant imaging studies should be performed promptly to confirm the source of infection. [Grade D]
• Use of a sepsis bundle may improve compliance with urgent management in women at high risk of sepsis. [Grade D]
• Administration of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics is recommended within one hour in women at high risk of sepsis,
with or without septic shock. [Grade C]
• In a critically ill pregnant woman, birth of the baby can be expedited if it would be beneficial to the woman or the baby or to
both.

A decision on the timing and mode of birth should be made by a senior obstetrician following discussion with the woman
and/or family if her condition permits. [GPP]
• During the intrapartum period, continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended.

question: When I'm measuring undermining on a post-op abdominal incision, how far do I advance the probe and where do I measure from?
reference: Insert the probe under the wound edge, directed almost parallel to the wound surface, and advance it until you feel resistance. The amount of undermining is the distance from the probe tip to the point where the probe is level with the wound edge. Document the location using clock terms (as with tunneling, where 12:00 points toward the patient's head).
source_text:
The location of the tunnel in the wound should be 
documented using the analogy of a clock face, with 12:00 pointing toward 
the patient’s head.

Undermining occurs when the tissue under the wound edges becomes 
eroded, resulting in a pocket beneath the skin at the wound’s edge. 
Undermining is measured by inserting a probe under the wound edge 
directed almost parallel to the wound surface until resistance is felt. The 
amount of undermining is the distance from the probe tip to the point at 
which the probe is level with the wound edge. Clock terms are also used 
to identify the area of undermining.

Wound Edges and Periwound Skin 
If the wound is healing by primary intention, it should be documented if 
the wound edges are well-approximated (closed together) or if there are 
any signs of dehiscence. The skin outside the outer edges of the wound, 
called the periwound skin, provides information related to wound 
development or healing. For example, a venous ulcer often has excess 
wound drainage that macerates the periwound skin, giving it a wet, 
waterlogged appearance that is soft and grayish white in color.

question: How long should I be scrubbing my hands and forearms before a case, and how far up do I need to go?
reference: Perform a preoperative surgical scrub for at least 2 to 5 minutes with an appropriate antiseptic, scrubbing the hands and forearms up to the elbows (Category IB). Before the first scrub of the day, also clean underneath each fingernail (Category II). Keep nails short, don't wear artificial nails (Category IB), and remove hand or arm jewelry (Category II). After scrubbing, keep your hands up and away from your body with elbows flexed so water runs from the fingertips toward the elbows, then dry with a sterile towel and don a sterile gown and gloves (Category IB).

question: If we're dealing with a VRE or MRSA outbreak in the unit, is it worth putting everyone in gloves for every patient, or just the colonized ones?
reference: Universal glove use is supported in that situation. In intensive-care units where VRE or MRSA have been epidemic, requiring all health-care workers to wear gloves for the care of all patients in the unit likely helped control the outbreaks. Gloves also prevent hand contamination in the majority of personnel having direct contact with patients colonized with C. difficile or VRE, and they prevent staff from picking up VRE on their hands after touching contaminated environmental surfaces — which matters because handwashing or hand antisepsis may not remove all pathogens once hands are heavily contaminated. In a prospective controlled trial, routine vinyl glove use for handling any body substance reduced the incidence of C. difficile diarrhea and substantially reduced asymptomatic C. difficile carriage on the glove wards but not on control wards. Note also that glove use should not replace hand hygiene — study findings on whether gloved staff wash their hands more or less often are conflicting.
source_text:
Two other studies, involving personnel caring for patients with

difficile or VRE, revealed that wearing gloves prevented hand
contamination among the majority of personnel having
direct contact with patients (45,58). Wearing gloves also prevented personnel from acquiring VRE on their hands when
touching contaminated environmental surfaces (58). Preventing heavy contamination of the hands is considered important, because handwashing or hand antisepsis may not remove
all potential pathogens when hands are heavily contaminated
(25,111).
Several studies provide evidence that wearing gloves can help
reduce transmission of pathogens in health-care settings. In a
prospective controlled trial that required personnel to routinely
wear vinyl gloves when handling any body substances, the
incidence of C. difficile diarrhea among patients decreased from

cases/1,000 patient discharges before the intervention to

cases/1,000 discharges during the intervention (226). The
prevalence of asymptomatic C. difficile carriage also decreased
substantially on “glove” wards, but not on control wards. In
intensive-care units where VRE or MRSA have been epidemic,
requiring all HCWs to wear gloves to care for all patients in
the unit (i.e., universal glove use) likely has helped control
outbreaks (357,358).
The influence of glove use on the hand-hygiene habits of
personnel is not clear. Several studies found that personnel
who wore gloves were less likely to wash their hands upon
leaving a patient’s room (290,320). In contrast, two other studies found that personnel who wore gloves were substantially
more likely to wash their hands after patient care (87,301).

question: For our open abdominal hysterectomy patients, what proportion should actually end up needing a PCA pump, and what should we be using for pain control instead?
reference: Patient-controlled analgesia should be needed in fewer than 5% of laparotomy patients — IV medication is reserved for breakthrough pain only. The mainstay should be multimodal analgesia including incisional infiltration with bupivacaine or liposomal bupivacaine, which has no systemic side effects when used appropriately and should be part of all ERAS protocols. Current data favor incisional injection over transversus abdominis plane blocks or thoracic epidural analgesia — one trial in total abdominal hysterectomy showed lower pain scores and less opioid use with local liposomal bupivacaine versus TAP blocks. Thoracic epidurals carry a roughly 30% failure rate, hypotension needing vasopressors, and delayed mobilization, and one trial showed 0.5 day longer length of stay with epidural compared with TAP block due to slower transition to oral analgesics.
source_text:
While intravenous medications 
may be required for breakthrough pain, patient-controlled analgesia 
should be required in <5% of patients undergoing laparotomy.

Incisional infiltration with either bupivacaine or liposomal bupivacaine 
has no systemic side effects when used appropriately, and should 
be incorporated into all ERAS protocols as a component of multimodal analgesia.37 180
The use of thoracic epidural analgesia and transversus abdominis plane blocks, both alternatives to local analgesia, has been 
frequently debated in patients undergoing major abdominal 
surgery.

Thoracic epidural analgesia has been shown to effectively reduce post-operative pain and stress,181 182 but with some 
untoward effects such as a 30% risk of failure,183 hypotension 
requiring vasopressors,184 and hindrance of early mobilization.185 
Transversus abdominis plane blocks are performed by injecting 
local anesthetic between the muscle layers of the trunk using 
ultrasound guidance, and has also been shown to reduce pain and 
opiate requirements after surgery.186 However, direct comparisons 
of thoracic epidural analgesia, transversus abdominis plane blocks, 
and incisional injection have not been performed and current literature has failed to show improvements over local injection.

One 
trial showed lower pain scores and less opioid use in patients 
randomized to local injection of liposomal bupivacaine compared 
with transversus abdominis plane blocks following total abdominal hysterectomy.187 Other investigations in laparoscopic surgery 
have also failed to show improvements with transversus abdominis plane blocks.188–191 A randomized trial of conventional epidural 
versus transversus abdominis plane block demonstrated a 0.5 day 
decreased length of stay with transversus abdominis plane blocks, 
likely due to a slower transition to oral analgesics with thoracic 
epidural analgesia.192 The weight of current data supports the use 
of incisional injection over transversus abdominis plane blocks or 
thoracic epidural analgesia.

question: My ankle arthrodesis patient is still in a cast — how long do we keep the VTE prophylaxis going before we think about stopping it?
reference: For foot or ankle surgery requiring immobilisation (such as arthrodesis or arthroplasty), pharmacological VTE prophylaxis should be considered, and you should consider stopping prophylaxis if the immobilisation continues beyond 42 days. Prophylaxis is also considered when total anaesthesia time was more than 90 minutes, or when the person's VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk.

question: Our unit does D&Cs in a small procedure room down the hall — should that room be counted as an operating room when we report our OR numbers?
reference: No, not unless it actually meets the definition of an operating room. An operating room is an enclosed room specifically dedicated to surgical procedures and equipped to deliver monitored anaesthesia, whether or not it is inside a hospital facility. Rooms used for procedures like dilation and curettage, endoscopy, or incision and drainage that are not suitable for other invasive operations are minor procedure rooms and should be excluded from the count unless they meet that full definition (dedicated, enclosed, and equipped for monitored anaesthesia).

question: We've just admitted a pregnant woman to the gynae ward with ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome — does she need LMWH even though she's only in her first trimester?
reference: Yes. Women admitted to hospital when pregnant, including admissions to the gynaecology ward with hyperemesis gravidarum or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, should usually be offered thromboprophylaxis with LMWH, unless there is a specific contraindication such as risk of labour or active bleeding. Her VTE risk assessment should be repeated on this admission (risk assessment is repeated whenever a woman is admitted to hospital for any reason or develops intercurrent problems), and the reasons for the recommendation should be discussed with her.

Risk assessment should be repeated if the woman is admitted to hospital for any reason or develops

Any woman with two current risk factors shown in Appendix I and Table 1 (other than previous VTE

Women admitted to hospital when pregnant (including to the gynaecology ward with hyperemesis
gravidarum or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome) should usually be offered thromboprophylaxis

question: One of my emergency medical admissions came in overnight — how quickly does she need to be seen by a consultant, and will she still be reviewed over the bank holiday weekend?
reference: For anyone admitted as a medical emergency, aim for consultant assessment within 14 hours of admission to determine her care pathway. After that, she should have a daily consultant review, including at weekends and bank holidays. If her clinical need warrants it, review should be more frequent — for example twice daily. These arrangements should be accompanied by local evaluation that takes account of current staffing models, case mix and severity of illness.

question: For our PPH prevention stock, what strengths of ergometrine and misoprostol are on the WHO essential medicines list, and is the combined oxytocin/ergometrine ampoule included?
reference: The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines includes ergometrine (hydrogen maleate) 200 µg in a 1 ml ampoule for injection, and misoprostol as 200 µg tablets and 25 µg tablets — the 200 µg tablets being for prevention and treatment of PPH where oxytocin is unavailable or cannot be safely used, and for management of incomplete abortion and miscarriage. Oxytocin (listed as IU in a 1 ml ampoule for injection) and ergometrine are listed separately; the fixed-dose combination of oxytocin plus ergometrine (5 IU/500 µg, e.g. Syntometrine®, which is 500 µg ergometrine maleate with 5 IU oxytocin) is NOT listed. Carbetocin is also not listed — note the heat-stable carbetocin formulation differs from the non–heat-stable one only in its excipients (inactive vehicle substances), and manufacturer's instructions on storage and transport should be given due consideration.

question: If a labouring woman with a penicillin allergy needs GBS cover for a fever, can we still just use clindamycin?
reference: No — clindamycin is no longer recommended as the routine alternative because GBS resistance to it reached 31% in 2022. For beta-lactam allergic women needing GBS prophylaxis in labour, substitute a cephalosporin or vancomycin. Any woman with pyrexia and suspected infection in labour should be offered an antibiotic regimen covering GBS plus continuous fetal monitoring, and be screened for sepsis with the source of infection identified and managed. Check your local formulary, as empirical choice should be tailored to local epidemiology and resistance.
source_text:
Maternal pyrexia is an important potential marker of infection,
but may not always be present in maternal sepsis and is not
necessarily related to the severity of illness.

Indeed, it is important to recognise that sepsis can present with hypothermia.

Pyrexia in labour can be managed with supportive measures
such as increased fluid intake, paracetamol, tepid sponging
and lowering the environmental temperature.

Non-sepsis
causes of maternal hyperthermia such as epidural anaesthesia and misoprostol are diagnoses of exclusion.

Women with a
fever during labour should be screened for sepsis as already described, and the underlying source of infection identified and
managed [84].

Women with pyrexia and suspected infection in
labour should be offered an antibiotic regimen which covers
GBS, [70, 71] and they should be offered continuous fetal monitoring [85]. [Evidence level 3]
If genital tract sepsis is suspected, GAS and E.Coli are likely
pathogens [4].

Prompt treatment with a combination of high-dose
broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, active against Gramnegative bacteria and capable of preventing exotoxin production
from Gram-positive bacteria, may be lifesaving.

The empirical
choice of antimicrobials should be tailored to local epidemiology and resistance.

Local formularies should be consulted,
narrowing the agent spectrum to that of the causative organism(s) once identified.

Early oral switch and a documented duration should be included in the individual's medical notes [61].

Source control should be a priority, e.g. surgery to drain pus,
expedited birth where necessary.

Women suspected of having
infected retained products of conception should be given antibiotics and surgery to remove the infected products of conception
should be performed promptly [4]. [Evidence level 4]
Increasing resistance of GBS to clindamycin (31% resistance in
2022) has necessitated recommendations for substituting cephalosporins or vancomycin for beta-lactam allergic women needing prophylaxis in labour [44, 71, 72].
source_title: GTG64 - Identification and Management of Maternal Sepsis
source_section: 6.1   |   How should Maternal Sepsis be Managed?

question: For a C-section, should I give the prophylactic antibiotic before the skin incision or wait until the cord is clamped?
reference: Either practice is acceptable — both are more effective than placebo for preventing post-caesarean infection — but giving the prophylactic antibiotic during the hour before incision is likely more effective than waiting until the umbilical cord is clamped. Prophylaxis before incision has been most effective for every other operation studied, and a recent meta-analysis showed no clear evidence of harm to the baby from this brief antibiotic exposure at birth. Note that the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists both recommend offering prophylactic antibiotics, but neither makes a conclusive recommendation on timing, so there is genuine controversy on this point.
source_text:
Prophylaxis is most effective when given before incision for every
other operation studied, and a recent meta-analysis did not show clear
evidence of harm to the child from this brief exposure to antibiotic at
the time of birth (264).

Prophylactic antibiotic administration during
the hour before incision is likely more effective than waiting until the
umbilical cord is clamped.

The Royal College of Obstetricians and
Gynaecologists recommend offering antibiotics prophylactically while
the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend
antibiotic administration for prophylaxis, but neither makes conclusive
recommendations regarding timing (269).

Clearly, there is controversy
on this question, and either practice is acceptable and more effective
for preventing post-caesarean infection than placebo (267).

Prophylaxis in children: Very few trials of surgical antibiotic
prophylaxis have been done in paediatric populations, but the issue
has been reviewed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, which
concluded that the basic biological principles of prophylaxis are
unlikely to be different in paediatric patients and adults (268).

They
recommend that the same basic principles be followed but that
the doses be adjusted according to standard dosing principles for
paediatric patients.

Subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis in patients
undergoing surgical procedures: Guidelines for subacute bacterial
endocarditis prophylaxis are available for patients who are at risk
for endocarditis and undergoing an operation.

The American Heart
Association recently released a new guideline, which has been
endorsed by the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the
Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society (269).
source_title: Safe Surgery Saves Lives: The Second Global Patient Safety Challenge

question: If my gloves still look clean after prepping one patient, can I just wash the gloves and keep them on for the next patient, or do I have to take them off and do hand hygiene?
reference: No — washing and reusing gloves between patients should be discouraged. In a study simulating clinical conditions, washing and reusing gloves between patient contacts left bacterial counts of 0–4.7 log on the hands after glove removal. Gloves must be removed after patient contact, and handwashing or hand disinfection performed after glove removal. Hand hygiene is required regardless of whether gloves were worn or changed, and failure to remove gloves after patient contact — or between 'dirty' and 'clean' body-site care on the same patient — counts as nonadherence to hand-hygiene recommendations.
source_text:
Hand hygiene is required regardless of
whether gloves are used or changed.

Failure to remove gloves
after patient contact or between “dirty” and “clean” body-site
care on the same patient must be regarded as nonadherence to
hand-hygiene recommendations (11).

In a study in which
experimental conditions approximated those occurring in clinical practice (321), washing and reusing gloves between
patient contacts resulted in observed bacterial counts of 0–4.7
log on the hands after glove removal.

Therefore, this practice
should be discouraged; handwashing or disinfection should
be performed after glove removal.

Lack of 1) knowledge of guidelines for hand hygiene, 2)
recognition of hand-hygiene opportunities during patient care,
and 3) awareness of the risk of cross-transmission of pathogens are barriers to good hand-hygiene practices.

Furthermore,
certain HCWs believe they have washed their hands when
necessary, even when observations indicate they have not
(89,92,295,296,322).

Perceived barriers to hand-hygiene behavior are linked not
only to the institution, but also to HCWs’ colleagues.

Therefore, both institutional and small-group dynamics need to be
considered when implementing a system change to secure an
improvement in HCWs’ hand-hygiene practice.

question: We're bringing a patient with suspected C. diff back from the OR — can I just use the alcohol foam between contacts, or do I have to go to the sink every time?
reference: You must use soap and water for hand hygiene, not hand sanitizer, because alcohol-based hand sanitizer is not effective against C. difficile spores. Enteric precautions are used whenever a GI pathogen such as C. diff or norovirus is present or suspected, and they are applied in addition to contact precautions. You should also wear a gown in the client's room to prevent inadvertent fecal contamination of your clothing from contact with contaminated surfaces, and after the client is discharged a special disinfecting process must be used, including disinfection of the mattress.
source_text:
Enteric Precautions
Enteric precautions are used when there is the presence, or suspected presence, of gastrointestinal pathogens such as Clostridium difficile (C-diff) or norovirus. These pathogens are present in feces, so health care workers should always wear a gown in the client room to prevent inadvertent fecal contamination of their clothing from contact with contaminated surfaces.

In addition to contact precautions, enteric precautions include the following:

Using only soap and water for hand hygiene. Do not use hand sanitizer because it is not effective against C-diff spores.

Using a special disinfecting process. Special disinfecting should be used after client discharge and includes disinfection of the mattress.
source_title: OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals - Infection Prevention Chapter
source_section: 9.6 Preventing Infection – Nursing Fundamentals 2e > Enteric Precautions

question: One of our new nurses gave the wrong medication in the OR because she skipped the double-check — do I write her up, or is there something else I should be looking at first?
reference: Don't jump to individual blame. Use a systems approach first to understand what happened and why before making any decision about personal accountability. Look at the contributing factors: was she new to the unit and unsupervised? Did she know the steps in the checking protocol? Was she even aware a checking policy existed? Was she unsure but had no one available to check with, and feared getting into trouble for delaying the drug? If any of those apply, the finding is that she wasn't prepared for the duty — that's a system failure, not a personal one. Personal responsibility for the error applies only if she was prepared, was being supervised, knew the protocols, and still skipped the check out of laziness, sloppiness, or wanting to finish early. Accountability is still a professional obligation, but alongside personal accountability there is system accountability — the system must examine itself. Also note this blame-free approach isn't just for students or novices; it applies equally to long-experienced staff. Practically, an inexperienced staff member who isn't being supervised should escalate and seek advice from a senior colleague, despite pressure to keep moving patients through.
source_text:
If a dental student administers the wrong
medication to a patient because he/she failed
to follow the protocol for checking medications,
should that student be held accountable?

An
analysis of such a case using a systems approach
would examine the factors that contributed to
the student not checking the medication: what
if the student was new to the dental clinic and
was not being supervised?; or if he/she did not
know the steps involved?; or was unaware that
a policy existed to help make sure the correct
medication is given to the correct patient?; or
if he/she was unsure, but there was no one
around with whom to check and the student
feared getting into trouble for delaying the
administration of the drug?

Systems thinking
would suggest that this student was not prepared
for such duties.

But if the student was prepared,
was being supervised by a dentist and was aware
of the protocols, but did not check the medication
because he/she was lazy or sloppy or wanted
to finish work early, then that student would be
responsible for the error.

Inexperienced health-care
workers may not always be supervised; in such
circumstances, they should seek advice from
a senior colleague, notwithstanding the pressure
to move patients through the service.

Most circumstances surrounding adverse events
are complicated, so it is best to use a systems
approach to understand what happened and
why before making any decisions about personal
accountability.

It is important to remember that
this blame-free culture does not apply only
to students, but also to other staff, even those
who have been in practise for a long time and
have many years of experience.

Accountability is a professional obligation and
no one thinks that individuals should not be held
accountable.

However, in addition to personal
accountability, there is also system accountability.

System accountability requires that the system
examine itself.
source_title: Patient Safety Curriculum Guide: Multi-professional Edition

question: For a major PPH, how do I dose carboprost — how much, how often, and what's the max number of doses?
reference: Carboprost 0.25 mg is given intramuscularly every 15 minutes, up to a maximum of 8 doses. If needed, carboprost 0.5 mg can also be given intramyometrially. This sits within the stepwise medical treatment sequence: rub up the uterine fundus and empty the bladder, oxytocin 5 iu slow IV (repeat if necessary), ergometrine 0.5 mg slow IV or IM, oxytocin infusion (40 iu in 500 ml), then carboprost, misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually, and consider tranexamic acid 1 g IV.

question: When we set a patient up with a system navigator at discharge, what timeframe are we watching for ED visits and readmissions as the marker of a good handoff?
reference: Within 30 days of the transition in care. For navigator support, the prioritized outcomes are emergency department visits within 30 days of a transition in care and readmission rates within 30 days of a transition in care, along with patient quality of life, whether a follow-up visit with a health or social service provider occurs, and patient satisfaction.

question: Can we add a VTE prophylaxis check to our surgical safety checklist for gynae cases, and are there any items we're not allowed to drop?
reference: Yes — the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist was deliberately kept brief rather than comprehensive, and teams are encouraged to add safety checks specific to their procedures, especially ones already routine in the facility. Confirming VTE prophylaxis is given as an explicit example: mechanical means (sequential compression boots or stockings) and/or medical means (heparin or warfarin) when indicated. Other suggested additions include availability of essential implants (e.g. mesh or a prosthesis), other equipment needs, and critical preoperative biopsy results, laboratory results or blood type. Each locale may reformat, reorder or revise the checklist to fit local practice, as long as the critical safety steps are still completed efficiently. However, the team communication items — briefings and debriefings — are of critical importance and must not be removed. Facilities are also cautioned not to make the checklist unmanageably complex.
source_text:
Modifying the Checklist
WHO Patient Safety | WHO Guidelines for Safe Surgery 2009

WHO Patient Safety

Integrated
Many institutions already have strategies
to insure the reliable performance of
many of the processes that are part
of the WHO Checklist. Integrating
new safety checks into the processes
is challenging but possible in nearly
all settings. The major additions to
existing routines involve the integration
of team communication, briefings, and
debriefings. These items are of critical
importance and should not be removed
from the Checklist.
In order to ensure brevity, the WHO Surgical Safety
Checklist was not intended to be comprehensive. Teams
may consider adding other safety checks for specific
procedures, particularly if they are part of a routine process
established in the facility. Each phase should be used
as an opportunity to verify that critical safety steps are
consistently completed. Additional steps might include
confirmation of venous thromboembolism prophylaxis by
mechanical means (such as sequential compression boots
and stockings) and/or medical means (such as heparin
or warfarin) when indicated, the availability of essential
implants (such as mesh or a prosthetic), other equipment
needs or critical preoperative biopsy results, laboratory
results or blood type. Each locale is encouraged to
reformat, reorder or revise the Checklist to accommodate
local practice while ensuring completion of the critical safety
steps in an efficient manner. As noted above facilities and
individuals are cautioned against making the Checklist
unmanageably complex.

question: We've got a 35-weeker with severe pre-eclampsia — do we need to deliver her now or can we hold off?
reference: Between 34 and 36 weeks plus 6 days with a viable fetus, expectant management may be an option rather than immediate delivery — but only if there is no uncontrolled maternal hypertension, no increasing maternal organ dysfunction and no fetal distress, and only where those parameters can be actively monitored. If any of those appear, that policy no longer applies. Note this is a weak recommendation based on very low quality evidence. At term, by contrast, early delivery is strongly recommended for severe pre-eclampsia.

question: How often should I be emptying my patient's urostomy pouch, and at what point does it need emptying?
reference: Empty the urostomy pouch regularly — most patients empty every two to four hours, or whenever the pouch becomes about one-third full. Overnight, the pouch can be connected to a drainage bag instead. Remember the patient has no voluntary control of urine, so scheduled emptying is essential.

reference: For inpatients with a low-risk VTE profile undergoing vaginal or laparoscopic urogynecologic procedures, early ambulation plus intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) until the patient can ambulate is recommended — pharmacologic prophylaxis is not automatic and should be decided based on your institution's VTE risk scoring. Individual and surgical VTE risk factors should have been thoroughly evaluated during the preoperative assessment. (For outpatient procedures in a low-risk patient, no thromboprophylaxis other than early ambulation is recommended.) This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence.

question: How soon after pelvic reconstructive surgery should I be pulling the Foley, and what do I need to check before she goes home?
reference: Remove the catheter as soon as feasible — preferably within 3–8 hours postoperatively rather than waiting until postoperative day 1. Early removal shortens length of stay and lowers infection risk, though it modestly increases the chance of recatheterization; it has been shown to be feasible, safe, and acceptable in women having major pelvic reconstructive surgery. If you do an early trial without catheter, monitor post-void residuals before discharge. A patient-reported subjective assessment of urinary force of stream correlates well with measured voided volume and may be used as an alternative to PVR checks. Keep in mind that transient postoperative voiding difficulty is common (after midurethral sling, only about 61% of patients passed the immediate postoperative voiding trial). Longer-term catheterization should be used only when there is a specific indication; if retention does occur, patient-driven self-discontinuation of a transurethral catheter at home is not inferior to office-based discontinuation and reduces patient encounters.

Trial without catheter/urinary drainage
Removal of the urinary catheter, preferably within 3–8 h,
shortens hospital length of stay and decreases infection risk
[108], but can modestly increase the risk of recatheterization
[109]. Early catheter removal is a feasible, safe, and acceptable alternative to the standard timing on postoperative day
1 in women undergoing major pelvic reconstructive surgical
procedures [110]. Longer term catheterization should only
be undertaken where there are specific indications [111].
Women who undergo FPMRS surgical procedures are at risk
of transient postoperative voiding difficulty. After midurethral
sling surgery, 61% of the patients passed their immediate postoperative voiding trial [112]. If early trial without catheter
is undertaken, the patient’s post-void residuals should be
monitored prior to discharge [113]. Patient-reported subjective assessment of the urinary force of stream correlates well
with the measured voided amount and may be an alternative
to post-void residual checks [114]. An alternative strategy
to inpatient or office-based trial without catheter is patientdriven self-discontinuation of a transurethral catheter. Studies suggest this is not inferior to office-based discontinuation
in the setting of postoperative urinary retention after pelvic
reconstructive surgery and results in fewer patient encounters
and improved patient experience [115].
Recommendation
Remove the urinary catheter as soon as is feasible with subsequent monitoring of post-void residual volumes.
Grade of recommendation: Strong
Quality of evidence: High

question: If labour looks slow but delay hasn't been formally confirmed yet, can we go ahead and start the oxytocin drip, and should we use a high starting dose to get things moving?
reference: No to both. Augmentation with intravenous oxytocin before delay in labour is confirmed is not recommended (very low quality evidence, weak recommendation). Once delay is confirmed, oxytocin alone is recommended for treatment, but a high starting and increment dosage regimen is not recommended for augmentation (very low quality evidence, weak recommendation) — so use a low starting dose with low increments. Amniotomy combined with oxytocin is recommended for confirmed delay, whereas amniotomy alone is not. Oral misoprostol should not be used for labour augmentation (strong recommendation).

question: My post-op hysterectomy patient is starting scheduled oxycodone — when do I need to start a bowel regimen and what do I begin with?
reference: Start the bowel management program with the very first opioid dose and continue it until the opioid is stopped. Begin with a stool softener such as docusate. If that isn't enough to maintain a normal bowel pattern, add a stimulant laxative such as sennoside (Senna), bisacodyl, or Milk of Magnesia — but stimulants shouldn't be used long-term because they can be habit-forming. Also encourage increased fluid and fiber intake and ambulation as appropriate, since opioids slow peristalsis and increase fluid reabsorption in the large intestine, producing hard, slow-moving stools.
source_text:
Constipation
Opioids slow peristalsis and cause increased reabsorption of fluid into the large intestine, resulting in slow-moving, hard stools. Nurses play an important role in preventing constipation for all clients taking opioids. A bowel management program should be initiated with the first dose and continued until the opioid is discontinued. A stool softener (such as docusate) is typically prescribed initially as part of the bowel management program. If needed, a stimulant laxative, such as sennoside (Senna), bisacodyl, or Milk of Magnesia may be added to maintain a normal bowel pattern. However, stimulants should not be taken long-term because they can be addictive. Clients taking opioids should be encouraged to increase fluid and fiber intake and ambulate, as appropriate. [12]
source_title: OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals - Comfort and Pain Chapter

question: What tidal volume and PEEP settings should we be using intraoperatively for our open abdominal gyn cases?
reference: Use a lung protective ventilation strategy: tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg with positive end expiratory pressure of 6–8 cm H2O. Studies in open abdominal surgery show this reduces pulmonary complications, and randomized trials suggest low tidal volumes, higher PEEP, and recruitment maneuvers may be protective intraoperatively.

question: My patient is still on her combined oral contraceptive pill and is going for surgery tomorrow — does she need VTE prophylaxis, and when should it start?
reference: Yes. Continued use of combined oral hormonal contraception up to the time of surgery is itself an indication for thromboprophylaxis, so she should be prescribed prophylaxis. For patients at risk of VTE, give either LMWH or unfractionated heparin, started pre-operatively (not waiting until after surgery), combined with mechanical methods such as graduated compression stockings and/or intermittent pneumatic compression, and continue it post-operatively. Ideally she should have been advised to switch to an alternative form of contraception before surgery; if she had been switching, the progestogens with the lowest thromboembolic risk are levonorgestrel, norethisterone, and norgestimate. This is a strong recommendation based on high-level evidence for combined oral hormonal contraception as a risk factor, with a strong recommendation for pre-operative prophylaxis.
source_text:
Changing from an oral to a transdermal estrogen preparation may reduce thromboembolic risk; of note, most patients taking HRT will
meet criteria to receive thromboprophylaxis.

Combined oral hormonal contraception. Combined oral hormonal
contraception is a risk factor for postoperative thromboembolism. The
risk of thromboembolism varies according to progesterone type, with
levonorgestrel, norethisterone, and norgestimate associated with the
lowest risk. Women should be encouraged to use an alternative form
of contraception preoperatively. Continued use of combined oral hormonal contraception is an indication for thromboprophylaxis [50,51].
Summary and recommendation:
Patients at risk of VTE should receive prophylaxis with either LMWH
or heparin, commenced preoperatively, combined with mechanical
methods, and continued post-operatively.
HRT is a relative risk factor for postoperative thromboembolism and
patients should be advised to consider stopping or switching to alternative preparations before surgery, taking into account the risks and beneﬁts. If HRT is continued, thromboprophylaxis should be considered.
Combined oral hormonal contraception is a risk factor for thromboembolism. Patients should change to another form of contraception
prior to surgery. If continued to the time of surgery, thromboprophylaxis
should be prescribed.

question: My post-caesarean patient was flagged as intermediate risk for VTE, but she's now on day 8 with a wound infection and still admitted — how long do I keep her on the LMWH?
reference: Intermediate-risk women normally get 10 days of postpartum thromboprophylaxis, but if there are additional risk factors that persist beyond 10 days postpartum — such as prolonged admission, wound infection or surgery in the puerperium — prophylaxis should be extended for up to 6 weeks, or until those additional risk factors are no longer present. High-risk women get the full 6 weeks. Also make sure a risk assessment is done at least once after delivery and before discharge, with arrangements for LMWH prescription and administration in the community (usually self-administered) if she is going home on it.
source_text:
7.5	 For how long should thromboprophylaxis be continued after delivery?

Risk assessment should be performed in each woman at least once following delivery and before
discharge and arrangements made for LMWH prescription and administration (usually by the
woman herself) in the community where necessary.

Thromboprophylaxis should be continued for 6 weeks in high-risk women and for 10 days in
intermediate-risk women (see Appendix I and Appendix IV).

In women who have additional persistent (lasting more than 10 days postpartum) risk factors,
such as prolonged admission, wound infection or surgery in the puerperium, thromboprophylaxis
should be extended for up to 6 weeks or until the additional risk factor/s is/are no longer present.

The prothrombotic changes of pregnancy do not revert completely to normal until several weeks
after delivery.

The time of greatest risk for VTE is the early puerperium and, although most VTE
occurs antenatally, the risk per day is greatest in the weeks immediately after delivery.8,9,17,52,53,94,105
For women at high risk of postpartum VTE, the recommended duration of thromboprophylaxis
is 6 weeks.

Although laboratory evidence from thromboelastography (TEG) suggests correction
of hypercoagulability by 4 weeks,106 clinical data from observational studies in Sweden,107 the
USA,8,105 Norway48 and the Netherlands10 suggest that the increased risk of VTE persists for 6
weeks postpartum, albeit less during weeks 5 and 6.

The triennial UK confidential enquiries
into maternal mortality between 1994 and 2005 suggest that the increased risk of fatal PE is
still present in weeks 5 and 6 (a total of 15 deaths compared to 21 in weeks 3 and 4) and all six
women who died from PE after caesarean section (2006–2008) died between 2 and 6 weeks
after delivery, whereas fatal events after that are very rare.3,4,101,102,108
There is little evidence to support recommendations regarding duration of postpartum
thromboprophylaxis in women at intermediate risk of VTE.
source_title: GTG37a - Reducing Risk of Thrombosis and Embolism during Pregnancy

question: The mesh implant we need was never sterilized and the surgeon wants me to flash it — can I do that, and when is flash sterilization actually appropriate?
reference: No — flash sterilization is not recommended for implantable devices because of the potential for serious infection. Flash sterilization is only intended for steam sterilization of patient care items needed for immediate use, such as reprocessing an instrument that was inadvertently dropped during the operation. It must not be used for convenience, to save time, or as a substitute for purchasing additional instrument sets, and it is not recommended as a routine sterilization method because of the lack of timely biologic indicators, no protective packaging after sterilization, risk of contamination in transport to the OR, and use of minimal cycle parameters (time, temperature, pressure). Even though some hospitals now keep flash units near the ORs and have biologic indicators that read out in 1 to 3 hours, flash sterilization should still be restricted to its intended emergency purpose until studies show comparable SSI risk to conventional sterilization.

have been published.212,314,320,321

Instrumentation defines flash sterilization as “the process

However,

Also, flash sterilization is not recommended for implantable devices(*)
because of the potential for serious infections.314,320,321
Flash sterilization is not recommended as a routine
sterilization method because of the lack of timely biologic
indicators to monitor performance, absence of protective

some of these concerns, many hospitals have placed

items.322-325 Nevertheless, flash sterilization should be
restricted to its intended purpose until studies are performed that can demonstrate comparability with conventional sterilization methods regarding risk of SSI.

question: We have carboprost in our fridge for the C-section — can we give it routinely with the oxytocin to prevent bleeding, or is it only for when she's already haemorrhaging?
reference: No — injectable prostaglandins like carboprost (or sulprostone) are not recommended for PPH prevention. Keep them for treatment of PPH, not routine prophylaxis. For prevention they don't improve the outcomes that matter most (severe PPH ≥1000 ml, need for blood transfusion, or need for additional uterotonics); the only benefit seen was a 39% risk reduction in PPH ≥500 ml versus placebo/no uterotonic. Against that, they cause significantly more vomiting and diarrhoea — diarrhoea has a number needed to harm of only 6, so roughly 1 in 6 women treated will be harmed. They're also costly and not available in all settings, so they're probably not cost-effective for prophylaxis. Note this applies to systemic injection; local/intrauterine injection at caesarean wasn't assessed, and this does not change their role in treating established PPH.
source_text:
In
these situations, another effective uterotonic can be considered instead of this
combination.

Injectable prostaglandins (carboprost or sulprostone) are not recommended for the
prevention of PPH. (Not Recommended)
Justification
"
" When used for PPH prevention, injectable prostaglandins (carboprost and
sulprostone) are not beneficial for substantive priority outcomes (severe PPH
[≥ 1000 ml], blood transfusion and the use of additional uterotonics) except PPH
(≥ 500 ml), for which they show a 39% risk reduction compared with placebo or
no uterotonic. However, they are associated with increased risk of vomiting and
diarrhoea. The associated risk of diarrhoea is particularly high with a number
needed to harm (NNH) of 6. Injectable prostaglandins are currently not available
in all settings and where they are available, the unit cost is high. While there is
no direct evidence on cost analysis regarding these uterotonics compared to no
uterotonics, they are probably not cost-effective because of lack of benefits for most
priority outcomes and substantial side-effects. As they are not widely available and
not routinely used for obstetric indications, their acceptability is not known and
the feasibility of implementation in clinical practice would vary according to local
availability. The potential costs of these uterotonics may prohibit access for women
in disadvantaged regions and thus would probably reduce equity.
"
" The narrative evidence supporting this recommendation and the corresponding SoF
table can be found in Web Annex 6.
Remarks
"
" Trials of systemic injectable prostaglandins for PPH prevention have used
carboprost or sulprostone.
"
" Local administration of injectable prostaglandins, such as intrauterine injections
during caesarean section, was not considered.
"
" This recommendation relates to the use of injectable prostaglandins for prevention
of PPH only; it does not relate to the treatment of PPH.

question: My pre-op patient was just started on an antihypertensive plus lifestyle changes — how often should she be getting her BP rechecked, and when can we stretch that out?
reference: Check BP monthly until her target BP is reached. Once her pressure is stable with 2 consecutive readings below target, the monitoring interval can be extended to every 3–6 months. Shorter intervals than monthly may be needed if she has severe hypertension, is not tolerating the drug therapy, or has target organ damage. Once she is stable and normotensive, she should also do self/home monitoring for one week every 3 months.

question: If a hysterectomy is running long, when do I need to give a second dose of the prophylactic antibiotic?
reference: Give a repeat dose of antibiotic prophylaxis when the operation lasts longer than the half-life of the antibiotic that was given. When planning prophylaxis you should take into account the timing, the pharmacokinetics (for example the serum half-life) and the necessary infusion time of the antibiotic. The initial dose is normally a single intravenous dose given on starting anaesthesia (given earlier if a tourniquet is used).

question: For a woman coming in with secondary PPH, what should we be checking before she's booked for a surgical evacuation, and who should be doing the procedure?
reference: Because ultrasound sensitivity and specificity for retained products of conception varies so widely, don't rely on the scan alone — the clinical picture must be taken into account before deciding on surgery, specifically the degree of bleeding and whether the cervical os is open. Ultrasound findings that suggest RPOC are an echogenic mass in the uterine cavity and an anteroposterior cavity diameter above the 90th centile on days 1–7 postpartum. Colour flow Doppler may be added (no strong evidence for it) but can help identify pseudoaneurysms and arteriovenous malformations, rare causes of secondary PPH. Surgical evacuation carries real morbidity — uterine perforation in about 1.5% and Asherman's syndrome — so it should be undertaken or supervised by an experienced clinician, and an appropriately trained clinician may perform the evacuation under direct ultrasound guidance.
source_text:
In a prospective observational
study187 of 79 women with secondary PPH, Mulic-Lutvica and Axelsson concluded that an echogenic mass
in the uterine cavity and an anteroposterior diameter of the cavity above the 90th centile (approximately

mm on days 1–7 postpartum) was associated with RPOC. Since the range of sensitivities and
speciﬁcities of ultrasound in the detection of RPOC is so wide, the clinical ﬁndings, including the degree of
bleeding and whether the cervical os is open, should be taken into account before the decision to
undertake surgery is made. It has been proposed that colour ﬂow Doppler imaging should be included in
the evaluation of the postpartum uterus, although, there is no strong evidence to support its use;178 its
use may facilitate the diagnosis of pseudoaneurysms and arteriovenous malformations, which are rare but
recognised causes of secondary PPH.188–190
Evidence
level 3
e135 of e149 ª 2016 Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Surgical evacuation of the uterus for RPOC is not without morbidity and can result in uterine
perforation (1.5%)180,191 and Asherman’s syndrome.192 It is, therefore, recommended that surgical
evacuation of retained placental tissue should be undertaken or supervised by an experienced clinician.
An appropriately trained clinician may consider performing uterine evacuation under direct ultrasound
guidance.
A 2002 Cochrane review (assessed as up-to-date in January 2008) addressed treatments for secondary
PPH.4 No trials were identiﬁed which met the review group’s inclusion criteria and no recommendations
were made regarding effective treatments. Uterotonics, such as misoprostol and ergometrine, have been
recommended in the management of secondary PPH, although evidence to support their use is
limited.178 Transcatheter arterial embolisation193 and balloon tamponade194 have been employed in cases
of secondary PPH with ongoing bleeding.

question: For a patient having an elective knee replacement, what dose of aspirin do we use for VTE prophylaxis and how many days does it run for?
reference: Aspirin 75 mg or 150 mg once daily for 14 days is one of the first-line options for people undergoing elective knee replacement whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk. The alternative first-line choices are LMWH for 14 days combined with anti-embolism stockings until discharge, or rivaroxaban (as per NICE TA170). If none of these can be used, consider apixaban (TA245) or dabigatran etexilate (TA157); if pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated, consider intermittent pneumatic compression continued until the person is mobile.

question: My post-op patient can't keep anything down and needs stronger pain relief — do I push for a PCA or an epidural, and does it matter what surgery she had?
reference: For patients who can't take an oral opioid, either PCA or an epidural can be offered, as there's no evidence favouring one mode over the other for most surgical patients. The exception is people having major or complex open-torso surgery, who may benefit from the early pain relief of a continuous epidural. When choosing between PCA and continuous epidural, take into account patient preference and whether she is able to use a PCA pump effectively. (Note also that oral opioids are recommended over IV where the patient can take oral medicines, since there's no difference in effectiveness and IV is more expensive; there's insufficient evidence to recommend spinal administration.)
source_text:
Opioids
There was no evidence showing a significant difference in effectiveness between oral and
intravenous opioids. Intravenous opioids are more expensive so the committee did not
recommend them for people who can take oral medicines.
For people who cannot take an oral opioid, the committee agreed that a choice of PCA
(patient-controlled analgesia) or epidural should be offered because there was no
evidence favouring either mode of administration for most people having surgery. An
exception is the group having major or complex open-torso surgery, who may benefit from
the early pain relief provided by a continuous epidural. The committee pointed out that
factors such as patient preference and ability to use a PCA pump effectively should be
taken into account when choosing between PCA and continuous epidural. The committee
looked at the possible benefits of spinal administration and agreed that there was
insufficient evidence to support a recommendation.

(Equivalent options are dalteparin 10 000 units daily or tinzaparin 9000 units daily, the latter also able to be split into two doses.) LMWH is the agent of choice postpartum — it is safe, easy to use, does not require monitoring, and no problems have been reported during breastfeeding.

question: If the placenta hasn't delivered on its own, what do we give and can I use ergometrine to help it along?
reference: Give an additional 10 IU of oxytocin IV or IM combined with controlled cord traction. Ergometrine is not recommended for a retained placenta because it can cause tetanic uterine contractions that may delay expulsion of the placenta. Prostaglandin E2 alpha (dinoprostone or sulprostone) is also not recommended in this situation. (Both are weak recommendations based on very-low-quality evidence.)

question: My post-op patient's temperature is normal but she just says she feels really unwell and her husband says she's not acting like herself — is that enough to start thinking sepsis?
reference: Yes. Sepsis can present non-specifically and without localising signs — for example someone just feeling very unwell — and the person may not have a high temperature, so a normal temperature does not rule it out. You should ask 'could this be sepsis?' in anyone with symptoms or signs of possible infection, and pay particular attention to concerns raised by the person and their family or carers, including changes from her usual behaviour. Assess her for a possible source of infection, factors that increase her risk of sepsis, and any indications of clinical concern such as new-onset abnormalities of behaviour, circulation or respiration. In a face-to-face setting, use a structured set of observations to stratify her risk. Take extra care with assessment if the history is difficult to obtain (for example English as a second language, or communication challenges associated with learning disabilities or autism).
source_text:
When to suspect sepsis

Think 'could this be sepsis?' if a person presents with symptoms or signs that
indicate possible infection. [2016]

Take into account that people with sepsis may have non-specific, non-localised
presentations, for example feeling very unwell, and may not have a high
temperature. [2016]

Pay particular attention to concerns expressed by the person and their family or

Assess people who might have sepsis with extra care if there is difficulty in taking

with communication challenges (such as those associated with learning

• possible source of infection (see the recommendations on finding and

• factors that increase risk of sepsis (see people who are most vulnerable to

question: On our oxytocin drips, what kind of pump-rate error should I be watching for when the fetal heart rate suddenly drops into the 70s?
reference: Check the infusion pump rate against what was actually ordered/expected — in this reported case the midwife found the pump running at 20 mu/min when she expected 12 mu/min, and the fetal heart rate was in the 70s when she rechecked the woman 30 minutes later. Attempts to bring the fetal heart rate back up failed and the woman needed an emergency caesarean section (the baby's Apgar scores were 3 at one minute, 6 at five minutes and 8 at ten minutes). The case is used to argue that routine use of a checklist-based protocol for increasing oxytocin would have prevented many of these system errors, so verifying the set rate against the intended rate at every oxytocin increase and at every check is the key safeguard.

question: If a mum refuses the routine uterotonic for preventing PPH after we've explained it, what do we do — and when should that conversation have happened?
reference: Her wishes must be respected. Application of the recommendations should be based on the woman's general condition and that of her baby, her wishes and preferences, and respect for her dignity and autonomy — even when her choices go against the care provider's advice. The counselling should happen in advance (antenatally/before the third stage), covering the need for a uterotonic to prevent PPH, the available uterotonic options, and their possible side-effects, delivered by a technically competent provider willing to engage in shared decision-making. Regardless of her decision, she should not be left unattended during the third stage of labour.
source_text:
Guiding principles
The GDG agreed that the following overarching principles are applicable to all
recommendations. These principles were consensus based, and were not directly derived
from a systematic process of evidence retrieval, synthesis and grading. They are intended to
underscore the importance of respect for women’s rights, choices and dignity as recipients
of care, and the need to maintain high ethical and safety standards in clinical practice. As
highlighted in the WHO framework for the quality of maternal and newborn health care (41),
experience of care is as important as clinical care provision for achieving the desired personcentred outcomes. It is critical for health care stakeholders to ensure that all pregnant
women receive relevant information from technically competent health care providers who
are sensitive to their needs, willing to engage in shared decision-making and respectful of
women’s choices and preferences (32).
These principles are not by themselves specific recommendations but are expected to guide
end-users in the process of adapting and implementing the guideline in a range of contexts
and settings.
Application of the recommendations should be based on consideration of the
general condition of the woman and her baby, her wishes and preferences, and
respect for her dignity and autonomy, even in situations where her choices go
against the advice of the care provider.
Women should be counselled in advance on the need to use a uterotonic to prevent
postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), the available uterotonic options, and their possible
side-effects.
Women should not be left unattended during the third stage of labour.
In order to ensure that a uterotonic is effective, it is essential that health systems
ensure that good-quality medicines are available wherever maternity services are
provided.
3. RECOMMENDATIONS AND SUPPORTING EVIDENCE
WHO RECOMMENDATIONS: UTEROTONICS FOR THE PREVENTION OF POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE

question: How many opioid tablets should we be sending our vaginal prolapse repair patients home with, and what should they be taking as their baseline pain control?
reference: Discharge with no more than 15 narcotic tablets — recent urogynecology data support ≤15 tablets to limit the consequences of excess opioids. Baseline pain control should be scheduled oral acetaminophen plus an NSAID (anti-inflammatory) after vulvar and vaginal surgery unless contraindicated; this is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. Opioids are reserved for breakthrough pain when acetaminophen and NSAIDs aren't sufficient, using the lowest dose for the shortest period. Educate the patient preoperatively about opioid risks and common side effects — constipation, nausea, vomiting, and somnolence. Also favor the oral route over IV for all postoperative medications in patients tolerating a diet, and use incisional local anesthetic injection to reduce the need for systemic medications.
source_text:
Postoperative multimodal medications
Postoperative pain control is an important factor affecting patient recovery and satisfaction. Poorly controlled
pain delays the return to normal bowel function, reduces
daily activity, and decreases ambulation [87]. Based on
high-level evidence, acetaminophen and NSAIDs should
be used postoperatively after vulvar and vaginal surgery
unless contraindicated [52, 65]. Many of the trials specific
to urogynecology utilize this and have shown reduction in
opioid utilization and postoperative pain as well as providing high patient satisfaction [59].
Opioids can be used for breakthrough pain when acetaminophen and NSAIDs are not sufficient. Preoperative
patient education should review the risks of opioid use and
stress using low doses for short periods of time if necessary.
Patients should also be educated on common side effects,
including constipation, nausea, vomiting, and somnolence.
The specific opiate chosen for treatment most likely has little impact on the incidence of pruritus and nausea/vomiting,
although greater differences between opioids were observed
regarding sedation and patient satisfaction, and selecting the
appropriate opioid may help to improve the overall pain control [88]. Recent data in urogynecology support discharge
with ≤ 15 tablets of narcotics to minimize potential consequences of excess opioids [56, 58–60].
A multimodal postoperative analgesic protocol successfully reduces opioid administration, both in the hospital and
after discharge. This can be accomplished using non-opioid
oral medications and incisional injection of local anesthetic
to decrease the need for systemic medications. In general,
oral administration of all postoperative medications in
patients who can tolerate a diet is preferable to the IV route.
Recommendation
Utilize preoperative multimodal medications and postoperative oral acetaminophen and anti-inflammatory drugs to
decrease postoperative opioid use.
Strength of recommendation: Strong
Quality of evidence: High
source_title: Joint report on terminology and clinical consensus: Enhanced Recovery After Urogynecologic Surgery (AUGS-IUGA)

question: For a delivery where mom is HIV-positive, how long should I wait before clamping the cord?
reference: Delay clamping for at least 1–3 minutes — late cord clamping is recommended even for women living with HIV or with unknown HIV status, because the proven benefits of a 1–3 minute delay outweigh the theoretical, unproven harms. Early cord clamping is generally contraindicated.
source_text:
Thus, the proven benefits of a 1 – 3 minute delay at least in
clamping the cord outweigh the theoretical, and unproven, harms.

Late cord clamping is recommended
even among women living with HIV or women with unknown HIV status.

However, the GDG considered that routine and frequent uterine

question: My hysterectomy patient is asking if she can have a drink this morning — how close to her surgery can she keep drinking clear fluids, and should I be offering her a carbohydrate drink too?
reference: She can drink water/clear fluids up until 2 hours before surgery — there is evidence this reduces postoperative headache, nausea and vomiting, and you should explain these benefits to her, as many patients wrongly believe all fluids must be avoided before surgery. Routine preoperative carbohydrate drinks are not recommended for most types of surgery, as the evidence only showed small reductions in postoperative thirst and headache with no substantial benefit for patient satisfaction or other side effects. However, carbohydrate drinks can be considered for people having major abdominal surgery, since these patients may need longer postoperative fasting periods and some evidence suggests a shorter hospital stay. There is no evidence on the best timing for giving carbohydrate drinks or clear fluids.
source_text:
Oral fluids
Some evidence showed that drinking water until 2 hours before surgery reduces
postoperative headaches, nausea and vomiting. The committee noted that many patients
are not aware of this and that there is a widespread belief that fluids should be avoided
before surgery. They agreed that there was sufficient evidence to recommend drinking
clear fluids before surgery, and that the benefits should be explained to patients.
There was not enough evidence to justify the routine use of preoperative carbohydrate
drinks for most types of surgery. A small amount of evidence suggested reductions in
postoperative thirst and headache in people given a carbohydrate drink before surgery.
However, the evidence did not show any substantial benefits in terms of patient
satisfaction or the occurrence of other side effects.
The committee noted that people having major abdominal surgery may need longer
postoperative fasting periods and therefore might benefit more than others from
preoperative carbohydrate drinks. Some evidence also suggested that length of hospital

question: What dose and route of ergometrine do we give to prevent postpartum haemorrhage, and who shouldn't get it?
reference: Give 200 µg of ergometrine/methylergometrine IM or IV. It is only recommended in settings where you can safely rule out hypertensive disorders beforehand, since it can cause hypertension — so it should be withheld in women with hypertensive disorders and used only where skilled health personnel are present. Expect possible side-effects including nausea, vomiting, hypertension, headache and abdominal pain. Compared with placebo or no uterotonic, it substantially reduces PPH of 500 ml or more and the need for additional uterotonics.
source_text:
The use of ergometrine/methylergometrine (200 µg, IM/IV) is recommended
for the prevention of PPH in contexts where hypertensive disorders can be safely
excluded prior to its use. (Context-specific recommendation)
Justification
"
" When used for PPH prevention, ergometrine/methylergometrine is associated
with substantial reductions in PPH (≥ 500 ml) and the use of additional uterotonics
when compared with placebo or no uterotonic. However, it is also associated with
side-effects including nausea, vomiting, hypertension, headache and abdominal
pain. There is no evidence of uncertainty about how much women value the health
outcomes associated with ergometrine/methylergometrine. Although ergometrine/
methylergometrine in the injectable form is widely available and generally
acceptable and feasible to use, its cost-effectiveness and impact on health equity
are not known because of the increased likelihood of side-effects, particularly
hypertension, which means that the presence of skilled health personnel is required
for its safe use.
source_title: WHO Recommendations for Uterotonics for Prevention of PPH

question: Our catheter policy lists some items as Category I and others as Category II — do I have to follow the Category II ones exactly, or is there room to individualize for my patient?
reference: Category II items are weak recommendations and are discretionary for the individual institution — they are not intended to be enforced. For these, different choices will be appropriate for different patients, and you should help each patient reach a management decision consistent with her or his values and preferences (most patients in that situation would want the recommended action, but many would not). Category I recommendations are strong: most patients should receive the recommended course of action, and they can be adopted as policy. You can also tell them apart by wording — Category I recommendations use active, certain language like "do" or "do not," while Category II recommendations use softer wording such as "consider," "is preferable," "is suggested," "is not suggested," or "is not recommended."
source_text:
Reviewing and Finalizing the Guideline

For patients: Most people in the patient’s situation would want the recommended course 
of action and only a small proportion would not; request discussion if the intervention is 
not offered.

For clinicians: Most patients should receive the recommended course of action.

For policymakers: The recommendation may be adopted as a policy. 
 
Category II recommendations are defined as weak recommendations with the following 
implications:

For patients: Most people in the patient’s situation would want the recommended course 
of action, but many would not.

For clinicians: Different choices will be appropriate for different patients, and clinicians 
must help each patient to arrive at a management decision consistent with her or his 
values and preferences.

For policymakers: Policy making will require substantial debate and involvement of many 
stakeholders. 
 
It should be noted that Category II recommendations are discretionary for the individual 
institution and are not intended to be enforced. 
 
The wording of each recommendation was carefully selected to reflect the recommendation's 
strength. In most cases, we used the active voice when writing Category I recommendations - 
the strong recommendations. Phrases like "do" or "do not" and verbs without auxiliaries or 
conditionals were used to convey certainty. We used a more passive voice when writing 
Category II recommendations - the weak recommendations. Words like "consider” and phrases 
like "is preferable,” “is suggested,” “is not suggested,” or “is not recommended” were chosen to 
reflect the lesser certainty of the Category II recommendations. Rather than a simple statement 
of fact, each recommendation is actionable, describing precisely a proposed action to take.

question: Which of our uterotonics can I keep at room temperature on the ward, and which ones have to stay in the fridge?
reference: Misoprostol tablets have no special storage requirements — just keep them in tightly closed containers protected from humidity — and a heat-stable formulation of carbetocin is available. Oxytocin, ergometrine and injectable prostaglandins all need refrigeration at 2–8 °C to prolong shelf life; oxytocin, ergometrine and injectable prostaglandins also need protection from light (carbetocin in its standard form likewise requires 2–8 °C storage). Combination products (oxytocin plus ergometrine, misoprostol plus oxytocin) follow the requirements of their individual components.

question: My pre-op patient has a large upper arm and I only have a standard cuff on the cart — how much will that skew her pressure, and how do I know if a cuff is the right size?
reference: A cuff that's too small will significantly overestimate blood pressure — for every 5 cm increase in arm circumference with an undersized cuff, systolic readings rise about 2–5 mmHg and diastolic about 1–3 mmHg. Under-cuffing a large arm is the single biggest source of error in clinic blood pressure measurement, accounting for 84% of all errors. To size correctly, the cuff bladder should encircle 80–100% of the arm circumference. Be aware of the opposite problem too: a cuff that is too large will underestimate the blood pressure. Also make sure the aneroid or electronic monitor has been calibrated regularly, since monitors can drift from a zero starting point with use and over-inflation, giving inaccurate readings.
source_text:
Discussion of Evidence
The most frequent error in the clinic-based blood pressure assessment is the utilization of an inappropriate
blood pressure cuff, with under-cuffing a large arm accounting for 84% of all errors (See Table 1) (CHEP, 2004;
Graves, Bailey, & Sheps, 2003). When the cuff is correctly sized, the bladder of the cuff should encircle 80 -100%
of the arm. Utilizing a blood pressure cuff that is too small may lead to a significant overestimation of blood
pressure. Fonseca-Reyes et al. (2003) found that when a cuff is too small, for every 5 cm increase in arm
circumference, there was a 2-5 mmHg increase in systolic blood pressure and a 1-3 mmHg increase in diastolic
blood pressure. In contrast, use of a cuff that is too large leads to an underestimation of blood pressure.
Regular calibration of aneroid and electronic blood pressure monitors is required in order to ensure that
blood pressure measurements begin from a starting point of zero. Monitors can drift from a zero starting
point due to use and over inflation, resulting in potentially inaccurate blood pressure readings. Monitors

question: We're prepping a patient with alcohol-based antiseptic and the surgeon plans to use diathermy — what precautions do I need to take before they start?
reference: Because alcohol-based skin preparations are flammable and can cause burns with diathermy: let the prep dry by evaporation before draping or starting, avoid pooling of the solution, remove any soaked materials, drapes or gowns before diathermy is used, don't use excessive quantities of alcohol-based antiseptic, and make sure no excess product is present before applying an occlusive dressing.
source_text:
Page 22 of

There was little evidence to support the use of povidone-iodine, but based on their clinical
experience the committee agreed that it should be an option when chlorhexidine is
contraindicated, for example, in people with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine.
There was no evidence on the use of skin antiseptics in babies. However, the committee
were aware of risks, such as burns, associated with their use in this population, and
wished to highlight this. The committee noted that the MHRA has published MHRA advice
on the use of chlorhexidine for skin disinfection in premature babies.
The committee also discussed that some operative procedures may require diathermy.
This means that precautions must be taken when using alcohol-based antiseptic solutions
because they are flammable and can result in burns. Along with using evaporation to dry
antiseptic skin preparations and avoiding pooling, the committee also agreed that soaked
materials, drapes or gowns should be removed before diathermy, excessive quantities of
alcohol antiseptics should not be used and no excess product should be present before
applying an occlusive dressing.
The committee agreed that further research is needed to establish the effectiveness of
different concentrations of chlorhexidine in reducing the risk of surgical site infections.
Therefore, the committee made a recommendation for research on antiseptic skin
preparation to examine this further.
source_title: Surgical Site Infections Prevention and Treatment (NG125)
