question: When I'm arguing for switching our unit to alcohol-based hand rub, how many hand hygiene opportunities per hour should I expect my ICU nurses to have, and does that cost more than the infections we'd prevent?
reference: Expect about 20 hand-hygiene opportunities per hour of patient care for nurses in intensive-care units, compared with about 8 per hour for nurses on pediatric wards. Observational studies also found HCWs washed their hands anywhere from an average of 5 times per shift up to 30 times per shift, with some nurses doing so under 100 times per shift. On cost: a promotion program including increased hand-rub use, poster production, and staff time was estimated at $57,000 or less per year (about $1.42 per patient admitted), with the extra alcohol-based hand-rub solution averaging $6.07 per 100 patient-days. Using a conservative estimate of $2,100 saved per infection averted — and crediting only 25% of the observed infection-rate reduction to better hand hygiene — the program was substantially cost-effective. Another study showed roughly $17,000 saved in 7 months from reduced vancomycin use after MRSA incidence fell. So preventing even a limited number of additional health-care–associated infections per year yields savings exceeding the incremental cost of better or more acceptable hand-hygiene products.
source_text:
Two studies provided certain quantitative estimates of the benefit of hand-hygiene–
promotion programs (72,74).

One study demonstrated a cost
saving of approximately $17,000 resulting from reduced use
of vancomycin after the observed decrease in MRSA incidence
in a 7-month period (72).

In another study that examined
both direct costs associated with the hand-hygiene promotion
program (increased use of hand-rub solution and poster
production) and indirect costs associated with health-care–
personnel time (74), costs of the program were an estimated
$57,000 or less per year (an average of $1.42 per patient
admitted).

Supplementary costs associated with the increased
use of alcohol-based hand-rub solution averaged $6.07 per
100 patient-days.

Based on conservative estimates of $2,100
saved per infection averted and on the assumption that only
25% of the observed reduction in the infection rate was associated with improved hand-hygiene practice, the program was
substantially cost-effective.

Thus, hospital administrators must
consider that by purchasing more effective or more acceptable
hand-hygiene products to improve hand-hygiene practices, they
will avoid the occurrence of nosocomial infections; preventing
only a limited number of additional health-care–associated
infections per year will lead to savings that will exceed any
incremental costs of improved hand-hygiene products.

Hand-Hygiene Practices Among HCWs
In observational studies conducted in hospitals, HCWs
washed their hands an average of five times per shift to as
many as 30 times per shift (Table 6) (17,61,90,98,274,288);
certain nurses washed their hands <100 times per shift (90).

Hospitalwide surveillance of hand hygiene reveals that the
average number of handwashing opportunities varies markedly between hospital wards.

For example, nurses in pediatric
wards had an average of eight opportunities for hand hygiene
per hour of patient care compared with an average of 20 for
nurses in intensive-care units (11).

question: If I'm sending a patient home and they deteriorate later, up to what time can they still get hold of their own GP practice before out-of-hours takes over?
reference: Standard GP hours are Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 18:30. Outside those hours, anyone needing urgent primary care is triaged and treated by an out-of-hours GP provider, so they will usually be seen by a primary care clinician who does not know them or their history and who may not have access to their complete clinical records. So advise patients that contact with their usual practice team is only assured within weekday hours up to 18:30; after that, and at weekends, they will go through the out-of-hours service (often at a more distant centre than their own surgery). Extended weekday and weekend access to the usual primary care team is being explored because it might reduce unscheduled use of secondary care emergency services and emergency admissions, but note that many current extended-access schemes are for pre-booked appointments only and do not provide emergency care.
source_text:
Why this is important
Continuity of care improves patient experience, aids clinical decision-making and could
reduce hospital admissions. GPs' knowledge of patients enhances trust and promotes
patient-centred care, especially when dealing with complex conditions. Currently, outside
of standard GP hours (Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 18:30), people who need urgent primary
care are triaged and treated by an out-of-hours GP provider and will usually be seen by a
primary care clinician who is not familiar with them or their history, and who might not
have access to their complete clinical records. Extended weekday and weekend access to
their usual primary care team might reduce people's unscheduled use of secondary care
emergency services. It might also increase opportunities to prevent exacerbations of
chronic disease and thus reduce emergency hospital admissions. There is also likely to be
less movement to secondary care if there is greater access to usual primary care because
GP surgeries are often more conveniently located than more distant out-of-hours centres.
Many extended access schemes currently in operation for general practice are for
prebooked appointments only and do not provide emergency care. The focus of this
research recommendation is on extending opening hours of practices for the full spectrum
of GPs' clinical work.

question: If our surgical scrub sink only has a PCMX product, is that as good as chlorhexidine for scrubbing in?
reference: Not reliably. One report found 3% PCMX had immediate and residual activity comparable to 4% chlorhexidine gluconate, but two other studies found PCMX inferior to both chlorhexidine gluconate and povidone-iodine. Overall, PCMX is not as rapidly active as chlorhexidine gluconate or iodophors, and its residual activity is less pronounced than chlorhexidine's. With repeated use (18 times/day for 5 consecutive days) it also showed less cumulative activity than chlorhexidine gluconate. The differences among studies are likely due to the PCMX concentration used (products range from 0.3% to 3.75%) and other formulation factors such as the presence or absence of EDTA. Note that in 1994 the FDA tentatively classified PCMX as Category IIISE — insufficient data to classify it as safe and effective — with evaluation ongoing. So if chlorhexidine gluconate or an iodophor scrub is available, prefer it for surgical scrubbing.

studies in which antiseptics were applied to abdominal skin,
PCMX had the weakest immediate and residual activity of
any of the agents studied (183).

However, when 30-second
handwashes were performed using 0.6% PCMX, 2%
chlorhexidine gluconate, or 0.3% triclosan, the immediate
effect of PCMX was similar to that of the other agents.

When
used 18 times per day for 5 consecutive days, PCMX had less
cumulative activity than did chlorhexidine gluconate (184).

When PCMX was used as a surgical scrub, one report indicated that 3% PCMX had immediate and residual activity
comparable to 4% chlorhexidine gluconate (185), whereas two
other studies demonstrated that the immediate and residual
activity of PCMX was inferior to both chlorhexidine gluconate and povidone-iodine (176,186).

The disparity between
published studies may be associated with the various concentrations of PCMX included in the preparations evaluated and
with other aspects of the formulations tested, including the
presence or absence of EDTA (7,182).

PCMX is not as rapidly active as chlorhexidine gluconate or iodophors, and its
residual activity is less pronounced than that observed with
chlorhexidine gluconate (7,182).

In 1994, FDA TFM tentatively classified PCMX as a Category IIISE active agent (i.e.,
insufficient data are available to classify this agent as safe and
effective) (19).

Further evaluation of this agent by the FDA is
ongoing.

The antimicrobial activity of PCMX is minimally affected
by the presence of organic matter, but it is neutralized by nonionic surfactants.

PCMX, which is absorbed through the skin
(7,182), is usually well-tolerated, and allergic reactions associated with its use are uncommon.

PCMX is available in concentrations of 0.3%–3.75%.

In-use contamination of a
PCMX-containing preparation has been reported (187).

Hexachlorophene
Hexachlorophene is a bisphenol composed of two phenolic
groups and three chlorine moieties.

question: Is P6 acupressure wristbands actually worth recommending for my patients with pregnancy nausea, and how strong is the evidence?
reference: The evidence for P6 acupressure is weak and inconsistent, so it can't be relied on. Across single small randomized trials: one trial (50 vs 50) found nausea severity on a 10 cm VAS was 1.7 points lower after 4 days of treatment (95% CI 0.99 to 2.41 lower) — low certainty; but other trials showed no benefit: no improvement in symptom intensity 28.3% vs 36.4% (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.44–1.39, i.e. 80 fewer per 1000, from 204 fewer to 142 more) — low certainty; mean nausea score after day 3 was 0.1 higher (1.49 lower to 1.69 higher) — low certainty; mean nausea score for days 1–3 was 0.39 higher (0.8 lower to 1.58 higher) — very low certainty; mean total Rhodes Index days 1–3 was 1.17 higher (1.52 lower to 3.86 higher) — very low certainty; and Rhodes Index on day 3 was 1.48 lower (4.1 lower to 1.14 higher) — very low certainty. All estimates came from single trials with very serious imprecision and mostly serious risk of bias, giving low to very low certainty overall.

question: If an OG or NG tube was placed during a robotic hysterectomy to decompress the stomach, when do we pull it — can it stay for the first few hours on the floor?
reference: No — it should come out before the patient is woken up. Gastric decompression with an oro- or nasogastric tube is acceptable during laparoscopic or robotic surgery to reduce the risk of gastric injury from trochar or Veress needle insertion, but the tube should be removed at extubation, i.e., before reversal of anesthesia. Routine nasogastric intubation otherwise should be avoided (high-level evidence, strong recommendation), since it increases postoperative pneumonia risk (6% vs 3%), doesn't reduce wound dehiscence or anastomotic leak, and about 88% of patients with a tube report moderate to severe discomfort. Early feeding instead is associated with faster return of flatus/stool and shorter length of stay, with only about 10% needing an NG tube later for sub-occlusive symptoms.
source_text:
Recommendation grade:
Strong.

Nasogastric intubation
Meta-analyses have concluded that nasogastric intubation increases
the risk of postoperative pneumonia (6% vs. 3%) after elective abdominal surgery. Moreover, nasogastric decompression does not reduce the
risk of wound dehiscence or intestinal leaks [92]. In a prospective randomized trial comparing early feeding to nasogastric decompression
after major open gynecologic oncology surgery, the authors found no
signiﬁcant difference in postoperative nausea and vomiting between
318
the two groups. Only 10% of the early feeding arm required nasogastric
tube insertion because of sub-occlusive symptoms. Conversely, 88% of
patients who had a nasogastric tube experienced moderate to severe
discomfort. Time to passage of ﬂatus or stools and length of hospital
stay was signiﬁcantly shorter in the early diet group [93].
One exception where gastric decompression by oro- or nasogastric
intubation may be of beneﬁt is during laparoscopic or robotic surgery,
whereby decompression may be used to reduce risk of gastric perforation by trochar or Veress needle insertion. The tube, however, should
be removed at extubation.
Summary and recommendation:
Routine nasogastric intubation should be avoided. Nasogastric
tubes inserted during surgery should be removed before reversal of
anesthesia.
Evidence level:
High.
Recommendation grade:
Strong.

question: If a pregnant patient on iron supplements asks me whether the iron is causing her heartburn or vomiting, what can I tell her about how common those side effects actually are?
reference: Pooled randomized trial data show these GI complaints are common in pregnancy regardless of iron. Heartburn (3 trials): 23.6% (166/702) with iron-containing supplements vs 20% (124/621) without iron or on placebo — RR 1.19 (95% CI 0.86-1.66), about 38 more per 1000 (28 fewer to 132 more), moderate-certainty evidence, so no clear increase. Vomiting (4 trials): 7% (52/747) with iron vs 6.8% (44/645) without — RR 0.88 (0.59-1.3), about 8 fewer per 1000 (28 fewer to 20 more), moderate certainty. So you can reassure her that iron has not been shown to significantly increase either heartburn or vomiting; the confidence intervals cross no effect. Maternal satisfaction was also similar (87.5% vs 96%, RR 0.91, 0.77-1.08, moderate certainty).

question: For a patient admitted acutely overnight, how quickly do we need to get a consultant to review them, and does that review need repeating?
reference: Early consultant review should happen after admission to hospital — with consultant review within 12 hours of admission being one of the specified topic areas — and thereafter there should be daily consultant review while the patient is in hospital. These are key aspects of care reaffirmed from the NHS seven day services clinical standards, alongside multidisciplinary care, structured handovers and liaison mental health services.
source_text:
Context
NICE's service guidance on emergency and acute medical care supports the next steps in
the NHS five year forward view. It presents a survey of the best available evidence on a
range of questions across the emergency and acute care pathway, which reaffirms key
aspects of care articulated in the NHS seven day services clinical standards, including the
role of early consultant review after admission to hospital, daily consultant review in
hospital, multidisciplinary care, structured handovers and liaison mental health services.
This guideline covers service organisation and delivery in the following topic areas referred
to NICE by the Department of Health in 2012:
• urgent and emergency care
• out-of-hours care
• 7-day services
• consultant review within 12 hours of admission
• acute medical admissions within the first 48 hours
• discharge planning to reduce readmissions.
Hospitals have found it increasingly challenging to maintain the flow of patients through
from admission to discharge. The guideline committee considered interventions that avoid
hospital admission and facilitate earlier discharge, when this can be achieved safely and
without an increase in readmissions.
A comprehensive review of the evidence was conducted on sometimes complex
interventions within this field. The guideline committee also took account of national
initiatives such as the Keogh urgent and emergency care review that began in
January 2013.
The guideline contains recommendations for practice and for research. Commissioners of
services should take note of both types of recommendation when planning services.
Commissioners are encouraged to read the evidence reviews, particularly the sections
headed 'Recommendations and link to evidence', for more details about the interventions,

question: My pre-op patient keeps saying she doesn't want to keep taking her blood pressure pills after surgery — what should I be drawing out of her to figure out if she'll actually stay on them?
reference: Explore her beliefs about the medication — specifically how strongly she believes it is necessary versus what concerns she has about taking it. Patients are active decision-makers, and adherence is more likely when belief in the medication's necessity outweighs concerns about taking it. Also assess her knowledge and beliefs about her hypertension, her motivation to manage it, her confidence (self-efficacy) that she can carry out the management behaviours, and her expectations about treatment outcomes and the consequences of not adhering — these all interact to influence adherence. Ask her to voice her wishes and expectations explicitly: patients whose expectations go unmet are less satisfied with care, less likely to follow treatment and healthcare advice, and report poorer health-related outcomes and greater healthcare utilization than those whose expectations are met.
source_text:
Discussion of Evidence
Clients’ knowledge and beliefs about their illness, motivation to manage it, confidence (self-efficacy) in
their ability to engage in illness-management behaviours, expectations regarding the outcome of
treatment and the consequences of poor adherence, all interact in ways not yet fully understood to
influence adherence behaviour (WHO, 2003).
Expectations are defined as verbal or explicit communication of clients’ wishes and desires to their health
provider. Clients whose expectations are unmet are less likely to be satisfied with their care, and are less
likely to adhere to recommended treatment and healthcare advice. They report poorer health-related
outcomes and increased healthcare utilization than those whose expectations are met (Ogedegbe, Mancuso &
Allegrante, 2004). Client’s beliefs about treatment influence treatment preference, adherence, and outcomes
(Horne & Weinman, 1999). Horne and Weinman’s (1999) cross-sectional study examined clients’ personal
beliefs about the necessity of their prescribed medication and their concerns about taking it in order to
assess relations between beliefs and adherence. His findings support the view that clients should be
regarded as active decision-makers who will be more motivated to use their medication as instructed if
their belief in its necessity outweighs their concerns about taking it (Horne, 1999).

question: For a pregnant patient starting treatment-dose enoxaparin for a VTE, which weight do I use to calculate the dose, and is it once or twice daily?
reference: Dose LMWH according to the woman's booking or early pregnancy weight — not her current weight later in pregnancy. There is insufficient evidence to say whether the total dose should be given once daily or split into two divided doses, so follow your local guideline, which should clearly specify the LMWH dosage used. For reference, in nonpregnant patients therapeutic doses are enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg once daily, dalteparin 10 000–18 000 units once daily depending on body weight, and tinzaparin 175 units/kg once daily. Earlier editions of this guidance (2001 and 2007) recommended twice-daily regimens in pregnancy (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily; dalteparin 100 units/kg twice daily), based on anti-Xa activity and limited safety/efficacy data for once-daily dosing, because pregnancy alters LMWH pharmacokinetics through changes in volume of distribution and renal glomerular filtration rate.
source_text:
6.2	 What is the therapeutic dose of LMWH in pregnancy?
LMWH should be given in doses titrated against the woman’s booking or early pregnancy weight.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend whether the dose of LMWH should be given once daily
or in two divided doses.
There should be clear local guidelines for the dosage of LMWH to be used.
In nonpregnant patients, the recommended therapeutic doses of LMWH vary according to
the manufacturer (enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg once daily; dalteparin 10 000–18 000 units once
daily depending on body weight; tinzaparin 175 units/kg once daily). During pregnancy,
changes in volume of distribution and renal glomerular filtration rate result in alterations
in the pharmacokinetics of LMWHs.95–99 Previous editions of this guideline (2001 and 2007)

question: My post-op patient has a moderate risk NEWS2 score and a raised lactate but I'm not sure whether that's enough to start IV fluids — what should I be basing that call on?
reference: Use the NEWS2 score to categorise risk rather than relying on any single hypoperfusion marker. For patients at high risk, give intravenous fluids unless contraindicated (for example in cardiac or renal failure). For moderate risk, indicators of organ hypoperfusion such as a high lactate or acute kidney injury can be used as additional markers to support the decision — but a moderate risk score on its own, without other hypoperfusion indicators, is still sufficient evidence of illness for clinicians to consider giving fluids, depending on the individual assessment. Lactate, mottled skin and capillary refill time should not be used in isolation to guide treatment: lactate can be raised for many reasons, and assessment of mottled skin is subjective and must be interpreted with caution in people with brown or black skin.
source_text:
Why the committee made the recommendations
When to give fluids
The committee reviewed evidence on indicators of hypoperfusion, to see if these could be
used to guide intravenous fluid administration.

The evidence was all low or very low
certainty.

There was a high risk of bias, and the evidence did not cover all of the indicators
of hypoperfusion specified in the review protocol.

Evidence was available for lactate, mottled skin and capillary refill time, but the committee
agreed that these could not be used to guide treatment decisions in isolation.

Lactate
could be high for numerous reasons.

Assessments of mottled skin can be quite subjective
and needs to be interpreted with caution in people with brown or black skin.

The
committee agreed that the person's risk should be categorised using their NEWS2 score.
• People assessed as being at high risk should be given intravenous fluids, unless giving
fluids is contraindicated (for example in people with cardiac or renal failure).
• For people at moderate risk, the committee agreed that indicators of organ
hypoperfusion such as a high lactate or acute kidney injury could be used as
additional markers to help decision making.

However, the committee also agreed that
dependent on the assessment of the individual a moderate risk score without other
indicators of hypoperfusion was sufficient evidence of illness for clinicians to consider
giving fluids.

• there was a high risk of bias
• some of the evidence was indirect: many of the studies looked at people in intensive
care units, and this group is not covered by the guideline
• some of the populations in the studies were small.

question: My ovarian cancer patient is really anxious in pre-op and asking for something to calm her down — can I give a sedative before she goes back?
reference: Routine preoperative sedatives should be avoided, and long-acting sedatives in particular should not be given within 12 hours of surgery because they impair immediate postoperative recovery. Psychomotor impairment has been seen up to 4 hours after surgery even with short-acting oral anxiolytics, which can interfere with the patient's ability to ambulate, eat and drink. A short-acting anxiolytic may be appropriate on a case-by-case basis for severe preoperative anxiety, so discuss it with anesthesia rather than giving it routinely.
source_text:
Carbohydrate loading: Strong.

Preanesthetic medication
Preoperative medications are widely used in major gynecological
surgery to decrease anxiety. However, routine administration of longacting sedatives within 12 h of surgery should be avoided due to its
effects on immediate postoperative recovery [37]. In 2009, a Cochrane
review of short-acting oral anxiolytics for outpatient surgery concluded
that patients were successfully discharged. However, an impairment in
psychomotor function was observed in some studies up to 4 h postoperatively, which may negatively inﬂuence the patient's ability to ambulate, eat and drink [37]. The use of short acting anxiolytics to address
severe preoperative anxiety may be appropriate on a case by case basis.
Summary and recommendation:
Routine administration of sedatives to reduce anxiety preoperatively
should be avoided in order to hasten postoperative recovery.
Evidence level:
Low.
Recommendation grade:
Strong.

Thromboembolism prophylaxis
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a major risk in gynecologic oncology patients with rates as high as 8% in endometrial cancer [38]
and 38% in ovarian cancer [39]. An analysis from the Million Women
study showed an increased risk of VTE 12 weeks postoperatively, with
a risk of 1/85 for oncologic surgery and 1/365 for gynecologic surgery
[40]. Patients undergoing oncologic surgery were at over 90 times the
risk of VTE in the ﬁrst 6 weeks. All gynecologic oncology patients with
major surgery N30 min should receive VTE prophylaxis with either
low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) or heparin [41]. Prophylaxis
should be commenced preoperatively, combined with mechanical
methods, and continued post-operatively [42].
source_title: Guidelines for pre- and intra-operative care in gynecologic/oncology surgery: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations - Part I

question: How long before the skin incision should I give the prophylactic antibiotic, and when do we have to stop it after surgery?
reference: Give the prophylactic antibiotic within the 60 minutes before incision, and stop prophylaxis within 24 hours of the end of the operation — this is what an expert panel convened by the US Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services recommended. Continuing prophylaxis longer is not advised, since studies show more resistant bacteria are recovered from patients who receive prophylaxis for prolonged periods.
source_text:
Other studies show that more resistant
bacteria are recovered from patients who receive prophylaxis for a long
time (252).

An expert panel assembled by the United States Center
for Medicare and Medicaid Services recommended that prophylactic
antibiotics be initiated during the 60 minutes before incision and
stopped within 24 hours of the end of the operation (14).

Many different antibiotics have been shown to reduce the incidence of
surgical-site infections.

The primary consideration is that the antibiotic
used is active against the spectrum of bacteria commonly encountered
during the procedure and recovered from surgical site infections.

There
is general agreement that the antibiotic agents used for prophylaxis
should be different from those usually chosen for first-line treatment
of established infections, although this supposition has never been
studied systematically.

A number of societies and organizations,
including the Surgical Infection Society (218), the Infectious Diseases
Society of America (217), the American Society of Hospital Pharmacists
(253), Johns Hopkins University (254), the Medical Letter (255) and
the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (256), have published
well-researched guidelines and recommendations for surgical antibiotic
prophylaxis.

Table II.6.9 gives recommendations published by various professional
societies and organizations.

Usually, a single first-generation
cephalosporin for operations not expected to encounter anaerobes
or a single second-generation cephalosporin with anaerobic activity
for anaerobic operations based on local susceptibility patterns is
sufficient.

For clean operations on the skin and subcutaneous tissues
that do not involve any portion of the gastrointestinal tract, a semisynthetic penicillin resistant to penicillinases, such as oxacillin or
cloxacillin, is probably effective, although there are limited published
data to support this recommendation.
source_title: Safe Surgery Saves Lives: The Second Global Patient Safety Challenge

question: For our morning gyn-onc cases, how long before anesthesia can patients have a light meal versus their carbohydrate drink, and does that change if they have gastroparesis?
reference: Encourage a light meal up until 6 hours before initiation of anesthesia, and clear fluids — including oral carbohydrate drinks — up until 2 hours before anesthesia. Oral carbohydrates should be used routinely since they reduce insulin resistance and improve well-being (extrapolated from non-gynecologic surgery data). However, patients with documented delayed gastric emptying or GI motility disorders should not receive oral fluids/carbohydrates on this schedule — they should fast overnight, or at least 8 hours before surgery. Oral carbohydrates are also not appropriate for emergency surgery patients, and there are insufficient data to make a recommendation in diabetic patients.
source_text:
In one randomized placebo-controlled trial, less 
post-operative nausea and vomiting, metoclopramide consumption, 
and improved patient satisfaction was noted 24 hours after abdominal myomectomy.44
A Cochrane review of abdominal, orthopedic, and cardiac surgery 
studies reported that preoperative carbohydrate treatment was 
associated with reduced post-operative insulin resistance, 
enhanced return of bowel function, and shorter hospital stay 
with no effect on post-operative complication rates.45 Large 
cohort studies in patients undergoing major colorectal surgery have 
shown that oral carbohydrates as part of an ERAS protocol significantly improved clinical outcome.46 47
Oral fluids including oral carbohydrates may not be administered 
safely in patients with documented delayed gastric emptying or 
gastrointestinal motility disorders as well as in patients undergoing 
emergency surgery.

Although obese48 and diabetic49 patients have 
been included in recent studies of oral carbohydrates and no issues 
with regard to safety have been reported, studies are insufficient to 
allow a general recommendation.

Summary and Recommendation:
Patients should be encouraged to eat a light meal up until 6 
hours, and consume clear fluids including oral carbohydrate 
drinks up until 2 hours, before initiation of anesthesia.

Patients 
with delayed gastric emptying should fast overnight or 8 hours 
before surgery.

Oral carbohydrates reduce insulin resistance and 
improve well-being and should be used routinely (extrapolated 
from non-gynecological surgery data).

There are insufficient data 
to make recommendations in diabetic patients.
source_title: Guidelines for perioperative care in gynecologic/oncology: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations — 2019 update

question: My post-op patient is still in a lot of pain on IV morphine alone — what dose of IV ketamine can we add on?
reference: If an IV opioid alone isn't giving adequate pain relief (or the patient is opioid sensitive with abnormal pain sensitivity), consider a single dose of IV ketamine at 0.25 mg/kg to 1 mg/kg. Ketamine has an additive analgesic effect and adding it to an IV opioid can reduce both pain and opioid consumption.
source_text:
Intravenous ketamine
There was evidence showing that adding intravenous ketamine to an intravenous opioid
can reduce both pain and opioid consumption. The committee noted that ketamine has an
additive analgesic effect. They agreed, based on their experience, that intravenous
ketamine is helpful if an intravenous opioid alone does not provide adequate pain relief, or
if the person is opioid sensitive (abnormal pain sensitivity). Based on the evidence and
their experience, the committee agreed that a single dose of 0.25 mg/kg to 1 mg/kg should
be considered in these situations.
source_title: Perioperative Care in Adults (NG180)

question: When is it actually appropriate to use vancomycin for our surgical prophylaxis instead of a cephalosporin, and who needs to sign off on that?
reference: Vancomycin is not recommended for routine surgical prophylaxis for any type of operation. It may be the prophylactic agent of choice only in specific circumstances — for example, when a cluster of MRSA mediastinitis or incisional SSI caused by methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci has been identified. There is no scientifically defined threshold that justifies its use; the decision must take into account local rates of MRSA isolates, SSI rates for the particular operation, and a review of infection prevention practices for compliance, and it should be made through consultation between the surgeons and infectious disease experts. An effective SSI surveillance program must also be in place, with careful, timely culturing of SSI isolates to identify species and determine susceptibility to prophylactic agents.

dosages, antimicrobial spectra and properties, and other
practical clinical information.

The routine use of vancomycin in AMP is not recommended for any kind of operation.242,266,283,292 However, vancomycin may be the AMP agent of choice in certain clinical
circumstances, such as when a cluster of MRSA mediastinitis or incisional SSI due to methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci has been detected.

A threshold
has not been scientifically defined that can support the
decision to use vancomycin in AMP.

The decision should
involve consideration of local frequencies of MRSA isolates,
SSI rates for particular operations, review of infection prevention practices for compliance, and consultation between
surgeons and infectious disease experts.

An effective SSI
surveillance program must be operational, with careful and
timely culturing of SSI isolates to determine species and
AMP agent susceptibilities.80
Agents most commonly used for AMP (i.e.,
cephalosporins) exhibit time-dependent bactericidal action.

question: If I use a 3% hexachlorophene scrub regularly, how long does its antibacterial effect last and is there any absorption risk I should worry about?
reference: Hexachlorophene has residual activity for several hours after use, and with repeated applications it gradually reduces bacterial counts on the hands (a cumulative effect) — though a single handwash or surgical scrub gives only modest efficacy. With repeated use of 3% preparations the drug is absorbed through the skin: personnel regularly handwashing with 3% hexachlorophene (and infants bathed with it) have blood levels of 0.1–0.6 ppm. Neurotoxicity (vacuolar degeneration) occurred in some infants bathed with it in the early 1970s, prompting a 1972 FDA warning against routine infant bathing, and current guidelines still recommend against routine hexachlorophene bathing of neonates because of potential neurotoxicity. Its spectrum is mainly against S. aureus, with relatively weak activity against gram-negative bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria.
source_text:
aureus and relatively weak activity against gram-negative
bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria (7).
Studies of hexachlorophene as a hygienic handwash and
surgical scrub demonstrated only modest efficacy after a single
handwash (53,143,188). Hexachlorophene has residual activity for several hours after use and gradually reduces bacterial
counts on hands after multiple uses (i.e., it has a cumulative
effect) (1,101,188,189). With repeated use of 3% hexachlorophene preparations, the drug is absorbed through the skin.
Infants bathed with hexachlorophene and personnel regularly
using a 3% hexachlorophene preparation for handwashing have
blood levels of 0.1–0.6 ppm hexachlorophene (190). In the
early 1970s, certain infants bathed with hexachlorophene developed neurotoxicity (vacuolar degeneration) (191). As a
result, in 1972, the FDA warned that hexachlorophene should
no longer be used routinely for bathing infants. However,
after routine use of hexachlorophene for bathing infants in
nurseries was discontinued, investigators noted that the incidence of health-care–associated S. aureus infections in hospital nurseries increased substantially (192,193). In several

question: We've got a wound protector opened for a laparotomy on a patient with known abdominal adhesions — anything I should flag to the surgeon, and can we re-sterilise the ring if it isn't used?
reference: Yes, flag two things. First, in patients with abdominal adhesions insertion of a wound protector can be difficult and may force the surgeon to enlarge the incision, with risk of small bowel injury and a longer operation; there is also concern about limited access to the surgical field once the device is in place. The surgeon must be familiar with handling the device at insertion, during the operative phase and at removal, so the wound isn't contaminated at these critical moments — especially with a high intra-abdominal bacterial load such as diffuse peritonitis. Second, no: these are single-use devices and must not be reused. Also note the evidence comes only from adult patients, so effectiveness is not established in children; no serious adverse effects were reported in the included studies, although they did not assess harms in depth.

question: At the start of my shift, what do I need to check before I do a full head-to-toe general survey on my post-op patient, and when do I call the provider?
reference: Before the general survey, do a brief primary survey to confirm the patient is medically stable — quickly assess mental status, airway, breathing, and circulation. If any signs indicate distress, notify the provider and initiate emergency care; changes in level of consciousness or abnormal vital signs are early warning signs of deterioration requiring prompt medical treatment. Once stability is confirmed, proceed with the general survey: overall observation of general appearance, behavior, mobility, communication, nutritional and fluid status, plus analysis of height, weight, and vital signs for out-of-range values needing follow-up. This primary survey is done at the beginning of every shift or patient visit.
source_text:
Basic Concepts

Basic Concepts 
When performing a general survey assessment, nurses use all of their 
senses to carefully observe the patient. They look at a patient and ask 
themselves, what are they seeing? They listen to a patient and ask 
themselves, what are they hearing, both verbally and nonverbally? They 
smell a patient’s odors and ask themselves, is there anything unusual we 
need to further assess? They observe a patient’s behaviors and make 
notes about their functioning and ability to complete daily activities 
according to their developmental level. 
Before performing a general survey assessment, it is important to first 
ensure the patient is medically stable by completing a brief primary 
survey. After ensuring the patient is medically stable, a general survey 
assessment is an overall observation of a patient’s general appearance, 
behavior, mobility, communication, nutritional, and fluid status. A general 
survey assessment also includes analyzing height, weight, and vital signs 
for values that are out of range and require additional follow-up. 
Primary Survey 
At the beginning of every shift or patient visit, nurses perform a brief 
primary survey to ensure their patient is medically stable. If any signs 
indicate patient distress, the provider is notified and emergency care is 
initiated. For example, changes in level of consciousness or abnormal vital 
signs often provide early warning signs that a patient’s condition is 
deteriorating and prompt medical treatment is needed.

Mental status, 
airway, breathing, and circulation are also quickly assessed and 
emergency actions taken as needed.

In a clinic setting, the patient is observed from the time they are called

question: What infection rate should we expect for hip and knee replacements going forward — is it still around 2% or is it climbing?
reference: It's projected to climb. The current infection risk cited for hip and knee arthroplasty is 2.18%, but by 2030 it is expected to rise to 6.5% for hip and 6.8% for knee arthroplasty. With the growing number of procedures (1.2 million prosthetic joint arthroplasties in 2011, projected to reach 3.8 million per year by 2030), total hip and knee prosthetic joint infections are projected to reach 221,500 cases per year by 2030, costing more than $1.62 billion. Infection is already the most common indication for revision in total knee arthroplasty and the third most common in total hip arthroplasty.
source_text:
Prosthetic Joint Arthroplasty Section
Prevention efforts should target all surgical procedures but especially those in which the human and financial burden is greatest.
In 2011, primary total knee arthroplasty accounted for more than
half of the 1.2 million prosthetic joint arthroplasty procedures (primary and revision) performed in the United States, followed by
total hip arthroplasty and hip hemiarthroplasty.24 Primary shoulder, elbow, and ankle arthroplasties are much less common. By
2030, prosthetic joint arthroplasties are projected to increase to
3.8 million procedures per year.25-27
Infection is the most common indication for revision in total
knee arthroplasty28 and the third most common indication in
total hip arthroplasty.28 By 2030, the infection risk for hip
and knee arthroplasty is expected to increase from 2.18%22 to
6.5% and 6.8%, respectively.25 In addition, owing to increasing
risk and the number of individuals undergoing prosthetic joint
arthroplasty procedures, the total number of hip and knee prosthetic joint infections is projected to increase to 221 500 cases
per year by 2030, at a cost of more than $1.62 billion.22,25 The
Prosthetic Joint Arthroplasty section contains recommendations
that are applicable to these procedures (eAppendix 1 of the
Supplement).
source_title: CDC Guideline for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection 2017

question: For our hysterectomy cases, do we need to prep the skin with an alcohol-based agent, and is a plastic adhesive drape or microbial sealant worth adding on top of it?
reference: Yes — intraoperative skin preparation should be done with an alcohol-based antiseptic agent unless it's contraindicated for that patient; this is a strong recommendation backed by high-quality evidence (Category IA). Adding a microbial sealant immediately after the skin prep is not necessary for preventing SSI (Category II, weak recommendation, low-quality evidence), and plastic adhesive drapes — with or without antimicrobial properties — are also not necessary for SSI prevention (Category II, weak recommendation, high to moderate-quality evidence).

question: For my post-op patient with suspected sepsis, what oxygen saturation should I be titrating to — and is it different if she's a COPD retainer?
reference: For patients aged 18 or over, give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 94% to 98%. If the patient is at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (for example a CO2 retainer), aim for a lower target of 88% to 92%. For patients aged 16 to 18, oxygen should be given if they have signs of shock or an SpO2 of less than 92% on air, and can also be considered at an SpO2 above 92% if clinically indicated. Bear in mind that pulse oximeters can under- or overestimate saturation, particularly when readings are borderline, with overestimation reported in people with dark skin, so interpret borderline values cautiously and check probe placement.
source_text:
1.10 Using oxygen for people with suspected sepsis
1.10.1
Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 94% to 98% for people aged
18 years or over or 88% to 92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
[2016]
1.10.2
Oxygen should be given to people aged 16 to 18 with suspected sepsis who have
signs of shock or oxygen saturation (SpO2) of less than 92% when breathing air.
Treatment with oxygen should also be considered for children with an SpO2 of
greater than 92%, as clinically indicated. [2016]
Be aware that some pulse oximeters can underestimate or overestimate oxygen
saturation levels, especially if the saturation level is borderline. Overestimation has
been reported in people with dark skin. See also the NHS England Patient Safety
Alert on the risk of harm from inappropriate placement of pulse oximeter probes.

question: If the surgeon is already moving on to close and we haven't finished the sign-out items, am I allowed to hold the team up as the checklist coordinator?
reference: Yes. The checklist coordinator can and should stop the team from progressing to the next phase of the operation until each step is satisfactorily addressed. Having a single person lead the checklist is essential to its success, because in the fast pace of the OR any step can be overlooked; designating one person to confirm completion of each step keeps safety steps from being omitted in the rush to move forward. Be aware this may irritate or alienate other team members and can create an antagonistic dynamic, which is why hospitals should choose carefully who fills the role — often the circulating nurse, though any clinician can coordinate it. Until the team knows the steps well, expect to actively guide them through the process. For sign-out before leaving the OR, the items to confirm are: the procedure performed, completion of sponge and instrument counts, labelling of any specimens, any equipment malfunctions or issues to address, and key plans and concerns for postoperative management and recovery.

Before leaving the operating room, the team will review
the operation that was performed, completion of sponge
and instrument counts and the labelling of any surgical

malfunctions or issues that need to be addressed. Finally,

Having a single person lead the Checklist process is
essential for its success. In the complex setting of an
operating room, any of the steps may be overlooked
during the fast-paced preoperative, intraoperative, or
postoperative preparations. Designating a single person
to confirm completion of each step of the Checklist can
ensure that safety steps are not omitted in the rush to move
forward with the next phase of the operation. Until team
members are familiar with the steps involved, the Checklist
coordinator will likely have to guide the team through this
Checklist process.
A possible disadvantage of having a single person lead
the Checklist is that an antagonistic relationship might
be established with other operating team members. The
Checklist coordinator can and should prevent the team
from progressing to the next phase of the operation until
each step is satisfactorily addressed, but in doing so may
alienate or irritate other team members. Therefore, hospitals
must carefully consider which staff member is most suitable
for this role. As mentioned, for many institutions this will
be a circulating nurse, but any clinician can coordinate the
Checklist process.

question: If we're out of oxytocin on the unit, is it actually acceptable to give something like misoprostol or ergometrine on its own for PPH prevention, or do those only count as add-ons?
reference: Yes — each uterotonic option was assessed on its own merit. The WHO guideline development group deliberately compared each individual uterotonic option (oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, ergometrine/methylergometrine, injectable prostaglandins, oxytocin plus ergometrine, misoprostol plus oxytocin) against placebo/no uterotonic first, specifically to determine whether each agent can be applied individually for PPH prophylaxis in situations where other uterotonic agents are not available. So single agents are considered as stand-alone prophylaxis, not just add-ons. Separately, the group then compared each option head-to-head against the others to identify the most efficacious agent with the best side-effect profile — the 'uterotonic of choice' — along with the route of administration and dosing regimen that should be used.
source_text:
If so, what route of administration and dosing regimen should be used?

For women in the third stage of labour (P), is the use of any uterotonic
agent(s) (oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, ergometrine/methylergometrine,
injectable prostaglandins, oxytocin plus ergometrine, misoprostol plus
oxytocin) for prevention of PPH (I) compared with other uterotonic agents
(oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, ergometrine/methylergometrine, injectable
prostaglandins, oxytocin plus ergometrine, misoprostol plus oxytocin) (C), safer
and more effective for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes?
If so, what route of administration and dosing regimen of such uterotonic
agent(s) should be used?
The GDG initially considered the comparisons of each uterotonic option (single agent or
combination regimen) with placebo/no uterotonic to assess the efficacy and safety of each
uterotonic option separately (PICO questions 1–6). This approach was taken to determine
if each uterotonic can be individually applied for PPH prophylaxis in situations where other
uterotonic agents are not available. Then, the GDG reviewed the comparative efficacy and
safety of each uterotonic option (single agent or combination regimen) with each of the
other uterotonic options to determine the most efficacious uterotonic agent with the best
side-effect profile – the uterotonic of choice (PICO question 7).

question: Ci sono prove solide che dicano quale prodotto usare per il lavaggio chirurgico delle mani, e per quanto tempo, per ridurre le infezioni del sito chirurgico?
reference: No: su questo punto le prove sono molto limitate ed eterogenee. question: What IV rate should I keep my post-op urogyn patient on until she's drinking, and when can I stop the fluids?
reference: Postoperatively, run IV fluids at about 40 mL/h — this rate has been shown to be adequate in urogynecology patients, including elderly patients, without an increase in complications. Continue the IV fluids only until the patient is tolerating oral fluids, then discontinue them once she is tolerating oral hydration.
source_text:
Perioperative management of intravenous fluids
Administration of IV fluids should consider age, anesthetics, analgesics, and length of procedure.

In addition,
because of liberalized fasting guidelines allowing for
intake of clear liquids up to 2 h before surgery, there is no
need to administer IV fluids to account for fasting losses.

The goal of intraoperative fluid administration should be
to maintain euvolemia.

This is especially important in the
geriatric population, as fluid overload may contribute to
congestive heart failure, electrolyte disturbances, edema,
and ileus.

One urogynecology-specific ERAS pathway with
the goal of euvolemia used rates of 2 mL/kg/h for intraoperative fluid administration in laparoscopic and vaginal
surgery with boluses of crystalloid for mean arterial pressure < 60 mmHg or < 20% of baseline [4].

Another used
a goal-directed fluid algorithm using the Masimo “Pleth
Variabilty Index,” which resulted in a decrease in fluids
administered of > 1L compared to non-ERAS patients
without any complications related to hypovolemia, including acute renal failure [29].

These studies provide a framework for fluid management.

Fluid administration should be
tailored to the specific clinical circumstances.

In general,
balanced salt solutions (Plasma-Lyte®, lactated Ringer’s)
should be utilized rather than normal saline to decrease the
risk of complications such as hyperchloremic acidosis [14].

If fluid resuscitation is needed, either crystalloid or colloid
may be used with no difference in outcome [30].

Postoperatively, IV fluids should be run until the patient is
tolerating oral fluids.

Rate of administration of 40 mL/h has
been shown to be adequate in urogynecology patients without an
increase in complications, including in elderly patients [29, 31].

Recommendation
The goal of intraoperative fluid administration should be
euvolemia.

In general, balanced salt solutions should be
utilized over normal saline.

IV fluids should be discontinued
once the patient is tolerating oral hydration.
source_title: Joint report on terminology and clinical consensus: Enhanced Recovery After Urogynecologic Surgery (AUGS-IUGA)

question: When we report our unit's CAUTI numbers, what exactly do we count on the top and bottom, and how do we express the rate?
reference: For CAUTI rates, use NHSN definitions. The numerator is the number of CAUTIs in each location being monitored, and the denominator is the total number of urinary catheter-days for all patients with an indwelling urinary catheter in that same location. Multiply by a standardization factor of 1000 so the rate is expressed as cases per 1000 catheter-days. The same denominator and standardization factor are used for the rate of bloodstream infections secondary to CAUTI, where the numerator is the number of episodes of secondary bloodstream infection (using NHSN definitions for laboratory-confirmed bloodstream infection). Tracking these rates lets your facility gauge the longitudinal impact of prevention strategies — note that current NHSN CAUTI definitions were developed for monitoring rates within a facility, though facility-to-facility comparisons may be requested by state requirements or external quality initiatives.

question: The next hysterectomy case is delayed and we're short one instrument set — can I flash sterilize the set from the previous case to keep things moving?
reference: No. Flash sterilization should only be used for patient care items that will be used immediately, such as reprocessing an instrument that was inadvertently dropped during a case. It should not be used for convenience, as a substitute for purchasing additional instrument sets, or to save time (Category IB). Instruments should otherwise be sterilized according to published guidelines (Category IB).

question: For a post-op obstetric patient I'm worried might be septic, which observations do I need to chart and how should I escalate?
reference: Record all vital signs — temperature, pulse rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturations and respiratory rate — on an early warning system that has been modified for obstetrics to allow for the physiological changes of pregnancy. Monitoring should be managed with a multidisciplinary approach, and there should be clear instructions for escalation using a structured SBAR (Situation–Background–Assessment–Recommendation) communication tool, with early escalation to a senior clinician. This is important because women who become unwell in pregnancy or around birth often deteriorate abruptly after a period of physiological compensation, which narrows the window for early detection.

question: My post-op patient is nil by mouth after an open abdominal hysterectomy and is expected to have severe pain — should I be setting her up for PCA or asking about an epidural?
reference: For patients who cannot take oral opioids, offer a choice of either PCA or a continuous epidural for postoperative pain relief. However, weigh the benefits of a continuous epidural for patients who are having major or complex open-torso surgery, are expected to have severe pain, or have cognitive impairment — this patient meets two of those criteria (major open-torso surgery and expected severe pain), so a continuous epidural is worth considering and discussing with the anaesthetist. Oral immediate-release opioids should only be offered when immediate postoperative pain is expected to be moderate to severe, and only once the person can eat and drink.

question: For our post-op pelvic reconstructive patients, which bowel regimen should I be sending home or starting on the floor — docusate with Senokot or docusate with polyethylene glycol?
reference: Prescribe a laxative regimen routinely, since constipation is common after pelvic reconstructive surgery. Docusate sodium combined with Senokot hastens return of gut function after surgery, whereas docusate sodium combined with polyethylene glycol does not — so the docusate/Senokot combination is the one to use (strong recommendation, high quality evidence). Additional safe, inexpensive measures that speed return of bowel function include drinking coffee, chewing gum, maintaining euvolemia, opioid-sparing analgesia, and early feeding.

question: My patient is going for a CT with IV contrast before her surgery — what do I need to check and how long should she be NPO?
reference: Keep her NPO for four to six hours before the scan if contrast is being used. Before sending her, check for previous allergies to iodine or other contrast dyes — if she's had a prior allergic reaction she may be prescribed diphenhydramine or corticosteroids beforehand. Verify kidney function by checking BUN, creatinine, and eGFR, since IV contrast can worsen kidney function; if those labs are abnormal, notify the provider before the contrast is given. Also check whether she takes metformin, as there may be restrictions on giving it before or after the procedure. Remove all jewelry before the procedure.

question: When I'm orienting to a new OR, what should I be checking about the unit's protocols before I rely on them for things like drug administration or setting up equipment?
reference: Ask which main protocols are used in that setting and get familiar with them, and specifically check when each one was last reviewed — a protocol is only effective if it's a living document, so also find out the process by which they get updated. Protocols that aren't updated in a timely way or aren't evidence-based are unhelpful, and having too many of them is also a problem. Don't rely on memory alone for treatment steps or drug doses; use pictures, diagrams and posted notices of the steps involved (including for switching equipment on/off and reading displays) to check your actions, which reduces working-memory load so you can focus on the task itself.
source_text:
Avoid relying on memory

remember lots of facts and information.

Students should look for pictures
and diagrams of the steps involved in
a treatment process or procedure.

Checking

reduce the load on the working memory,
freeing the student to focus on the task
at hand, such as taking a medical history
or administering an appropriate drug.

This is a major reason that protocols are
so important in health care–they reduce reliance
on memory.

On the other hand, having too
many protocols is unhelpful, especially if they
are not updated in a timely manner or are not
evidence-based.

Students should ask about

familiar with them.

It is important to check

Finding

question: We're taking a PPH patient to theatre — is she better off with a spinal or a general?
reference: An experienced anaesthetist should assess her promptly and choose the mode of anaesthesia based on her haemodynamic status. Central neuraxial (regional) anaesthesia is the technique of choice in obstetric patients and has contributed to reduced maternal mortality, since general anaesthesia carries increased morbidity and mortality in pregnancy because of physiological changes. However, general anaesthesia may be preferable if she is haemodynamically unstable or has a coagulopathy. A senior anaesthetist should be involved early to help assess and continue resuscitation, and she may need high dependency or intensive care postoperatively with an obstetric early warning score to pick up ongoing or concealed bleeding.
source_text:
D
Anaesthetists play an important role in the multidisciplinary team involved in the management of patients
with PPH. A senior anaesthetist should be consulted early to help assess, initiate and continue prompt
resuscitation of these patients, using their expertise in ﬂuid and transfusion therapy as well as their
experience in managing critically ill patients.10
If the patient needs to go to theatre for a surgical intervention, an experienced anaesthetist should
promptly assess the patient in order to decide on the most suitable mode of anaesthesia, depending on
the patient’s haemodynamic status. Central neuraxial anaesthesia has become the anaesthetic technique of
choice in the obstetric population and this has resulted in a reduction in maternal mortality.133
While general anaesthesia in obstetric patients is associated with increased morbidity and mortality when
compared with regional anaesthesia due to the physiological changes that occur in pregnancy,9 it may be
preferable in patients who are haemodynamically unstable or who have a coagulopathy.
The patient may need high dependency or intensive care in the postoperative period. An obstetric early
warning score system would help in the early identiﬁcation of continuous bleeding, especially in cases
which are not apparent, as recommended by CMACE (see Appendix IV).131

question: How often should I be checking and changing the incontinence pads on my post-op patient who's still incontinent and at risk for skin breakdown?
reference: Check incontinence pads frequently — every two to three hours — and change them as needed to keep the patient dry. Frequent changing of soiled pads prevents exposure to the chemicals in urine and stool that erode skin. Alongside this, apply a moisture barrier ointment, which can significantly decrease skin breakdown and pressure injury formation, and keep bed linens clean, dry, and wrinkle free, since soiled, wet, or wrinkled sheets contribute to skin breakdown.

question: When I'm writing a problem-focused nursing diagnosis for my post-op patient, what has to be documented before I can call it accurate — and how do I pick what to aim my interventions at?
reference: A problem-focused diagnosis requires both related factors (etiology) and defining characteristics to be present. Related factors are antecedent factors with a demonstrated partnered relationship to the human response, and they must be modifiable by independent nursing interventions — whenever possible, aim your interventions at these etiological factors. Defining characteristics are the observable cues or inferences that cluster as manifestations of the problem — things you can see, hear, touch, or smell. Problem-focused diagnoses and syndromes must have related factors; health promotion diagnoses only need them if they help clarify the diagnosis.

question: For a pregnant patient from a malaria-endemic area in Africa, when do we start her sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine doses and how far apart do they need to be spaced?
reference: Start intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) in the second trimester, and give doses at least one month apart, aiming for the patient to receive at least three doses. This is recommended for all pregnant women in malaria-endemic areas of Africa (a context-specific recommendation).

question: When I'm cutting the new wafer, how much skin around the stoma can I leave exposed before the fit is wrong?
reference: No more than 1/8 inch (2 mm) of peristomal skin should be exposed for a correct fit. Trace the pattern onto the paper backing of the wafer and cut it to that size — and if a pattern is already available, cut the new wafer before you remove the old pouch. After removing the paper backing, place the wafer with the stoma centered in the cutout and press gently to remove air and seal it to the skin.

question: For a woman who already got prophylactic oxytocin after delivery, do I still need to do continuous fundal massage, or is checking tone enough?
reference: Continuous uterine massage is not recommended for PPH prevention in women who have received prophylactic oxytocin — it can cause maternal discomfort, ties up a dedicated staff member, and may not reduce blood loss. However, you should still monitor uterine tone by abdominal palpation in all women, so that postpartum uterine atony is identified early.
source_text:
Recommendations for PPH prevention
The contribution of each component of the ‘active management of the third stage of
labour’ was examined in light of new available evidence, and relevant recommenda
tions were made. Box 1 presents recommendations concerning the use of uteroton
ics for the prevention of PPH. All women giving birth should be offered uteroton
ics during the third stage of labour to prevent PPH and IM/IV oxytocin (10 IU) is
recommended as the uterotonic drug of choice. Other injectable uterotonics (i.e.
ergometrine/methylergometrine, or the fixed drug combination of oxytocin and
ergometrine) and misoprostol are recommended as alternatives for the prevention
of PPH in settings where oxytocin is unavailable. Box 2 contains recommendations
related to cord management and uterine massage. The importance of controlled
cord traction (CCT) was revisited because of new evidence. This intervention is now
regarded as optional in settings where skilled birth attendants are available, and
is contraindicated in settings where skilled attendants do not assist with births.
Early cord clamping is generally contraindicated. Continuous uterine massage is
not recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH for women who have received
prophylactic oxytocin, because the massage may cause maternal discomfort, re
quire a dedicated health professional, and may not lead to a reduction of blood loss.
However, surveillance of the uterine tonus through abdominal palpation is recom
mended for all women for the early identification of postpartum uterine atony. Table

question: Quanto devo strofinare mani e avambracci prima di calzare i guanti sterili — cambia se uso il sapone antimicrobico o il gel alcolico?
reference: Sì, i tempi sono diversi. Con un sapone antimicrobico adatto si frizionano mani e avambracci per il tempo indicato dal produttore, di solito 2-5 minuti. Con la soluzione alcolica (ABHR) si applica una quantità sufficiente su mani e avambracci asciutti per il tempo indicato dal produttore, di solito 1,5 minuti, lasciando poi asciugare completamente prima di calzare i guanti sterili. I due prodotti non devono essere combinati; è preferibile un prodotto con efficacia prolungata. Se la qualità dell'acqua non è garantita, è consigliabile usare ABHR.

question: My post-op patient is nil by mouth and vomiting after her laparoscopic hysterectomy — can I give her an IV NSAID for pain, and which one should I ask for?
reference: Yes. IV NSAIDs should normally be avoided for immediate postoperative pain, but they are appropriate when the person cannot take oral medicine — which applies here. In that situation, ask for a traditional NSAID rather than a COX-2 inhibitor. Once she can tolerate oral intake, oral ibuprofen is the recommended option for immediate postoperative pain of any severity (the exception being patients who have had surgery for hip fracture, who follow the hip fracture analgesia recommendations).
source_text:
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
1.6.7
Offer oral ibuprofen to manage immediate postoperative pain of all severities
(including pain after dental surgery) unless the person has had surgery for hip
fracture (see the recommendations on analgesia in the NICE guideline on hip
fracture).
1.6.8
Do not offer an intravenous NSAID to manage immediate postoperative pain
(including pain after dental surgery) unless the person cannot take oral medicine.
1.6.9
If offering an intravenous NSAID to manage immediate postoperative pain,
choose a traditional NSAID rather than a COX-2 (cyclo-oxygenase-2) inhibitor.

question: The oxytocin vials in our theatre cupboard say they're fine at room temperature — can I just leave them out, and what temperature should they actually be kept at?
reference: No — oxytocin should always be stored refrigerated regardless of what the manufacturer's label says. Label claims of room-temperature stability may not have been tested under the much warmer conditions found in some countries, and different formulations have different stability characteristics. Both oxytocin and ergometrine (alone or in combination) require refrigerated transport and storage, protected from light, at 2–8 °C, to prevent degradation and safeguard quality. Where electricity is limited or inconsistent so this cold chain can't be maintained, misoprostol or heat-stable carbetocin may be more feasible options, provided heat-stable carbetocin is locally available at a cost comparable to other effective uterotonics.
source_text:
While some manufacturer labelling
may seem to indicate that oxytocin is stable at room temperature, stability may not have

been tested in the much warmer conditions that may be prevalent in some countries, and
different formulations have different stability characteristics. To prevent its degradation
and to safeguard its quality, oxytocin should always be stored in refrigeration, regardless
of labelling.
As oxytocin and ergometrine (as single or combination agents) require refrigerated
transport and storage (protected from light and stored at 2–8 °C) (42,45), their use may
be less feasible in settings with limited or inconsistent electricity. Misoprostol or the
heat-stable formulation of carbetocin may be more feasible in such settings, provided
that heat-stable carbetocin is available locally at a comparable cost to other effective
uterotonics.
Ergometrine/methylergometrine is contraindicated in women with hypertensive
disorders, and hence can only be used in settings where women can be screened for
these conditions. It may therefore be less feasible to use this option in settings with few
skilled birth attendants and limited capacity for screening for hypertensive disorders of
pregnancy.
It is advised that programmes to implement uterotonics for PPH prevention ensure
women are adequately informed in advance about the need to use a uterotonic to prevent
PPH, the available uterotonic options, the possible side-effects of these options and their
rights to choose what care they receive.
source_title: WHO Recommendations for Uterotonics for Prevention of PPH

question: My post-op patient has a suspected wound infection and a NEWS2 of 3 — how quickly does someone need to review her, and do I have to start antibiotics straight away?
reference: A NEWS2 of 1 to 4 with suspected or confirmed infection puts her at low risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. You need to arrange review by a registered health practitioner within 1 hour of her being assessed as low risk, and perform blood tests if indicated. Antibiotics do not have to be given immediately: request assessment by a clinician with core competencies in caring for acutely ill patients (FY2 level or above) to consider deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for a period after her first NEWS2 score was calculated (on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration), using that time to gather information for a more specific diagnosis. Once a decision to give antibiotics is made, do not delay administration any further.
source_text:
Low risk of severe illness or death from sepsis
A person is at low risk of severe illness or death from sepsis if they have suspected or
confirmed infection and a NEWS2 score of 1 to 4 (see recommendation 1.6.2 on evaluating
risk of severe illness or death from sepsis), or a NEWS2 score of 0 and cause for clinical
concern (see recommendations 1.6.3 and 1.6.4 on taking causes for clinical concern into
account when evaluating risk of severe illness or death from sepsis).

For people aged 16 or over at low risk of severe illness or death from sepsis:
• arrange for registered health practitioner review within 1 hour of the person
being assessed as at low risk
• perform blood tests if indicated. [2024]

question: For a woman with HIV coming in for delivery, what should we be doing intrapartum and right after birth to cut down the transmission risk to the baby?
reference: Labour and delivery carry a high risk of HIV transmission, so keep to the key practices: make sure recommended antenatal visits have happened, especially high-risk management in the late third trimester; deliver in a facility with a trained skilled birth attendant; avoid unnecessary instrumentation and avoid premature rupture of membranes, using a partograph to monitor the stages of labour; and for the newborn, use non-invasive suction of nasogastric secretions and wash away blood. Antenatally she should also get at least the minimum package of recommended visits and pregnancy care, with consideration of STI screening, nutritional support, and infant feeding and family planning counselling.

question: For our laparoscopic urogyn cases, when should we be injecting local into the port sites — at insertion or at closure?
reference: Either works: injecting the port sites with local analgesic at the time of port insertion and/or at closure is known to reduce the need for postoperative analgesia. This is part of using regional techniques where appropriate, alongside nerve blocks, transverse abdominal plane blocks, and infiltration of the surgical field with local anesthetic, as part of a multimodal intraoperative analgesia plan (e.g., acetaminophen, ketorolac, lidocaine infusions, and/or dexmedetomidine) that minimizes opioids.

question: For a patient who's completely bedfast after surgery, how often should I be turning her and doing skin checks, and how high can I put the head of the bed?
reference: For a patient scoring 1 (bedfast) on the Braden activity subscale: turn/reposition every 1-2 hours and post a turning schedule, and perform skin assessment/inspection every shift. Keep the head of bed elevated no more than 30 degrees, or position prone if appropriate. Also use pillows to elevate pressure points off the bed, elevate heels off the bed and/or use heel protectors, teach or perform frequent small shifts of body weight, consider a specialty bed, and consider a physical therapy consult for conditioning and wheelchair assessment.

question: If I hand a scalpel or needle to someone else during a case, who's responsible for disposing of it — me or whoever used it last?
reference: The person who uses the sharp is responsible for disposing of it safely. Practically, that means taking a sharps bin to the patient/point of use so the user can discard it immediately. Don't overload or use a sharps bin that is full, and never leave a sharps bin somewhere children can reach it. Needles collected from patients should go into a sharps container placed inside a safe box to minimize risk to community pharmacists, and any needlestick injury must always be reported in line with local policy.

question: My post-op patient had chemo about three weeks ago and is now spiking a temp — do I need to suspect neutropenic sepsis and where does she need to go?
reference: Yes. Suspect neutropenic sepsis in anyone who becomes unwell and has had systemic anticancer treatment within the last 30 days — so a patient treated three weeks ago falls inside that window. The same applies to people receiving or who have received immunosuppressant treatment for non-cancer reasons, using clinical judgement about their condition, history and the treatment given to decide whether past treatment could still cause neutropenia. Refer anyone with suspected neutropenic sepsis immediately for assessment in secondary or tertiary care, and treat neutropenic sepsis, whatever the cause, in line with NICE's guideline on neutropenic sepsis in people with cancer. For pregnant or recently pregnant people with suspected sepsis, also consider using an early warning score to assess them, in any setting.

question: For a woman admitted in preterm labour, when do we actually start antibiotics, and which one do we use if her membranes have ruptured?
reference: Antibiotics are only indicated if the membranes have ruptured. If she is in preterm labour with intact membranes and no clinical signs of infection, do not give routine antibiotics (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). If she has preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), and erythromycin is the antibiotic of choice (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Do not use amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid (co-amoxiclav) in these women (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).

question: During the time-out before we make the incision, what exactly am I as the scrub nurse supposed to speak up about, versus what the surgeon and anaesthetist cover?
reference: Before skin incision, the surgeon covers the critical steps of the procedure, the risk of heavy blood loss, any special equipment needed (instruments, implants, intraoperative imaging, frozen section pathology) and any likely deviation from routine practice. As the nurse, you should tell the team about any critical safety concerns you have and about any special equipment that is unavailable or not properly prepared. The anaesthetist states any critical safety concerns of their own — particularly any difficulty preparing for resuscitation after heavy blood loss, or patient comorbidities that add anaesthetic risk. The surgeon is responsible for ensuring that team members — especially nurses, anaesthetists and surgical assistants — are aware of these points before incision.

question: My patient is on therapeutic LMWH for a DVT and is booked for a caesarean tomorrow — how long before the section do I need to stop her LMWH, and how long must anaesthetics wait before siting a spinal or epidural?
reference: Stop the therapeutic LMWH 24 hours before the planned delivery (the same applies for induction of labour). Regional anaesthesia or analgesia should not be undertaken until at least 24 hours after the last therapeutic dose of LMWH. Afterwards, LMWH should not be given for 4 hours after a spinal or after the epidural catheter has been removed, and the epidural catheter should not be removed within 12 hours of the most recent injection. If she were on subcutaneous unfractionated heparin instead, this should be stopped 12 hours before, and intravenous unfractionated heparin stopped 6 hours before induction or regional anaesthesia.
source_text:
9.1	 Should anticoagulant therapy be altered during labour and delivery?

When VTE occurs at term, consideration should be given to the use of intravenous unfractionated
heparin which is more easily manipulated.

The woman on LMWH for maintenance therapy should be advised that once she is in established
labour or thinks that she is in labour, she should not inject any further heparin.

Where delivery is planned, either by elective caesarean section or induction of labour, LMWH
maintenance therapy should be discontinued 24 hours prior to planned delivery.

Regional anaesthetic or analgesic techniques should not be undertaken until at least 24 hours
after the last dose of therapeutic LMWH.

LMWH should not be given for 4 hours after the use of spinal anaesthesia or after the epidural
catheter has been removed, and the epidural catheter should not be removed within 12 hours of
the most recent injection.

Where possible, anticoagulant therapy should be altered to avoid an unwanted anticoagulant effect
during delivery.

Women should be advised not to inject any further heparin if they are in established
labour or think they are in labour.

For elective delivery, LMWH should be stopped 24 hours before induction of labour or caesarean
section.

Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin should be discontinued 12 hours before and
intravenous unfractionated heparin stopped 6 hours before induction of labour or regional
anaesthesia.167 Women who present in labour shortly after injecting LMWH can be reassured that
bleeding complications are very uncommon with LMWH (see section 6.1).

If spontaneous labour
occurs in women receiving therapeutic doses of subcutaneous unfractionated heparin, careful
monitoring of the APTT is required (see above for use of APTT in pregnancy).

If it is markedly
prolonged near delivery, protamine sulfate may be required to reduce the risk of bleeding.
