question: If my post-op patient still has her Foley in, how fast does her risk of bacteriuria climb each day, and at what point is she essentially guaranteed to be colonized?
reference: With an indwelling catheter the daily risk of bacteriuria is about 3% to 10%, and it approaches 100% by 30 days of catheterization — 30 days is also the cutoff used to separate short-term from long-term catheterization. Even with a sterile closed drainage system, bacteriuria eventually occurs over time, either through breaks in the closed system (intraluminal route) or by the extraluminal route. With prolonged catheterization, urinary pathogens universally form biofilm on the catheter and drainage system surfaces, where organisms live in a sessile state that is resistant to antimicrobials and host defenses and virtually impossible to eradicate without removing the catheter.
source_text:
The marked reduction in risk of bacteriuria with the 
introduction of the sterile, closed urinary drainage system in the1960’s23 suggests the

Page 24 of 61 
importance of the intraluminal route. However, even with the closed drainage system, 
bacteriuria inevitably occurs over time either via breaks in the sterile system or via the 
extraluminal route.24 The daily risk of bacteriuria with catheterization is 3% to 10%,25,26 
approaching 100% after 30 days, which is considered the delineation between short and longterm catheterization.27

Formation of biofilms by urinary pathogens on the surface of the catheter and drainage system 
occurs universally with prolonged duration of catheterization.28 Over time, the urinary catheter 
becomes colonized with microorganisms living in a sessile state within the biofilm, rendering 
them resistant to antimicrobials and host defenses and virtually impossible to eradicate without 
removing the catheter. The role of bacteria within biofilms in the pathogenesis of CAUTI is 
unknown and is an area requiring further research.

The most frequent pathogens associated with CAUTI (combining both ASB and SUTI) in 
hospitals reporting to NHSN between 2006-2007 were Escherichia coli (21.4%) and Candida 
spp (21.0%), followed by Enterococcus spp (14.9%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (10.0%), 
Klebsiella pneumoniae (7.7%), and Enterobacter spp (4.1%). A smaller proportion was caused 
by other gram-negative bacteria and Staphylococcus spp 5.

Antimicrobial resistance among urinary pathogens is an ever increasing problem. About a 
quarter of E. coli isolates and one third of P. aeruginosa isolates from CAUTI cases were 
fluoroquinolone-resistant. Resistance of gram-negative pathogens to other agents, including 
third-generation cephalosporins and carbapenems, was also substantial 5. The proportion of 
organisms that were multidrug-resistant, defined by non-susceptibility to all agents in 4 classes, 
was 4% of P. aeruginosa, 9% of K. pneumoniae, and 21% of Acinetobacter baumannii. 29

question: Se togliamo il drenaggio addominale precocemente invece di aspettare la sesta giornata o il calo del volume drenato, aumentiamo il rischio di infezione della ferita?
reference: No, non risulta una differenza dimostrata: le evidenze disponibili (di qualità molto scarsa) non mostrano né un beneficio né un danno chiaro della rimozione precoce del drenaggio rispetto a quella tardiva sui tassi di SSI (OR 0.86; IC 95%: 0.49–1.50). Il risultato resta invariato anche quando la rimozione tardiva è definita come una giornata specifica (dalla sesta in poi: OR 0.63; IC 95%: 0.07–5.70) oppure in base al volume drenato (OR 0.93; IC 95%: 0.51–1.70). Da tenere presente che queste evidenze riguardano solo pazienti adulti — non ci sono studi pediatrici — e non esistono dati sulla mortalità attribuibile a SSI. Inoltre non sono stati inclusi in questi confronti gli studi che confrontavano rimozione in prima vs. seconda giornata o poche ore vs. 24 ore dopo l'intervento.

question: My hypertensive pre-op patient says she has a glass of wine most nights — what daily and weekly alcohol limit should I be telling her, and how much wine counts as one drink?
reference: For women (and lighter weight men), advise a maximum of one standard drink per day or 9 drinks per week. For men the limit is two standard drinks per day or 14 drinks per week. One standard drink equals 5 oz/142 mL of wine (12% alcohol), 1.5 oz/43 mL of spirits (40% alcohol), or 12 oz/341 mL of regular strength beer (5% alcohol) — so a large pour of wine may be more than one standard drink. Alcohol consumption should be discussed routinely, with a recommendation to limit use as appropriate.
source_text:

Nurses will routinely discuss alcohol consumption with the client and recommend limiting alcohol
use, as appropriate, to a maximum of:
■Two standard drinks per day or 14 drinks per week for men;
■One standard drink per day or 9 drinks per week for women and lighter weight men.
Level of Evidence = III

question: When we're counting a maternal sepsis case, how long after delivery does it still count as pregnancy-related sepsis, and how common is it as a cause of maternal death?
reference: Sepsis is counted as maternal when it occurs during pregnancy or up to six weeks after the end of pregnancy, defined in the broadest sense as death from a primary infective cause. Globally, sepsis accounts for 11% of all maternal deaths. In the UK between 2019–21, 241 of 2,066,997 women who gave birth died, and 78 of those deaths were due to sepsis (direct or indirect) — 10% of all maternal deaths were due to sepsis and 14% were due to COVID-19 infection. Of the 78 sepsis deaths, 60% were attributable to viral infections, and the overall sepsis mortality rate was reported per 100,000 maternities (95% CI 1.89–3.25 per 100,000). The non-significant rise in UK sepsis deaths between 2016–18 and 2019–21 was mostly accounted for by SARS-CoV-2 infection in unvaccinated women.

question: One of my patients on the gyn floor has C. diff diarrhea and we're in the middle of an outbreak — is my alcohol foam enough after I pull off my gloves, or do I need to go to the sink?
reference: Go to the sink. No hand hygiene agent used in antiseptic handwashes or rubs — alcohols, chlorhexidine, hexachlorophene, iodophors, PCMX, or triclosan — is reliably sporicidal against Clostridium or Bacillus species. Washing with soap and water (either non-antimicrobial or antimicrobial) helps physically remove spores from the hands. Normally, after glove removal you may either wash with non-antimicrobial or antimicrobial soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand rub, but during an outbreak of C. difficile-related infection, washing with soap and water after removing gloves is the prudent choice. Also keep wearing gloves whenever you care for patients with C. difficile-associated diarrhea.

(including alcohols, chlorhexidine, hexachlorophene,
iodophors, PCMX, and triclosan) used in antiseptic handwash
or antiseptic hand-rub preparations are reliably sporicidal
against Clostridium spp. or Bacillus spp.

(120,172,224,225).

Washing hands with non-antimicrobial or antimicrobial soap
and water may help to physically remove spores from the surface of contaminated hands.

HCWs should be encouraged
 to wear gloves when caring for patients with C. difficileassociated diarrhea (226).

After gloves are removed, hands
should be washed with a non-antimicrobial or an antimicrobial soap and water or disinfected with an alcohol-based hand
rub.

During outbreaks of C. difficile-related infections, washing hands with a non-antimicrobial or antimicrobial soap and
water after removing gloves is prudent.

HCWs with suspected
or documented exposure to B. anthracis-contaminated items
also should be encouraged to wash their hands with a nonantimicrobial or antimicrobial soap and water.

Reduced Susceptibility of Bacteria to
Antiseptics
Reduced susceptibility of bacteria to antiseptic agents can
either be an intrinsic characteristic of a species or can be an
acquired trait (227).

Several reports have described strains of
bacteria that appear to have acquired reduced susceptibility
(when defined by MICs established in vitro) to certain antiseptics (e.g., chlorhexidine, quaternary ammonium compounds, and triclosan) (227–230).

However, because the
antiseptic concentrations that are actually used by HCWs are
often substantially higher than the MICs of strains with
reduced antiseptic susceptibility, the clinical relevance of the
in vitro findings is questionable.

question: How long can I leave a warm compress or ice pack on my post-op patient's incision site, and is there anywhere I shouldn't put them?
reference: Heat (heating pads, warm compresses) should be applied for 5-20 minutes depending on the client's tolerance; it causes vasodilation and increases blood flow. Cold (cool baths, moist cool compresses) should be applied for no longer than 20 minutes; it causes vasoconstriction, reduces blood flow, and numbs nerve sensations. Neither heat nor cold should be applied over medication patches or implanted devices.

question: We're out of oxytocin — what can I give instead for third-stage PPH prevention, and at what dose?
reference: When oxytocin is unavailable, use another injectable uterotonic — such as ergometrine/methylergometrine or the fixed drug combination of oxytocin and ergometrine — or give oral misoprostol 600 µg. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. Oxytocin 10 IU IV/IM remains the first-choice uterotonic when available, and a uterotonic should be given during the third stage of labour for all births.
source_text:
The GDG also found insuffi
cient evidence to recommend self-administration for the prevention of PPH and the
measurement of blood loss over clinical estimation (see Box 9).

Box 1: Recommendations for the prevention of PPH – uterotonics

The use of uterotonics for the prevention of PPH during the third stage of labour is recom
mended for all births. (Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)

Oxytocin (10 IU, IV/IM) is the recommended uterotonic drug for the prevention of PPH.
(Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)

In settings where oxytocin is unavailable, the use of other injectable uterotonics (e.g. er
gometrine/methylergometrine or the fixed drug combination of oxytocin and ergometrine)

question: For our outpatient gyn cases in the ambulatory surgery suite, do we follow the same SSI prevention practices as we do for inpatient OR cases, or is there a separate standard?
reference: The same practices apply. The CDC SSI prevention recommendations make no distinction between surgical care delivered in ambulatory, same-day, or outpatient operating rooms and care provided in conventional inpatient operating rooms — this was anticipated since roughly 75% of U.S. operations were projected to be done in ambulatory/same-day/outpatient ORs by the turn of the century. Note, however, that the recommendations do not specifically cover procedures performed outside the operating room (e.g., endoscopic procedures) or invasive procedures such as cardiac catheterization or interventional radiology, although many of the SSI prevention strategies could likely be applied or adapted to those settings. They also do not specifically address burns, trauma, transplant procedures, healthcare-worker-to-patient bloodborne pathogen transmission, or the details of pediatric surgical practice — though in general, SSI prevention measures effective in adult surgical care are indicated in pediatric care as well.
source_text:
Thus, some of the recommendations in Part II are based on a strong theoretical rationale
and suggestive evidence in the absence of confirmatory scientific knowledge.

It has been estimated that approximately 75% of all
operations in the United States will be performed in “ambulatory,” “same-day,” or “outpatient” operating rooms by the
turn of the century.4 In recommending various SSI prevention methods, this document makes no distinction between
surgical care delivered in such settings and that provided in
conventional inpatient operating rooms.

This document is
primarily intended for use by surgeons, operating room
nurses, postoperative inpatient and clinic nurses, infection
control professionals, anesthesiologists, healthcare epidemiologists, and other personnel directly responsible for
the prevention of nosocomial infections.

This document does not:
●Specifically address issues unique to burns, trauma, transplant procedures, or transmission of bloodborne
pathogens from healthcare worker to patient, nor does it
specifically address details of SSI prevention in pediatric
surgical practice.

It has been recently shown in a multicenter study of pediatric surgical patients that characteristics
related to the operations are more important than those
related to the physiologic status of the patients.5 In general, all SSI prevention measures effective in adult surgical
care are indicated in pediatric surgical care.
●Specifically address procedures performed outside of the operating room (e.g., endoscopic procedures),
nor does it provide guidance for infection prevention for
invasive procedures such as cardiac catheterization or
interventional radiology.

Nonetheless, it is likely that many
SSI prevention strategies also could be applied or adapted
to reduce infectious complications associated with these
procedures.
●Specifically recommend SSI prevention methods

question: For a patient scheduled for a hysterectomy tomorrow morning, when do I tell her to do her pre-op wash, and does it have to be a chlorhexidine product?
reference: Tell her to shower or bathe her full body at least the night before surgery. The agent can be either plain (nonantimicrobial) soap, antimicrobial soap, or an antiseptic agent — an antiseptic such as chlorhexidine is not specifically required, and the wash should cover the whole body.

IMPORTANCE The human and financial costs of treating surgical site infections (SSIs) are
increasing.

The number of surgical procedures performed in the United States continues to
rise, and surgical patients are initially seen with increasingly complex comorbidities.

It is
estimated that approximately half of SSIs are deemed preventable using evidence-based
strategies.

OBJECTIVE To provide new and updated evidence-based recommendations for the
prevention of SSI.

EVIDENCE REVIEW A targeted systematic review of the literature was conducted in MEDLINE,
EMBASE, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library from 1998 through April 2014.

A modified
Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach
was used to assess the quality of evidence and the strength of the resulting recommendation
and to provide explicit links between them.

Of 5759 titles and abstracts screened, 896
underwent full-text review by 2 independent reviewers.

After exclusions, 170 studies were
extracted into evidence tables, appraised, and synthesized.

(antimicrobial or nonantimicrobial) or an antiseptic agent on at least the night before the
operative day.

question: When my post-op laparotomy patients on our ERAS pathway ask how long before they can walk around without much trouble, what timeframe should I tell them — and is it faster with laparoscopic surgery?
reference: For open surgery (laparotomy) on an ERAS pathway, patients reported returning to mild or no interference with walking at a median of about 5 days, compared with 13 days in pre-ERAS patients. With minimally invasive surgery on an ERAS pathway, patients reported return to mild or no interference with walking at a median of only 2 days. You can also tell laparotomy patients that ERAS patients reported returning to mild or no fatigue in about 10 days, versus 30 days before ERAS.
source_text:
For example, economic recovery and 
return to work may lag behind emotional or physical dimensions 
of recovery.

In one study, patients on an ERAS pathway reported 
return to mild or no fatigue in 10 days compared with 30 days for 
the pre-ERAS cohort, while returning to mild or no interference with 
walking after laparotomy was reported at a median of 5 days for 
ERAS patients compared with 13 days in the pre-ERAS group.177 
Patients undergoing minimally invasive surgery on an ERAS 
pathway reported a return to mild or no interference with walking 
at a median of 2 days.152
Consistent collection and documentation of patient reported 
outcomes within ERAS programs can help institutions monitor, 
understand, and compare patterns of recovery.

Patient reported 
outcomes, including symptom burden assessment, can also be 
tracked to guide individual post-operative care.

The RECOvER 
checklist, which outlines best practices for reporting on ERAS 
studies, recommends including references to validation of study 
instruments when reporting patient reported outcomes.232 Careful 
consideration of instrument selection should go beyond whether 
the instrument was validated in a gynecologic surgical population, 
but should include thoughtful evaluation of the specific content 
and purpose of the instrument, responsivity in the gynecologic 
surgical population, designed recall period, minimally important 
difference, and mode of administration.

Timing of measures should 
include a pre-operative baseline assessment, with the remainder of 
measurements designed thoughtfully based on an a priori hypothesis to balance patient burden with expected fluctuations in the 
patient reported outcome responses.

Wearable technologies that 
track functions such as steps, distance walked, sleep, and other 
physiologic processes can also contribute to the documentation and understanding of functional recovery and post-operative 
mobilization.

question: When I'm setting up for a case, what exactly counts as standard precautions — is it just hand hygiene and gloves, or is there more I need to be doing for every patient?
reference: Standard precautions apply to every patient, not just those with a known infection, and they include more than hand hygiene and gloves. They consist of: performing appropriate hand hygiene; wearing personal protective equipment when indicated; implementing category-specific, transmission-based precautions; encouraging respiratory hygiene; and following environmental infection control measures, including proper handling of sharps, laundry, and hazardous/contaminated waste. Beyond these, additional infection control measures include appropriate use of aseptic and sterile technique when performing procedures — maintaining a sterile field and equipment, and applying and safely removing sterile gloves and PPE — to protect the patient from transmission of microorganisms. Consistently following standard and transmission-based precautions as outlined by the CDC is how healthcare-associated infections are prevented; over 2 million patients in America contract an HAI each year and 99,000 die from one.
source_text:
Perform appropriate hand hygiene

Use standard precautions

Use category-specific, transmission-based precautions

Maintain a sterile field and equipment

Apply and safely remove sterile gloves and personal protective equipment

Dispose of contaminated wastes appropriately

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), over 2 million patients in America contract a healthcare-associated infection, and 99,000 patients die from a healthcare-associated infection every year. [1] Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are unintended and often preventable infections caused by care received in a health care setting. Healthcare-associated infections can be prevented by consistently following standard precautions and transmission-based precautions outlined by the CDC (2020). Standard precautions are used when caring for all patients and include performing appropriate hand hygiene ; wearing personal protective equipment when indicated; implementing category-specific transmission precautions; encouraging respiratory hygiene; and following environmental infection control measures, including handling of sharps, laundry, and hazardous waste. Additional infection control measures include the appropriate use of aseptic technique and sterile technique when performing nursing procedures to protect the patient from transmission of microorganisms. [2] Each of these strategies to keep patients and health care workers free of infection is discussed in further detail in this chapter.

question: Our OR runs off an oxygen concentrator instead of pipeline oxygen — what FiO2 should I actually expect it to deliver, and do I still need a cylinder in the room?
reference: With an oxygen concentrator, the delivered fraction of inspired oxygen varies between 0.93 and 0.99 rather than being a true 100%, so you should expect a maximum in that range. Yes, you still need a back-up source of oxygen such as a reserve cylinder — there should always be one available regardless of whether the hospital system is based on liquid oxygen, central cylinder banks or concentrators. Before starting anaesthesia there must also be a method for confirming the oxygen supply is adequate. Note that concentrators vary in capacity: some supply a whole hospital, others are intended as the oxygen source for a single machine.
source_text:
In both systems, a vaporizer is needed to deliver an accurate
concentration of the volatile agent.

In hospitals with unreliable compressed gas supplies, continuousflow anaesthesia machines cannot function safely; in this situation,
drawover equipment or machines based on oxygen concentrators have
considerable advantages.

When anaesthesia machines are purchased,
the local environment must be taken into account to ensure that the
machine will function correctly and can be maintained or repaired.

Gas Supplies in anaesthesia: Oxygen is essential for almost
all anaesthesia and must be readily available during induction,
maintenance and recovery.

Many patients require additional oxygen
postoperatively as well.

Oxygen may be supplied to operating rooms
in cylinders or via pipelines from a central oxygen distribution point.

Hospital oxygen systems may be based on liquid oxygen plants,
large cylinders in central banks or oxygen concentrators.

Whichever
system is used, there must be a method for confirming that the oxygen
supplies are adequate before starting anaesthesia.

There should
always be a back-up source of oxygen, such as a reserve cylinder.

Medical gas pipeline systems, connectors, pressure regulators and
terminal units should meet national standards for identification,
construction and installation.

All safety regulations for the preparation,
storage, identification and use of medical gases, anaesthetic drugs and
related materials must be met.

Wherever anaesthetic gases are used,
scavenging systems within the airway circuit should be in place to
reduce the risk for long-term exposure.

When oxygen concentrators are installed, users must be aware that
the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) delivered can vary between 0.93
and 0.99.

Concentrators differ in size: some are capable of supplying
an entire hospital, while others are designed to be used as the oxygen
source for a single machine.

Air is commonly used during anaesthesia.

question: My pre-op patient just refused her ordered medication — what do I need to document and who do I have to notify?
reference: Patients have the right to refuse medication. Document the patient's refusal along with any education or explanation you provided in your attempt to administer the medication, and notify the prescribing provider.

question: During the time out, who am I supposed to ask about the patient's allergies, and what do I do if I know about an allergy the anaesthetist hasn't mentioned?
reference: As Checklist coordinator, direct the allergy question (and the next two questions) to the anaesthetist — ask whether the patient has a known allergy and, if so, what it is. If you are aware of an allergy that the anaesthetist does not know about, you must speak up and communicate that information to them.
source_text:
Does the patient have a known allergy ?
The Checklist coordinator should direct this and the next two questions
to the anaesthetist. First, the coordinator should ask whether the
patient has a known allergy and, if so, what it is. If the coordinator
knows of an allergy that the anaesthetist is not aware of, this
information should be communicated.

question: My post-op patient has expressive aphasia and can't tell me her pain level — what's the best way to set up communication with her at the bedside?
reference: Modify the environment to cut excess noise and reduce emotional distress, and adjust your style: stand in front of her while speaking, listen attentively, present one idea or thought at a time, speak slowly without shouting, use written communication, or ask the family to help interpret her speech. Phrase questions so she can answer with a simple 'Yes' or 'No,' but be aware that clients with expressive aphasia may give automatic responses that are incorrect — so repeat back what she said to confirm accuracy, and instruct her to speak slowly. Offer alternative communication methods such as a writing tablet, flash cards, eye blinking, a communication board with pictures and letters, hand signals or gestures, or a computer. Ensure the call light is within her reach and that the central call light system is marked to indicate she has difficulty with speech. Monitor her for frustration, anger, depression, or other reactions to her impaired speech, and collaborate with the family and a speech therapist to develop a plan for effective communication.

question: If one of my post-op patients who's pregnant has a swollen calf and pleuritic chest pain, do I wait for the ultrasound and CTPA results before we start anticoagulation?
reference: No — don't wait. Any pregnant woman with symptoms or signs suggestive of VTE should have objective testing arranged expeditiously, and treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) should be given in the meantime until the diagnosis is excluded by that objective testing, unless treatment is strongly contraindicated. This urgency is because untreated DVT progresses to PE in 15–24% of patients, PE in pregnancy may be fatal in almost 15% of cases, and in 66% of those deaths occur within 30 minutes of the embolic event. Follow your hospital's agreed protocol for diagnosing suspected VTE in pregnancy, which may involve obstetricians, radiologists, physicians and haematologists.
source_text:
How is acute VTE diagnosed in pregnancy?
Any woman with symptoms and/or signs suggestive of VTE should have objective testing performed
expeditiously and treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) given (see section 6)
until the diagnosis is excluded by objective testing, unless treatment is strongly contraindicated.
Individual hospitals should have an agreed protocol for the objective diagnosis of suspected VTE
during pregnancy. This may recommend the involvement of obstetricians, radiologists, physicians
and haematologists.
Women presenting with symptoms and/or signs suggestive of VTE should have objective
testing performed expeditiously. If DVT remains untreated, 15–24% of these patients will
develop PE. PE during pregnancy may be fatal in almost 15% of patients, and in 66% of these,
death will occur within 30 minutes of the embolic event.14,15
All hospitals should have a protocol for the diagnosis of suspected VTE in pregnancy which may require
multidisciplinary team involvement.
source_title: GTG37b - Thrombosis and Embolism during Pregnancy Acute Management

question: My pre-op patient says she's ready to quit smoking before her surgery — what steps should I walk through with her, and when do I set up the follow-up call?
reference: Use the "5 A's": Ask (identify and document smoking status at every visit), Advise (urge her to quit in a clear, strong, personalized way), Assess (determine whether she's willing to make a quit attempt now), Assist (since she is willing, provide counseling and pharmacotherapy to help her quit), and Arrange (schedule follow-up contact in person or by telephone, preferably within the first week after her quit date). Also gather details such as what products she smokes or vapes, how many packs per day if cigarettes, how long she has smoked/vaped, and whether she has tried quitting before and which strategies worked best.

question: For a robotic hysterectomy where we can't keep tidal volumes low, what ventilation targets should we be aiming for and is a higher tidal volume a problem?
reference: The lung-protective target is a low tidal volume of about 6 cc/kg ideal body weight with plateau pressure kept under 30 cmH2O. During robotic and laparoscopic hysterectomy this may be difficult or impossible because pneumoperitoneum, steep Trendelenburg, and high BMI reduce chest wall compliance. If adequate oxygenation and ventilation can't be maintained with a low-tidal-volume strategy, using higher tidal volumes does not appear to be detrimental.
source_text:
Standardized anesthetic protocol
Standardized anesthetic protocols are a cornerstone of
ERAS pathways.

Anesthetic regimens should be designed
to facilitate rapid recovery.

Routine administration of sedatives to reduce anxiety preoperatively should be avoided
[2].

General and regional anesthesia and local anesthesia
plus sedation [21] have all been used successfully for urogynecological surgery.

There is no evidence that one approach
is superior to the others for operations in which multiple
techniques are possible.

Anesthetic choice should depend
on patient characteristics, the specific operation, and institutional factors.

If general anesthesia is chosen, sevoflurane and desflurane
are preferred over isoflurane because of their fast-on, fast-off
properties.

Propofol-based total IV anesthesia also facilitates rapid recovery.

It has the added benefit of decreasing
the risk of PONV [22].

Nitrous oxide, on the contrary, may
increase the likelihood of PONV.

However, with aggressive PONV prophylaxis (see below), this increased risk is
eliminated.

Also, propofol may be more environmentally
sustainable than anesthetic gases, especially desflurane and
nitrous oxide [23].

Lung-protective ventilatory strategies (low-tidal volume
of approximately 6 cc/kg ideal body weight and maintenance
of plateau pressure < 30 cmH2O) have been advocated for
intraoperative mechanical ventilation [24, 25].

This approach
may be difficult or impossible during robotic and laparoscopic hysterectomy because of factors that decrease chest
wall compliance such as pneumoperitoneum, steep Trendelenburg position, and high body mass index.

However, use
of higher tidal volumes does not appear to be detrimental if
adequate oxygenation and ventilation cannot be maintained
using low-tidal volume strategies [26].

Residual neuromuscular blockade is associated with respiratory complications,
increased length of stay, and mortality.

If nondepolarizing
neuromuscular block is used, it should be fully reversed at
the end of the operation [27].
source_title: Joint report on terminology and clinical consensus: Enhanced Recovery After Urogynecologic Surgery (AUGS-IUGA)

question: For tetanus toxoid in pregnancy, does a single dose actually cut newborn tetanus deaths, or do we need to get two or three doses in before delivery?
reference: The evidence favours completing two or three doses. With one dose only, neonatal tetanus deaths were 9/224 (4%) vs 19/270 (7%) in controls — RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.26–1.24), about 30 fewer deaths per 1000 but with a confidence interval crossing no effect (very low certainty). With two or three doses, there were 0/341 (0%) vs 27/347 (7.8%) — RR 0.02 (0 to 0.3), roughly 76 fewer deaths per 1000 (low certainty). All-cause neonatal death also only clearly improved with two or three doses: 14/341 (4.1%) vs 46/347 (13.3%), RR 0.31 (0.17–0.55), about 91 fewer per 1000 (moderate certainty), whereas one dose showed no benefit (RR 1.08, 0.65–1.79). Any dose reduced neonatal tetanus cases (9/565 vs 49/617; RR 0.2, 0.1–0.4).

question: For a mom who delivered here on the ward, how long do we need to keep her and baby before discharge, and when should we book her follow-up visits?
reference: After a facility birth, keep the mother and newborn in the facility for postnatal care for at least 24 hours after birth. Then schedule at least three more postnatal contacts: on day 3 (48–72 hours after birth), between days 7 and 14 after birth, and at six weeks after birth. (If a birth happens at home instead, the first contact should occur as early as possible within 24 hours of birth, followed by the same three additional contacts.)

question: We're trying to get an enhanced recovery pathway going on our gynae ward — who actually needs to be on the core team, and who do we escalate to if staff aren't following it?
reference: The core team of stakeholders should include a surgeon, an anaesthetist, specialist nurses and managers, and a designated local 'ER champion' can facilitate the work. That core team needs training so they understand the current service, can identify and implement improvements, measure impact and feed back to the wider clinical team. Sustainable change also needs commitment from all stakeholders across primary, secondary and social care, including high-level clinical and management teams within the hospital — without that senior support the change won't be sustained. If staff aren't following the pathway, the issues to address are that locally agreed pathways and protocols (based on the ER Pathway documentation) must be developed for local ownership and then actively advertised and promoted, since staff may otherwise be unaware of changes or not value them. Every member of the multidisciplinary team needs to understand the pathway and that their role is vital. Baseline and continuing data collection of clinical and service evaluation outcomes (a national ER audit tool allows benchmarking against other sites) with dissemination of results can help improve compliance and empower frontline staff, and further support is available from NHS Improving Quality.
source_text:

Adopting ER challenges traditional practice – it can be

of a pathway such as carbohydrate loading, and further
training may be required in laparoscopic surgical techniques.

Successful implementation requires a commitment from all
stakeholders in primary, secondary and social care, including
high-level clinical and management teams within hospitals.

Without this support, the change will not be sustainable.

question: When I'm pulling a Foley on my post-op patient, what's the right breathing cue and what do I do if it won't budge?
reference: Ask the patient to take a deep breath and exhale, and withdraw the catheter on expiration. If you meet resistance, stop pulling. Before removal, take off any securement device on the upper thigh, attach a 10-mL syringe to the balloon port and remove all the fluid, holding the plunger as you detach the syringe. After removal, inspect the catheter to confirm it came out intact and discard it in the wastebasket or facility-approved receptacle, then cleanse the perineal area (or let the patient do it), discard catheter materials and waste, remove gloves, and perform hand hygiene. Document the procedure and assessment findings and report any concerns per agency policy.

Attach the 10-mL syringe into the balloon port and remove all the fluid

question: If a woman gets IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis during labour, does her baby need anything, and what's the time window that matters?
reference: Yes. Any baby whose mother received parenteral antibiotics for confirmed or suspected invasive bacterial infection at any point during labour, or in the 24 hours before or after birth, needs a careful assessment for risk factors and clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection, which then guides investigations and management including whether the baby needs antibiotics. Babies with any risk factors or clinical indicators should be managed per NICE NG195 (Neonatal infection: antibiotics for prevention and treatment), which also covers specific investigations and advice to parents. Note also that intrapartum GBS prophylaxis should be offered to women with maternal pyrexia or signs of sepsis in labour. Separately, if the mother has invasive group A strep (iGAS), the baby should routinely receive antimicrobial prophylaxis — and if either mother or baby has iGAS postpartum, both should be treated with antibiotics, as GAS and PVL-producing S. aureus can be transmitted during birth and breastfeeding and cause severe neonatal infection.

question: We've got a septic mum at 30 weeks who may need delivering tonight — who makes the call on timing and mode of birth, and what do I need to have ready for the baby and for monitoring in labour?
reference: The decision on timing and mode of birth must be made by a senior obstetrician, after discussion with the woman and/or her family if her condition permits — birth can be expedited if it would benefit the woman, the baby, or both, and decisions must be individualised. If preterm birth is anticipated, magnesium sulfate should be considered if indicated, and antenatal corticosteroids should be considered for fetal lung maturity in women with sepsis. During the intrapartum period, continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended, and caution is required if fetal blood sampling is being considered. A senior anaesthetist should also make an individual risk assessment regarding the type of anaesthesia and the need for invasive monitoring.

question: Can I apply these SSI prevention recommendations to our pediatric gynae cases, or are they adult-only?
reference: Not all of them. Some of the recommendations are either not applicable to pediatric patients or their effectiveness in children is unproven because the supporting evidence is lacking. So for pediatric cases you can't assume the recommendations carry over — each one has to be checked for whether it was developed with pediatric applicability in mind.

question: My patient going home after her hysterectomy is on VTE prophylaxis — what exactly do I need to cover with her and her husband before she leaves?
reference: As part of the discharge plan, give her and her family members or carers verbal AND written information on three things: (1) the signs and symptoms of DVT and pulmonary embolism, (2) how she can reduce her VTE risk — for example keeping well hydrated and, if possible, exercising and becoming more mobile, and (3) the importance of seeking help if DVT, PE or other adverse events are suspected. Note this is separate from the information given before prophylaxis was started on admission, which covers her individual VTE risks and consequences, the importance of prophylaxis and its side effects (e.g. pharmacological prophylaxis can increase bleeding risk), and the correct use of the prophylaxis such as anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression.

Giving information and planning for discharge

On admission ensure that people understand the reason for having a risk
assessment for VTE and bleeding. [2018]

For people admitted to hospital who are at increased risk of VTE, give them and
their family members or carers (as appropriate) verbal and written information on
the following before offering VTE prophylaxis:
• the person's risks and possible consequences of VTE
• the importance of VTE prophylaxis and its possible side effects – for example,
pharmacological prophylaxis can increase bleeding risk
• the correct use of VTE prophylaxis – for example, anti-embolism stockings,
intermittent pneumatic compression
• how people can reduce their risk of VTE (such as keeping well hydrated and,
if possible, exercising and becoming more mobile). [2018]

Be aware that heparins are of animal origin and this may be of concern to some
people (See Religion or belief: a practical guide for the NHS). Discuss the
alternatives with people who have concerns about using animal products, after
discussing their suitability, advantages and disadvantages with the person.

question: For a woman being induced with misoprostol, what dose and dosing interval do we use for the oral versus the vaginal route — and is there anyone we shouldn't give it to?
reference: Oral misoprostol is given as 25 µg every 2 hours; low-dose vaginal misoprostol is given as 25 µg every 6 hours. Both are strongly recommended for induction of labour (moderate quality evidence). Misoprostol should not be used for induction of labour in women with a previous caesarean section (strong recommendation, low quality evidence). In the third trimester, for women with a dead or anomalous fetus, oral or vaginal misoprostol is recommended for induction.

question: For my pre-op patient who's frail and end-of-life with a high chance of deteriorating, do I need to get advance care planning started now while she's on the ward, or is that something community services sort out after discharge?
reference: Advance care planning should be offered to anyone approaching the end of life who is at risk of a medical emergency — this applies to people in hospital as well as in the community, so it should be offered now rather than deferred to community services. It must be done with close collaboration between the patient, their family and carers, and all professionals involved in their care.

there is close collaboration between the person, their families and carers, and the
professionals involved in their care.
See also the NICE guideline on end of life care for adults: service delivery.

question: For our gyn-onc patients, who should actually be in on the pre-op counseling session, and does having the patient's family member there make any difference?
reference: Pre-op counseling should be delivered in both written and oral form, and the patient along with a relative or care provider should meet with all members of the team — surgeon, anesthetist, dietician, and nurse. Patients with gynecologic cancer prefer to be well informed, and nurse support at the time of diagnosis has been shown to reduce stress levels for up to 6 months. Dedicated pre-operative counseling is recommended routinely for all patients (evidence level: moderate; recommendation grade: strong), as studies show benefit with no evidence of harm.
